en: The indicators of the subject matter, the means of valid cognition, and the authorities on dharma.
The determination of the essential nature of dharmas,
the decision regarding the relative strength of the means of knowledge such as Śruti, and the determination of the place [of performance].
Forbidden places,
the customs of countries, and the customs of the ages.
The characteristics of the Kali Yuga, the definition of the sacraments, and the rite of conception.
The *puṃsavana* rite,
the *sīmantonnayana* rite, and the duties of a pregnant woman.
The birth-rite, the naming ceremony, and the first outing.
Piercing the ears, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony.
The sacraments for women,
the duties prior to initiation,
and the commencement of learning.
The primary time for his initiation is [as follows];
the secondary times for initiation are [as follows];
the skins are [as follows].
Garments, staffs, and girdles.
The sacred thread,
the fire-ritual,
and the grounds for being honored.
The wandering for alms,
the duties of one who has been initiated, and the praise of the Vedas.
Praise of Learning;
the Rule for Vedic Study; the Commencement Ceremony.
The conclusion of the term,
the days when study is suspended, and the limit of the period of studentship.
The two types of religious studentship (*brahmacārin*); the combination and the option regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*); and the return home (*samāvartana*).
Marriage, the nature of *sāpiṇḍya*, and the definition of having common *pravara*s.
The cessation of sapinda-relationship and common lineage; the justification for the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter;
and the characteristics of a maiden.
Justification for marrying a woman of a different caste;
characteristics of a suitable bridegroom; and the proper times for the giving away of a maiden.
The fruit of giving a daughter in marriage,
the prohibition against remarriage, and the determination of who may give a daughter in marriage.
Having bowed to Vāgīśvarī and Gaṇeśa for the sake of favoring the learned, [this work on] the dissolution of marriages and the varieties of marriage [is composed].
The Smṛticandrikā is composed for the benefit of the entire world.
For nothing at all is written here by me according to my own intention;
rather, everything is based on the scriptures, and therefore it should be accepted without fear.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists precisely of the *Dharmaśāstras* composed by Manu and others; since these alone are rooted in the Veda, they are the authorities regarding Dharma. Therefore, for the sake of facilitating their comprehension, the authors of those treatises are first presented. Among them, Viṣṇu states: "Of those [authorities], [the foremost are] Manu, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Ātreya, Uśanas, and Yama."
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara.
Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Guru, Pracetas,
Nārada, the Yogi, Bodhāyana, and Pitāmaha.
Sumantu, Kaśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīna, and Vyāghra; Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgya, and likewise Kārṣṇājini.
"Jābāli, Jamadagni, and Logākṣi, who was born from Brahmā—these six sages are recorded as the founders of Dharma. Now, one might ask: is this an exhaustive enumeration?

Not so; for if that were the case, Vatsa, Marīci, Devala, Pāraskara, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Likhita, Chāgaleya, and others would not be authors of *dharmaśāstra*. Nor should it be said that this should be so, because they too, as authors of *smṛti* scriptures rooted in the Veda, are no different from Manu and the others. For this very reason, Śaṅkha included the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) when he listed: "Manu, Yama, Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Gautama, Saṃvarta, Ātreya, Hārīta, Kātyāyana, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śātātapa, Pracetas, Yājñavalkya, and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that the enumeration is merely for the sake of illustration. On this point, Aṅgiras says:
Jābāli, Nāciketa, Skanda, Logākṣi, Kāśyapa, Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra, Śaṃtanu, and likewise Janaka.
"Vyāghra, Kātyāyana, Jātūkarṇa, Kapiñjala,
Bodhāyana, Kaṇāda, and likewise Viśvāmitra—
these, the wise declare, are the Upasmṛtis. [3] Thus.
Now, the Purāṇas: the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata;
and another, the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh.
The Āgneya is the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is the ninth;
the tenth is the Brahmavaivarta, and the Laiṅga is the eleventh.
The twelfth is indeed the Vārāha, the thirteenth is the Skānda,
the fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma.
The Matsya, the Gāruḍa, and likewise another, the Brāhmāṇḍa.

The Veda is a means of valid cognition because it is independent of any speaker; likewise, tradition (smṛti) and custom (ācāra) are also means of valid cognition because they are rooted in that [Veda]. Their being rooted in it consists in their expressing the meanings set forth therein. And so says Bhṛgu:
"Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all of that is stated in the Veda, for it consists of the knowledge of Brahman."

Śaṅkha also says: "In that regard, the Smṛtis have the Veda as their foundation. This too applies only to those [Smṛtis] whose purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), and not to those whose purpose is seen (dṛṣṭārtha). And so says the Purāṇa:
"All these [Smṛtis] have the Veda as their foundation, with the exception of those whose purpose is seen.
Now, if the Smṛti-śāstra has its foundation in the Veda by virtue of being devoted to matters taught in the Veda, then that alone would suffice; what is the use of a separate Dharma-śāstra?
Anticipating this objection, Marīci says:
"Vedic words are difficult to understand, and those that are scattered are considered supplementary (khila).
It is by those who know them that these very words, whose meanings are made clear, are established within the Smṛti-tantras."

Thus, the authority and the purposefulness of the Purāṇas are established. For this very reason, after presenting the four Vedas, the Śruti says: "Itihāsa and Purāṇa are the fifth. Nor should one suspect the lack of authority of the Śruti and other scriptures on the basis of arguments such as their being of human origin, because such reasoning is unstable and because its defects have been pointed out. And so Manu says: "That twice-born man who, relying on the science of logic (hetuśāstra), would despise both of these [the Veda and the Smṛti], he should be cast out by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda."
Both Śruti and Smṛti [are authoritative]. Yama also says:
"Those Dharmaśāstras which were indeed composed by these [sages] in ancient times—these are the authorities; they must not be subverted by mere reasoning."
"He who would destroy these by means of [mere] arguments sinks into blind darkness.
The mention of the *dharmaśāstra* is intended to indicate the *purāṇas* and other such texts as well. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says:
"The *purāṇa*, the law of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), and medical science..."
"The four established by direct command are not to be sublated by logical arguments.

Thus, the authority of the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* is also uncontradicted; for they too provide the practical application of the very same collection of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) composed by Manu and others, by means of the application of mantras as understood from their own Vedic branches (*śākhā*). And so Devala says:
"Manu and the others are proclaimed as the authors of the Dharmaśāstra."
"The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras, who are the practitioners of that [dharma], have thus declared.
Thus ends the section on the establishment of means of proof regarding the authorities for dharma in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the authorities on Dharma, Yājñavalkya states therein:
"The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas)..."
"The Vedas are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of Dharma.

Here, "Purāṇa" refers to the *Brāhma* and others; "Nyāya" is logic (*tarka*); "Mīmāṃsā" is the investigation of Vedic statements; and "Dharmaśāstra" refers to the *Smṛtis* of Manu and others. Together with the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*) such as grammar and so forth, these constitute the four Vedas. These fourteen are the causes and authorities for knowledge regarding Dharma, and thus for Dharma itself by way of knowledge. Manu also says: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the *Smṛti* and the conduct of those who know it."
"And also the conduct of the virtuous, as well as self-satisfaction.

This is the meaning: the Veda is the root of Dharma, the authority for Dharma. Likewise, the Smṛti and the Śīla of those who know the Veda are also authorities; "Śīla" means the avoidance of passion, hatred, and so forth. "Ācāra" refers to practices such as the tying of the marriage-thread (kaṅkaṇabandhana) and the like. "Self-satisfaction" means that among optional matters, whatever brings pleasure to one's own soul when performed, that too is an authority. Vyāsa also says: "They say that the root of Dharma is the Veda, an uncreated mass of texts."
And for those who know that [Dharma], it consists of tradition, conduct, and virtuous behavior pleasing to the mind.
The virtuous are the refined (*śiṣṭa*). And so Manu says: "The conduct of the refined, the tradition (*smṛti*), and the Vedas—these are the threefold definition of Dharma.
The meaning is that "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He [Manu] himself also describes the nature of the refined:

"Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been acquired through righteous means (*dharma*), they are to be known as cultured Brahmins (*śiṣṭa-brāhmaṇas*), who are the authorities for the scriptures and direct perception. In this context, the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*) of the Veda are the supplements. And so says Bṛhaspati:
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me."
Those for whom the Veda (*śruti*) is the direct cause for the comprehension of *dharma* are so described.

Now, if the conduct of those who know the Vedas is authoritative, then would not even Indra’s, Candra’s, and others’ sexual advances toward Ahalyā, Tārā, and so forth be authoritative? But that is not the case. Therefore, how can conduct be authoritative? To this Gautama says: “A transgression of *dharma* and violence are observed [among them]; yet, due to their extraordinary power (*tejoviśeṣa*), no sin accrues. Violence includes such acts as Paraśurāma’s decapitation of his mother.

It is said: True, there was indeed the approaching of Ahalyā by Indra and others; nevertheless, due to the particular excellence of splendor produced by their asceticism (*tapas*), no transgression occurs for those yogins. For people such as ourselves, however, because that [splendor] is absent, a transgression certainly occurs when one commits such an act. Thus Āpastamba says:
"By virtue of their particular excellence of splendor, no transgression exists for them.
Observing this, one who is inferior (weak) perishes if he practices [such acts]."

"In matters" means in those cases where the Dharma is the authority. And these "learned ones" (*śiṣṭas*) are at least ten in number. Thus says Gautama: "In a matter not explicitly prescribed by tradition, what is commended by learned men who are at least ten in number, who possess the capacity for reasoning (*ūhavat*), and who are free from greed, should be performed. The meaning is that whatever they have declared to be commendable, that is the duty to be performed. Bodhāyana also says: "In their absence, a council of at least ten is pure. "In their absence" means in the absence of direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and so forth. Yājñavalkya also says:
"A council consists of four who know the Vedas and the Dharma, or even those possessing the threefold knowledge (*traividya*)."
She says: "That alone would be the Dharma which [is declared] by the one who is most proficient in the knowledge of the Self.

Here, *dharma* refers to the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). Those who possess the three branches of knowledge are the *traividya*; their assembly is the *traividyam*. The intended meaning is that an assembly consists of either those who know the three Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, or those who know the Dharma. And so Manu says: "One who knows the *Ṛgveda*, one who knows the *Yajurveda*, and likewise one who knows the *Sāmaveda*..."
"A council consisting of at least three members is to be known as authoritative for the resolution of doubts regarding the Dharma.

Thus, even if he is alone—one who knows the supreme inner self (*adhyātma*), the best among those who know the inner self, and a knower of the Dharma—whatever matter he declares according to the Dharma, that too shall be the Dharma. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Whatever those people who know the Dharma and are elders learned in the three Vedas declare to be the Dharma..."
"In both causing a downfall and effecting a downfall, that is indeed the law; there is no doubt in this matter.
Regarding this, Yama states that it is a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) just like the Vedas and other such authorities:
"The Vedas are a source of valid knowledge, the Smṛtis are a source of valid knowledge, and speech endowed with righteousness and purpose is a source of valid knowledge."
One for whom authority does not exist should not treat the word of authority as authoritative.

The intention is that the statement of one for whom the Veda and other such sources do not constitute valid authority is itself not authoritative; therefore, it should be rejected. For this very reason, Pracetas says:
"That which those who have not studied the Mīmāṃsā, those who follow external scriptures, and others who are devoid of the Veda might say—one should not do that; dharma is ordained from the Veda."
Likewise, tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is also an authority in some cases; thus Manu says:
"By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that, he does not come to harm."
Tradition (*sampradāya*) is the practice handed down through one's own family lineage. That too must be observed when there is a conflict with the scriptures (*śāstra*). And so Sumantu says:
"O Bhārata, where the course of the scriptures differs regarding all ritual acts—just as there is a distinction between the oblation offered after sunrise and that offered before sunrise."
In that regard, O mighty-armed one, a wise man should practice the conduct handed down through his family lineage; that is weightier even than what is declared in all the scriptures.

Likewise, Āpastamba states that the consensus of those who know the Dharma is also an authoritative means of knowledge: "The consensus of those who know the Dharma and the Vedas are authoritative. And Manu says that this [Dharmaśāstra] must also be studied because it is useful for the Dharma and because the hearing of rewards is mentioned for its study:
"Just as the study of the Veda, so too this Dharmaśāstra must be studied by a Brāhmaṇa who constantly desires heaven."
Yama also said: "The retention of this treatise on Dharma brings merit, fame, long life, and likewise leads to heaven,
just as does the retention of the Vedas."
By the study of the Dharmaśāstra, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The Śruti and Smṛti are indeed considered the two supreme eyes of the Brahmins;
one who lacks one of them is called one-eyed, and one who lacks both is declared blind."

"Having studied the four Vedas along with the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Pada and Krama recitations, those devoid of memory do not shine, just as a night without a moon. Thus says Manu as well.
"A Brāhmaṇa who studies this treatise with firm vows is never stained by the defects of action born of mind, speech, or body.
Here, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration for the twice-born (dvijāti) in general. For this very reason, Yama says:
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Vaiśya who studies this treatise purifies seven preceding ancestors and seven descendants as well.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu: "This must be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa,
and it must be correctly expounded by the learned, and not by anyone else."
That [statement] is intended to exclude the Śūdra from eligibility. For this very reason, Yama, referring to the eligibility of the Śūdra, says:

"Therefore, his eligibility exists neither in the Vedas nor in the Smṛtis. Thus, it is established that eligibility for Vedic study belongs only to the twice-born. The same should be understood regarding the performance of the duties prescribed therein. For this very reason, Manu says:

"He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the *niṣeka* and ending with the *śmaśāna* has been prescribed by means of mantras—only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. Here, *niṣeka* refers to the conception rite (*garbhādāna*), and *śmaśāna* refers to the funeral rites (*pretakarma*). Vyāsa also says:
"Therefore, for the twice-born who desire purity of dharma, the performance of Vedic rites proceeds without [the need for] Smārta [rites].
Furthermore, that which is composed by Śākya and others is not to be practiced, because it lacks a foundation in the Vedas. This has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
One should avoid all those words of the Arhat and the Cārvākas, even if they have been recited by Buddhists and others; for they are all the words of deceivers.
Vyāsa also says: "Whatever else there might be that purports to designate the Dharma, know that to be far removed from it; delusion is considered its basis."
When it is asked, "What, then, should be performed?", he himself says:
"One should diligently practice that which was formerly remembered by the sages who were the best among the knowers of the Veda's meaning; but one should avoid what is forbidden."

"For those who know the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas have, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, prescribed a certain dharma; one should not deviate from that dharma. Thus says Kātyāyana on this point.
Where an action is prescribed but the specific limb of the agent is not mentioned,
it should be understood that the right hand is intended, for it is the hand that brings actions to completion.
Where no fixed direction is prescribed for rites such as recitation and fire-offerings, three directions are declared there: the eastern, the northern, and the Aparājita (northeastern).
Whether sitting, standing, or bowing, where no such rule is specified,
it should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing.
If one should somehow perform an action otherwise than it was begun due to delusion,
one should complete it from the very point at which it became altered.
If one should realize that this has been performed by me incorrectly, one should perform it again at that very moment; there is no repetition of all ritual acts.

"Generally, however, that action in which the constituent parts (*aṅga*) are performed again is [the one to be repeated]; but when a constituent part is not performed, there is neither repetition nor is that [action] performed. Now, is the performance here to be carried out by including all the constituent parts prescribed in the *Smṛtis*, or not? If there is no inclusion [of all parts], then—
Just as the scriptural injunction has been stated by synthesizing all the Vedic branches,
so too has the traditional injunction been stated by synthesizing all the Smṛtis.

In such cases, there would be a contradiction. If, on the other hand, there were a comprehensive synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*), then it would be impossible to perform [the rite], because a synthesis of contradictory elements is untenable.

It is replied: True, if there were a synthesis of everything. However, that which is not prescribed in one's own [branch] is performed from another source only to the extent that it completes what is lacking; thus, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"That which is not prescribed in one's own branch, but is foreign and non-contradictory..."
"That should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other rites.
With this very intention it was said: "Because of the synthesis of all Smṛtis. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Whether much or little, whatever rite is proclaimed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra..."
When its meaning has been established as "those two," then everything would be accomplished.
This [statement] intends that [the rule] is self-sufficient; for he himself says:

"But whatever is not stated in one's own treatise (ātmatantra), one should perform according to another’s treatise (pāratantrika). Thus ends the section on the authorities of dharma in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

The definition of the nature of *dharma* has been stated: *dharma* is that which has the Vedas and other means of valid cognition as its authority. Regarding that *dharma*, Viśvāmitra states its general characteristic:
"That which, when being performed, is praised by those who know the scriptures and worldly affairs..."
"That which they censure is dharma; that which they praise is declared to be adharma. So too says Manu:
"That which is practiced by the learned, by the virtuous, and always by those free from hatred and passion..."
"Understand that dharma which is approved by the heart.
Likewise, he himself has stated specifically:
"Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, and control of the senses..."
"Modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.

(14) Thus: *dhṛti* is fortitude; *kṣamā* is the absence of mental agitation even when an offense has been committed; *dama* is the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); *asteya* is the non-appropriation of what is not given; *śauca* is both external and internal purity; *indriyanigraha* is the turning back of the senses from prohibited objects; *hrī* is the desisting from improper actions; *vidyā* is the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*); *satya* is speech that accords with reality, and it should be understood as being only that which is pleasant. And so says Manu:

"One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth; nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma. Thus [it is said]. *Akrodha* means the absence of anger. This group of ten is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of dharma, meaning its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Vyāsa also says:
"Truth, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, modesty, forgiveness,
uprightness, knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and meditation— this is the eternal dharma.
He himself stated the definitions of truth and the other virtues as follows:
Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings; self-restraint is the subduing of the mind;
austerity is the practice of one's own duty; and purity is the avoidance of mixing with others.
Contentment, renunciation of sense-objects, modesty, desisting from improper action, forbearance, endurance of the pairs of opposites, and straightforwardness, which is equanimity of mind.
"Knowledge is the thorough awakening to the meaning of reality; tranquility is the pacification of the mind;
compassion is the desire for the welfare of living beings; and meditation is a mind free from objective referents. And likewise, he [the Blessed One] has said this even within other teachings:
Charity, sacrifice, honoring the virtuous, the preservation of the Vedas, and straightforwardness—
this is to be known as the supreme dharma, which bears fruit both in this world and after death.
O King, Kapila has declared that for human beings, freedom from attachment to enjoyments as well as the contemplation of the Self is the supreme good.
"Seeing all things with equanimity, freedom from the sense of 'mine,' and non-attachment—
this, the sage Pañcaśikha declared, is the supreme good for human beings. Thus also said Sumantu.
That dharma which proceeds by relying upon a single caste is called the dharma of caste (varṇadharma), just as, for example, the initiation ceremony (upanayana).

But that qualification which proceeds by relying upon the status of a specific stage of life (āśrama) should indeed be considered the duty of that stage, just as the carrying of the alms-bowl and staff [is the duty of the mendicant].
That which proceeds by taking into account both caste-status (varṇatva) and stage-of-life (āśramatva) is the dharma of caste and stage; for example, the girdle made of muñja grass.
That which proceeds by virtue of a quality is called a "quality-dharma," such as the protection of subjects by one who has been consecrated as a sovereign.
"That dharma which proceeds by depending upon a single cause is to be known as *naimittika* (contingent), just like the rule for penance (*prāyaścitta-vidhi*).
Thus ends the determination of the nature of dharma in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
The determination of the relative strength and weakness of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof;
now, regarding the strength and weakness of *śruti* and so forth, Manu says:
"But where there may be a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of those have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise. [16]

Where there is a twofold division of two Vedic texts (śruti) due to mutual contradiction, both dharmas are established by the Veda; for even those earlier than Manu and others have stated that "those two are dharmas. The intention is that because these two are characterized by equal authority, there is an option (vikalpa) between them. By this very principle, it is also stated that when there is a contradiction between two Smṛtis, there is likewise an option. For this reason, Gautama says in the section on Smṛti: "In the case of a contradiction between those of equal strength, there is an option. However, in the case of a contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti, there is simply the sublation of the Smṛti. As Logākṣi has said:

"But when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is weightier; when there is no conflict, that which is prescribed in Smṛti should always be performed just like that which is Vedic. Thus, in the case of custom (ācāra) as well, there would certainly be its sublation when it conflicts with Smṛti, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Dharma is that which is enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti; in their absence, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is authoritative. The same should be understood regarding the pronouncements of an assembly (pariṣad). This has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:

"Just as the abandonment of Smṛti occurs when it contradicts the Veda, so too should one abandon a worldly statement due to its sublation by Smṛti. Furthermore, where there is a contradiction between a statement of Manu and another Smṛti, that which was spoken by Manu alone is superior. Thus said Aṅgiras:

"That unsurpassed Dharmaśāstra which was previously proclaimed by Manu—indeed, no speech that transgresses it is for one's own welfare. (17) Thus, a statement belonging to another, if it transgresses what was spoken by Manu, does not lead to one's own knowledge. Bṛhaspati also says:
Because it is based upon the Veda, the authority of Manu is considered preeminent;
however, any Smṛti that contradicts the meaning of Manu is not commended.

The Śruti also states: "Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed medicine. However, where there is a conflict between two duties (*dharma*), Vyāsa says that only the lighter one is to be set aside: "That duty which obstructs another duty is by no means a duty; but that duty which is non-obstructive is called a duty, and that is established as success."

"Therefore, when there is a conflict between two duties, having ascertained their relative weight, the wise man should make his decision regarding the duty according to that which is more significant. Thus ends the determination of the relative strength of the Śruti and other authorities in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the region.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"That which lies between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī..."
They call that region created by the gods Brahmāvarta.
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pāñcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages, immediately following Brahmāvarta.

[18] Immediately following this, the meaning is "slightly less than that. That region which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
Vinasana is the place where the Sarasvati disappears.
"From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, and between those two very mountains—the wise know this region as Āryāvarta. Thus [it is said].
And here, each preceding region is more excellent than the one following it. Thus Sumantu says:
"Brahmāvarta is the supreme land; next is the land of the sages (Ṛṣideśa);
the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is inferior to that, and beyond that is Āryāvarta."
Furthermore, as stated by Manu: "That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as a land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas."

Thus, this [definition] is to be understood as applying when the four aforementioned regions cannot be obtained, because it is mentioned immediately after them. Furthermore, this is not intended to exclude other regions altogether. As Viṣṇu says:
"That country in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a Mleccha country; beyond that is Āryāvarta."

Therefore, it should be understood that wherever the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) exists, or where the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya-vyavasthāna*) is established, that is a land of Dharma (*dharmadeśa*). Accordingly, the Ādipurāṇa states: "A land of Dharma is one that is rich in black antelopes, barley, *darbha* grass, and likewise the four castes and stages of life; such a place the wise should resort to."

The intended meaning is that a land devoid of these [virtues] is a *mleccha* country. By using the term "*mleccha* country," he indicates the prohibition of performing religious rites (*dharmakriyā*) there. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "One should not place faith in a *mleccha* region, nor should one go to such a region. Also in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"Even if they perform hundreds of sacrifices in the midst of unrighteousness, the twice-born do not see any higher good; for heaven has a great bolt against those who go there."

With this very intention, Yājñavalkya also said: "In whatever region the black antelope roams, learn the laws (dharmān) there. The word "through the performance of dharma" is to be supplied [to complete the sense], because that region is a means for the practice of dharma. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:

"That region where the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) naturally roams at all times should be known as the land of Dharma (*dharmadeśa*), the means for the twice-born to accomplish their religious duties. Here, "by nature" (*svabhāvāt*) means "without being driven. Regarding the *Āryāvarta*, Śaṅkha says: "As far as the black antelope roams, so far shall be the *Āryāvarta*. Following the term "*Āryāvarta*," Vasiṣṭha also states: "As far as the black antelope roams. A specific rule concerning one born in the *Āryāvarta* is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*.
Whether he be a twice-born or even a non-twice-born, one born in Āryāvarta should not cross the Narmadā, the Sindhu, or the Karatoyā.
Having crossed beyond Āryāvarta without performing a pilgrimage to sacred fords, a twice-born man is purified by the Aindava penance, provided he has likewise obtained the permission of his parents.

The Karatoyā River. Manu has stated an exception even regarding those places thus mentioned: "One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by heretics or twice-born men who have strayed from their duty, nor in one infested by outcaste persons. Thus it is said.
Vyāsa also says: "A person devoted to dharma should diligently avoid regions inhabited by those who subsist like Śūdras, by other unrighteous people, or by Mlecchas."
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) states an exception:
"Even in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, one may dwell where the Jāhnavī flows through its midst;
that is an exceedingly meritorious land, resorted to even by men."
By residing in Kurukṣetra and Vārāṇasī,
a person who is non-violent and devoted to truth, having abandoned sin, shall go to heaven.
There can be no dwelling on the Gaṅgā without the destruction of all the Kṣatriyas;
for death at Kāśī is superior, even without the sacred field of Prajāpati.
[21] Residence at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean does not come to men in this world without merits.
Kurukṣetra is the site of the destruction of all kṣatriyas. Vyāsa also says:
"Those regions, those provinces, those mountains, and likewise those hermitages, in the midst of which flows that most excellent river, the holy triple-pathed Gaṅgā."
Also in the Ādipurāṇa:
"Wherever the Gaṅgā is most excellent, that region is a forest of asceticism;
it should be known as a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra) when situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "A righteous person should dwell at Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Kāśī, Naimiṣa, Amarakaṇṭaka, on the Gaṅgā, or on the banks of the Sarayū."
Vyāsa also says: "The Antarvedī, Madhyadeśa, and the sacrificial Brahmāvarta;
likewise the confluence of the Sarayū river, Puṣkara, and Naimiṣa."

"The twice-born should resort to these countries for residence. Here, the mention of "the twice-born" is intended to include the Śūdra as well, because Manu records that the Śūdra may seek refuge in a country only in times of distress. "The twice-born should diligently resort to these countries."
"But a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in whatever place he chooses.
[22] Now, the forbidden regions:
Regarding this, Bodhāyana states: "The Ānartas, the Aṅgas and Magadhas, the Saurāṣṭras, the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha),
the Apāsyas, and the Sindhu-Sauvīras— these are of mixed origin."
Vyāsa also says:

"One should avoid these regions: Aṅga, Vaṅga, Andhra, and whatever other lands are inhabited by barbarian tribes (mleccha), as well as those countries where the black-spotted deer (kṛṣṇasāra) does not roam."
In the Ādipurāṇa as well:
"Those born in Kāñcī, Kosala, Saurāṣṭra, Devarāṣṭra, Dvikaccha, Sauvīra,
and Koṅkaṇa— these eight are severely censured."
Where these five rivers flow forth from the mountain, there are the regions known as Āraṭṭa; a noble person should not dwell among them day after day.
Having gone to the western bank of the Padma river— the confluence of the Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāśī—
one incurs hell by residing there for a time exceeding that prescribed for sacred pilgrimage sites.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas, as well as the Vindhyas and Mālavakas,
and that which lies south of the Narmadā and north of the Sindhu.
The Pauṇḍras, the Surāṣṭras, the Caidyas, the Keralas, and the Māgadhas—
[23] one should not perform marriage, śrāddha, or sacrifice with them.
Whatever sinful regions there may be inhabited by wicked people,
having gone to those meritless lands, one partakes of the full measure of sin.

"Having gone at will to these regions—Saurāṣṭra, Sindhu-Sauvīra, Āvantya, Dakṣiṇāpatha, and Kaliṅga—a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. This should be understood as referring to regions devoid of the previously mentioned black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) and other such animals, since even those regions serve as means for the practice of dharma. However, Bodhāyana prescribes an expiation for traveling to Sindhu-Sauvīra and similar directions.

"Having gone to the Sindhus, Sauvīras, Saurāṣṭras, as well as those dwelling in the borderlands (pratyanta), and to Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, one deserves purification. Here, "borderland" (pratyanta) refers to a frontier region. And thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, [one should not marry] those who are low-born nor those from the borderlands."
Also in the Ādipurāṇa:
"A twice-born man who has gone to these regions— Saurāṣṭra, Sindhu, Sauvīra, Āvantya, and Dakṣiṇāpatha— deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again."

Having gone to Himavat, Kauśika, Vindhya, or the western shore of the Padma river without undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), one deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again.
"Therefore, having gone to the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā at dawn,
we shall perform great penance for the sake of purifying our residence in this border region.
Thus, the favor shown toward regions for the sake of providing a livelihood to the twice-born in times of distress is demonstrated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
[He conquered] Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and the mountain-dwellers situated near them;
as well as Sindhu, Sauvīra, Saurāṣṭra, Kerala, Andhra, and Kāmala.
"A twice-born man should never abandon [these places] for the sake of residence unless there is an emergency;
however, having gone to these [forbidden] regions, he should return upon their cessation.
Thus ends the determination of forbidden regions in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the local customs.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana states: "There are five types of divergent practices in the South: eating with those who have not been initiated (*anupanīta*), eating with one's wife, eating food that has been kept overnight, marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle or a paternal aunt, and [the sale of wool]. Likewise, in the North: the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade with people from both sides of the sea, the profession of arms, and sea-voyages. One becomes blameworthy by performing [these acts] in the other region; in each case, the authority of the local custom (*deśaprāmāṇya*) alone shall prevail. This is the meaning: the Southerner (*dākṣiṇātya*) does not become blameworthy for eating with the uninitiated and so forth when doing so in the Northern region (*udīcya*), but he is blameworthy in his own country. Likewise, the Northerner does not become blameworthy for selling wool and so forth when doing so in the Southern region, but he is blameworthy in his own country. Why? Because of the authority of the local custom; that is to say, because authority is dependent upon the specific locality. Bṛhaspati also says:
[25] The twice-born of the South marry the daughters of their maternal uncles;
in the Middle Country, there are laborers and Śibis who eat beef.
In the east, men were eaters of fish and women were unfaithful;
in the north, women were drinkers of liquor and were to be touched by men even during their menstrual periods.
"Those born together [as twins] take as their wife the brother's widow who has no husband.
Regarding these, he himself states that their authority depends on regional custom:
"And whatever laws have been established for regions, castes, and families..."
"In that same manner they must be protected; otherwise, the subjects become agitated.
Thus says Devala as well:
"In whatever regions there are gods, and in whatever regions there are twice-born [Brahmins]..."
In whatever regions there is water, and whatever soil exists in each place;
In whatever places there is a particular purity and whatever kind of righteous conduct exists, one should not despise those things there; for such is the dharma in that very place.
"In whatever country, city, village, or even in a city of those learned in the three Vedas,
one should not deviate from that dharma which is prescribed there.
Thus, when the authority of local customs (*deśadharma*) would follow without distinction, Manu says:

"And that which has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, one should establish as the law for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not contradictory [to scripture]. (26) The meaning is this: whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and is not in conflict with authoritative sources such as the Śruti, one should establish that as the *dharma* for specific regions, families, and castes. And thus says Gautama: "The customs of regions, castes, and families, when not contradicted by the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*), are authoritative. In this regard, however, contradictions are occasionally observed. For example:
However, contradictions are now observed among the Southerners:
the marriage of one’s own mother’s son, which is censured because of the mother’s kinship.
The taking of a brother's wife by one who is not her husband, as well as the giving away of a daughter within the family, is seen in other countries and is considered extremely reprehensible.
Likewise, brother-marriage is also observed among the Persians;
similarly, regarding those twice-born who have eaten at a śrāddha on the eleventh day and so forth.
Regarding these, some teachers do not desire the giving [of grain] again at the *śrāddha* ceremony;
others say that after giving grain in the spring, one should give it again in the autumn, doubled in amount.
When the doubled wealth has entered, they seize the field of kinship;
when it has not entered, it is enjoyed by others, and that [loss] is publicly lamented.
In this way, one should turn back many contradictory practices;
however, the authority of local customs, caste laws, and so forth, remains valid provided they do not conflict [with the sacred scriptures].
"Therefore, having examined all the treatises, the king should act according to the scripture.
Likewise, even that which is contrary to worldly custom must be abandoned. Regarding this, Varāhamihira said:
"First, having reflected upon the local customs, whatever the established practice is in each region, that alone should be followed."
The wise who follow the path of the world avoid that which is hated by the world, just as those who know the stars avoid an ill-omened day.
Thus ends the section on local customs (*deśadharma*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the duties pertaining to the ages (*yugadharma*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
The duties of men are different in the Kṛta age, others in the Tretā and Dvāpara,
and still others in the Kali age, in accordance with the decline of the ages.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā, knowledge alone;
in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone; and in the Kali age, charity alone.
Austerity (*tapas*)—meaning *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth—is the supreme, that is, the primary [duty]. Bṛhaspati also says:
"In the Kṛta age, austerity is the duty; in the Tretā age, knowledge is remembered [as the duty];
in the Dvāpara, sacrifice is proclaimed [the duty]; in the Tiṣya [age], charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are the duties]."
Tiṣya is the Kali age; Parāśara [is the authority] as well. For it is said: "In the Kṛta age, the Dharma is that of Manu; in the Tretā, that of Gautama;
in the Dvāpara, Śaṅkha and Likhita; in the Kali, the Smṛti of Parāśara is prescribed."
One should abandon the country in the Kṛta age, leave the village in the Tretā age,
[abandon] a single family in the Dvāpara age, but [abandon] the perpetrator alone in the Kali age.
[28] In the Kṛta age one falls by conversing with such a person; in the Tretā, by physical contact;
in the Dvāpara, by taking his wealth; and in the Kali age, one falls through performing religious acts together with him.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"That which is a duty performed in a year during the Kṛta age is accomplished in three seasons during the Tretā;
in the Dvāpara it is done in three fortnights, and in the Kali age it is accomplished in a single day."
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"That which [is accomplished] in ten years in the Kṛta age, in one year in the Tretā,
and in one month in the Dvāpara, that is accomplished in a single day and night in the Kali age."
Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In the Tretā age, dharma was practiced annually; in the Dvāpara, it is recorded as being monthly.
A wise man should practice it according to his capacity, and in the Kali age, he may attain its fruit in a single day."
In the Viṣṇudharmottara as well:
"Puṣkara should be resorted to in the Kṛta age, likewise Naimiṣa in the Tretā;
Kurukṣetra in the Dvāpara, but in the Kali age one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā."
Thus ends the section on the duties of the ages (*yugadharma*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the duties of the Kali age (*kalidharmāḥ*).
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age by chanting the praises of Keśava.
"In this Kali age, a person attains an extraordinary excellence of dharma with very little effort; therefore, O knowers of dharma, I am pleased with the Kali age.
Thus it is said in the Ādipurāṇa as well.
But that dharma which belongs to the Kṛta age is not to be practiced in the Kali age,
because in the Kali age both women and men are addicted to sin.
"In the Kali age, there is no true learning, no pure meaning, and no purity of mind;
therefore, truth alone is beneficial for men. Thus it is said. "Kārta" means pertaining to the Kṛta Yuga. Likewise, even the prohibited dharmas are mentioned in that very same place.
Long-term observance of celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot,
marriage within the maternal sapinda lineage of one's clan, and likewise the killing of a cow.

In the Kali age, the human horse-sacrifice, liquor, and even the ritual sacrifice must be avoided by the twice-born; likewise, the procreation of offspring through the husband's brother, and the giving away of a daughter who has already been given in marriage, are forbidden.
In the Kali age, the slaughter of a cow in sacrifice must not be performed, nor should the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) be used.

In the Brāhma [Purāṇa]: "In the Kali age, one should not perform these five: the remarriage of a woman already wedded, the granting of the eldest son's share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother’s wife, and [carrying] a water-pot. [30] Thus it is said.
Likewise, others who know the Dharma have stated that the authority of legal tradition (samaya) is as follows:

the appointment of a brother-in-law for the procreation of offspring upon a widow; and the marriage ceremony performed by another bridegroom for a girl or a woman whose virginity has not been violated.
The marriage of twice-born men with girls of a different caste,
and the killing of murderous aggressors— even those who are foremost among the twice-born— by means of righteous warfare.
The acceptance of a twice-born man who has traveled by boat upon the ocean, even after he has been purified;
the initiation for a sacrificial session (sattra) for all [castes]; and the carrying of a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
The Great Journey (mahāprasthāna), the injury to cows during the Gosava sacrifice,
and likewise the taking of the Soma-cup of wine in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice are all included [as exceptions].
The taking up of the *agnihotra* offering-ladle together with the *sahālīḍha* [vessel] is prescribed as the entry into the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprasthāśrama*).
Wealth, the study of the Vedas, the contraction of sin,
as well as the rules for expiation, and even the penance ending in death for Brahmins.
Association with thieves and others [is a cause for] the expiation of great sins;
likewise is the act of stealing cattle from gods, guests, and ancestors.
The adoption of sons other than the *datta* and *aurasa* types,
as well as association with those of equal caste who have been tainted by vices— even if they have since been purified— is [forbidden].
If an improper union has occurred, there must be the abandonment of the teacher’s wife;
likewise, after the collection of the bones, physical contact [with her] is forbidden.
The office of officiating priest for Brahmins, as well as the selling of Soma,
eating only every sixth mealtime through fasting, and taking food from one of low-caste occupation;

Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, a physician, and a plowman may be eaten by a householder; however, he must keep himself at a great distance from visiting their sacred bathing places.
The conduct toward the wife of a guru is said to be like that toward the guru himself;
likewise, for the foremost of the twice-born, there are modes of livelihood in times of distress, such as not providing for the morrow.

The acceptance of wives from among the foremost of the twice-born for the sake of progeny, the wandering of Brahmins, and the practice of blowing upon the sacrificial fire with the mouth— all these are for the sake of the people.
For the forcible seizure of a wicked woman is ordained by rule;
however, for an ascetic, the practice of begging alms from among all castes is prescribed by rule.
In the case of new water, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed for ten days by the Guru;
likewise, for a Śūdra, the act of cooking and so forth may be performed for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
Likewise, there is death by leaping from a cliff or into fire, as well as death by drowning;
and the practice of sipping water for purification (ācamana) by the learned from milk that remains after satisfying the cows.
In disputes between father and son, the determination of punishment for witnesses—
wherein the state of being a householder at evening is [the criterion] according to the wise who are devoted to truth— is thus established.
These actions were established by wise and high-souled beings at the beginning of the Kali age for the sake of protecting the world, according to a fixed system.
"And the consensus of the virtuous shall also be authoritative, like the Veda.
Thus it was also stated by Āpastamba: "The consensus of those who know dharma and the Vedas are authoritative."
Thus ends the General Exposition on Saṃskāras in the Smṛticandrikā.

Now, the section on sacraments (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*) is stated briefly. Regarding this, Gautama says: "The *garbhādhāna* (conception), *puṃsavana* (male-impregnation), *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), *jātakarman* (birth-rite), *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving), *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food), *caula* (tonsure), *upanayana* (initiation), the four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*), the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), union with the partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*), the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*)—namely those for the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman—and these seven forms of domestic sacrifice (*pakayajñasaṃsthā*): the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *caitrī*, and the *āśvayujī*; the seven forms of oblation sacrifice (*haviryajñasaṃsthā*): the *agnyādheya*, *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *āgrayaṇa*, *cāturmāsya*, *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and *sautrāmaṇī*; and the seven forms of Soma sacrifice (*somasaṃsthā*): the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*. These constitute the forty sacraments. Furthermore, there are eight personal qualities (*ātmaguṇa*): compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of fatigue, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of greed. The Vedic vows refer to the *prājāpatya* and others. The "bath" is the *samāvartana* (graduation). "Union with the partner in dharma" is marriage. The "five sacrifices" are the *devayajña* and the rest. The *aṣṭakā* is a specific type of *śrāddha*. The *pārvaṇa* is that performed on the lunar festival days (*parvan*), characterized by the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) ritual. The *śrāddha* here refers to the monthly *śrāddha*. The *śrāvaṇī* is the offering to the serpents (*sarpabali*). The *āgrahāyaṇī* is the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. The *caitrī* is the rite known as *holākā*. The *āśvayujī* is the rite known as the *indradhvajahoma*. The others are well-known.
Some say that there are seven *pākayajñas*: the *aupāsanahoma*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *aṣṭakā*, the *māsiśrāddha*, the *sarpabali*, and the *īśānabali*.
Bṛhaspati has stated the characteristics of personal virtues:
"But when [one behaves] always toward one's circle of kinsmen, toward a friend, or toward an enemy..."
But one who has fallen [into misfortune] must be protected; this is proclaimed as compassion.
Whether suffering is produced by others externally or internally,
when one does not become angry nor retaliates, that is proclaimed as patience (kṣamā).
She does not destroy the virtues of the virtuous, she praises even those of meager merit, and she takes no delight in the faults of others; this is proclaimed as freedom from envy (*anasūyā*).
Avoiding the company of the wicked and remaining steadfast in one's own duty— this is proclaimed as the avoidance of the impossible and as purity.
Whatever action causes the body to suffer, even if it is very auspicious, that should not be done at all; that is called "effortlessness."
The constant practice of what is commendable and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—
this indeed is declared to be auspiciousness by the seers who perceive the truth.
For one should give even a little with a joyful inner heart;
whatever is given day after day, however small, is indeed remembered as being free from stinginess.
"Twice-born men should practice contentment with whatever has come to them;
they should not long for the wealth of others—this is proclaimed as freedom from desire.
Thus Manu says that he who possesses these forty purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and the eight qualities of the self attains union (*sāyujya*) with Brahman.
"Refined by former purificatory rites and further refined by subsequent ones,
the Brāhmaṇa who is eternally endowed with the eight qualities attains the state of Brahman, the world of Brahmā, from which he does not fall again. Thus it is said.

The preceding *saṃskāras* are those beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception), while the subsequent ones are the *pākayajña*s and so forth. Regarding this, Hārīta says: "Saṃskāra is indeed of two kinds: Brāhma and Daiva. That which begins with *garbhādhāna* is the Brāhma, being based on the Smṛtis (*smārta*). The Daiva consists of the *pākayajña*, *haviryajña*, and *soma* sacrifices. One purified by the Brāhma *saṃskāras* attains equality, residence in the same world (*salokatā*), and union (*sāyujya*) with the *ṛṣis*. Purified by the subsequent Daiva [saṃskāras], one attains equality, residence in the same world, and union with the gods. This is intended with reference to *saṃskāras* performed even when devoid of [excellent] qualities. For this very reason, Gautama states: "He who possesses these forty *saṃskāras* but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union or residence in the same world with Brahman. Therefore, it should be understood that this result characterized by the attainment of union with Brahman belongs only to him who possesses both these forty *saṃskāras* and the eight qualities of the self. Furthermore, among these, only the *saṃskāras* from *garbhādhāna* up to *upanayana* (initiation) are mandatory for all; the *snāna* (graduation) and others are not. If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the rule: "One may enter [the stage of] renunciation at will, or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*). Moreover, these *saṃskāras* belong only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). As Yājñavalkya says: [text follows].
"The [four] castes are the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; however, the first three are the twice-born (dvija).
For them, the rites beginning with *niṣeka* and ending with the *śmaśāna* are indeed performed with mantras.

Here, *niṣeka* refers to those for whom the first rite, *garbhādhāna* (conception), is performed; *śmaśāna* refers to the funeral rites for the deceased. By stating that "the rites of the twice-born are performed with mantras," he implies that the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of a Śūdra are performed without mantras. For this very reason, Yama says in the section concerning sacraments:

"A Śūdra also of such a kind should be consecrated with the sacraments, though without mantras. This refers to the intention that the sacraments should extend up to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*). For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is initiation (*upāyana*), Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and fruit-bearing rites. However, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, a prohibition of all sacraments other than marriage for the Śūdra is shown: "A Śūdra may always receive the sacrament of marriage alone. [36]

Therefore, because they are both prescribed and prohibited by injunctions, they should be understood as optional alternatives. Manu also states that for the twice-born alone, the sacramental rite is accompanied by mantras:
"By means of meritorious Vedic rites, beginning with the *niṣeka*, the purifying refinement of the body of the twice-born must be performed, which is beneficial both in this world and after death."
Because they are accomplished through Vedic mantras, Vedic rites are purifying for the Vedic practitioners by means of neutralizing their sins. As that very [author] has said:
"By means of the oblations performed in the womb, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, he wipes away the taints of the seed and the womb from the twice-born."

The seed is the semen and blood; that which is produced from their defects is the "seed-born" impurity (*baijika*). That which is produced by dwelling in the womb is the "womb-born" impurity (*gārbhika*). The mention of *homa* (fire-oblation) is intended to indicate even those rites such as *garbhādhāna* (conception), which do not consist of oblations. For this very reason, after describing the rituals beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure), Yājñavalkya states:
"In this way, the sin arising from the seed and the womb is pacified.
Thus ends the section on the definitions of sacraments (*saṃskāra-paribhāṣā*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), Yājñavalkya states:
"The fertile period (*ṛtu*) for women consists of sixteen nights; during that time, one should approach them on the even nights."

The period of sixteen nights beginning from the appearance of the menses is the *ṛtu*—the time for conception for women. During that period, if he desires a son, he should approach her on even nights; if he desires a daughter, on uneven nights. And so says Manu:
"Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights. Therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on even nights. [37]

And likewise Āpastamba says: "From the fourth day until the sixteenth, they teach that approaching one's wife during her fertile period on successive even nights leads to the excellence of progeny. Vyāsa also says:
"On the fourth night, a son would be born who is devoid of long life and wealth;
on the fifth, a woman [gives birth to] a mother of sons; on the sixth, a son of middling quality."
On the seventh day, she bears no offspring; on the eighth, a lordly son;
on the ninth, a fortunate woman; and on the tenth, an excellent man.
On the eleventh day, a woman is born who is unrighteous; on the twelfth, a supreme man;
and on the thirteenth, a daughter there who causes the intermixture of castes.
One who possesses the banner of Dharma, is grateful, self-knowing, and firm in his vows,
is born on the fourteenth lunar day as a lord of the world accompanied by multitudes of attendants.
Likewise, a highly fortunate queen, devoted to her husband, who has come into the presence of the King,
gives birth on the fifteenth day to many sons.

"Endowed with the characteristics of knowledge, truthful in speech, and having conquered his senses, a man who is a refuge for all beings is born on the sixteenth day. Thus it is said. Even when approaching women during the even nights, he should approach only those not otherwise prohibited; regarding those prohibited ones, Manu says:
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
"Of these, the first four [nights], as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are recommended. Thus it is said.
Among those sixteen nights, one should avoid the four nights beginning from the onset of menstruation. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states:

"One should not summon her on the first, nor the second, nor the third, nor the fourth night. However, some say that one should avoid the four nights following the ritual bath (*snāna*). This is because, by the very prohibition of touching her prior [to the bath], going to her is also prohibited, and because a penance is prescribed for having intercourse with her. Therefore, the statement "sixteen nights of women are the fertile period (*ṛtu*)" should be understood as referring to the period after the bath. But that is not correct; for the sixteen nights of women are traditionally known as the natural fertile period.
Along with four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
This is because it contradicts the statement of Manu; for indeed, there are no nights considered contemptible after the ritual bath. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"A woman in her menses attains purity by bathing on the fourth day."

On the contrary, the previously mentioned [view] alone is superior, because of the hearing of censures such as: "This very thing is the murder of a Brahmin among women, namely the appearance of menses month after month; he who is born from that is accursed. As for what was stated by Hārīta concerning the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), namely, "on the fourth day, when she has bathed, and on even nights," that should be understood to mean the fourth day *after* the cessation of the menstrual flow. For this very reason, Gobhila says: "When she is in her season and the blood has ceased, that is the time for union," and by stating, "The nights of the season for women are sixteen," he declares a prohibition against conception during the daytime. For this same reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the season by day; those born by day are eunuchs, of little vigor, and short-lived. Yājñavalkya also mentions a specific rule regarding the act of lying together.

"Proceeding in this manner, one should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla. When the Moon is well-situated, a man, approaching her once, shall procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks. The meaning is that when the Moon is well-situated—that is, when there is strength in the Moon—one should avoid Maghā and Mūla, and by approaching an emaciated or thin woman only once, one shall procreate a son possessed of auspicious marks. This is also stated in the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra).
Having avoided the fires of the ancestors (Pitṛ), Pūṣan, and Nirṛti, a man who is himself serene should approach his well-pleased wife;
one who is robust should approach her when she is emaciated, and one desiring a son should approach her during her fertile period.

"One obtains a son possessing excellent characteristics; this is the truth. The constellation Maghā belongs to the Pitṛs; Revatī belongs to Pūṣan; Mūla belongs to Nirṛti; and Dhiṣṇya is a constellation. At that time, emaciation is achieved through the very observances prescribed for a woman during her menstrual period. When the cessation of the flow occurs, emaciation should then be brought about by means of light food and so forth, for the sake of producing a son. And for the sake of increasing the male seed, the man should consume unctuous foods and the like. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "If the female seed is in excess, a girl will be born; if the male seed is in excess, a boy will be born."
Therefore, for the sake of increasing semen, one should consume aphrodisiac and unctuous foods.
"One should make the woman's [uterine] passage narrow; thus one shall produce a son.
"Vṛṣya" refers to a substance that increases virility. Manu also says:
"A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female is born when the female seed is in excess."
"When equal, it is a male; when both male and female, or when diminished and small, there is the reverse.
When the two seeds are equal, it means a non-male, that is, a neuter (*napuṃsaka*). Or, if it is both male and female, then there is a division of the seeds. Regarding this, Yama says:
"If, at the time of union, the man is deluded by passion..."
"One should emit the semen in two ways; there a twin is born.

When [the semen] is exhausted, essence-less, or scant, the opposite occurs: namely, non-conception. Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of fertile periods (*ṛtu*), Devala states the sequence for approaching [the wife]:
"When the fertile periods coincide, one should approach her according to the order starting with the Brahmin [husband]."
"Or else, for the sake of protection, he may go according to the order of their marriage, even among those who are childless.

Here, *tīrtha* means the fertile period (*ṛtu*). When there is simultaneity [of fertile periods], he should approach them according to the order of their castes or the order of their marriages; that is to say, he should go first to those who are childless. By this, it is stated that one must never, under any circumstances, let the fertile period pass by. For this very reason, Manu says: "He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife."

"Excluding the forbidden days (parvan), he who observes that vow should approach her out of a desire for pleasure. Here, "observing that vow" means observing the vow for the procreation of a son. By this, it is enjoined that even without a desire for pleasure, one should approach her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) for the sake of obtaining a son; otherwise, a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Parāśara:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him..."
"He incurs the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt about this. Thus [says the scripture]. Bodhāyana also says:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him..."
"His ancestors lie within that semen for a month.

[42] Thus, because of the mention of "proximity," it should be understood that there is no fault in the absence of proximity. Furthermore, even when in proximity, as long as one is incapable, there is indeed no fault. And so says the Smṛti:
"He who does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses, while he is in her presence..."
One incurs the sin of killing an embryo, and the offspring one has obtained perishes.

This [rule] pertains to one who has not yet fathered a son, because the following Vedic scripture—“A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the sages by means of studentship (*brahmacarya*), to the gods by means of sacrifice (*yajña*), and to the ancestors by means of progeny; he alone is free from debt who has a son, performs sacrifices, and has lived as a student”—is satisfied by the procreation of even a single son. And it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
“He should approach his wife during her fertile period until a son is born.
But is there not also an injunction for the procreation of further sons, such as: “Beget ten sons upon her”?

True, but this [text] would not be prescriptive; rather, it is for the purpose of praising many offspring. For this very reason, Nārada says: "In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided he sees the face of his born son while the son is living."
"The worlds of those with sons are infinite; for one without a son there are none"—such is the Vedic revelation (śruti).
The intention is that by the mere birth of an eldest son, the father becomes free from his debt. And so says Manu:
"By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son."
"And because he is indeed free from debt to the ancestors, he therefore deserves everything.
For this very reason, that same [author] stated that for others there is also birth through karma:
"That in which one pays off a debt, and by means of which one attains infinity..."
"He alone is the son born of dharma; they know the others to be born of desire.
By this, it is established that this rule regarding approaching one's wife during her fertile period applies only to one who has not yet fathered a son.
Thus ends the section on *garbhādhāna* (conception) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the *puṃsavana* rite, Yājñavalkya states:
"The *garbhādhāna* [should be performed] during the fertile period; the *puṃsavana* before the movement [of the fetus]."

The meaning is that the rite called *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child) should be performed before the movement of the fetus. Baijavāpa states a specific rule: "In the second or third month, prior to the fetus moving. Following the term *puṃsavana*, Pāraskara also says: "In the second or third month, on a day when the moon is conjoined with a male asterism (*punnakṣatra*). The male asterisms are enumerated in the *Ratnakośa*: Hasta, Mūla, Śravaṇa, Punarvasu, Mṛgaśiras, and likewise Tiṣya (Puṣya).
"These auspicious lunar mansions [are prescribed] for rites intended for males.
Here, "dhiṣṇyāni" refers to the *nakṣatras* (lunar mansions). Bṛhaspati, however, prescribes the *puṃsavana* rite at the time of fetal movement:
"One should perform the *garbhādhāna* during the fertile period; the *savana* rite should be performed when the fetus begins to move."

Thus [ends] the *puṃsavana*; now follows the *sīmantonnayana*. Regarding this, Lōgākṣi says: "One should perform the *sīmantonnayana* in the third month of pregnancy. Āpastamba also says: "The *sīmantonnayana* is performed in the first pregnancy during the fourth month. Baijavāpa also says: "Now, the *sīmantonnayana* is performed in the fourth, fifth, or even the sixth month. In the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* it is also said: "In the first pregnancy, the *sīmantonnayana* is performed in the seventh month. Yājñavalkya also [says the same].

"In the sixth or eighth month, the *sīmantonnayana* [should be performed], as well as these birth-rites (*jātakarman*) when they have arrived. The meaning is: "when these [months] have arrived, the child is born. Śaṅkha also says: "The *sīmantonnayana* is performed at the time of fetal movement, or until the delivery. Regarding this, Śaunaka has stated a specific rule: "During the waxing fortnight, on a day when the moon is conjoined with a masculine asterism. Furthermore, because this *sīmantonnayana* is a consecration of the field (the womb), it should be performed only once, not for every conception. Thus says Hārīta: "Twice-born women undergo the consecration by means of the *sīmantonnayana* only once."
"Whichever womb she gives birth to, all of it shall be consecrated. Thus says Devala as well:
"A woman, having been consecrated once, is consecrated for all her pregnancies."
Some perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite at every conception, regarding it as a sacrament for the embryo (*garbhasaṃskāra*). Thus says Viṣṇu:
"The *sīmantonnayana* rite is intended as a sacrament for the woman.
And some apply it to each individual embryo because it is a sacrament for the embryo.
Regarding the birth of a child from a woman for whom the *sīmanta* ceremony has not been performed, Satyavrata says: "If a woman should somehow give birth while the *sīmanta* has not been performed,
she, having taken up her son, deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again according to the rule."
The application of these various positions should be understood according to the specific rules of each respective *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Thus ends the section on the *Sīmantonnayana* in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follow the duties of the pregnant woman.
In that regard, Kāśyapa:
[46] One should not sit upon refuse heaps such as pestles and mortars;
one should not plunge into water, and one should avoid empty dwellings.
One should not step upon an anthill, nor should one be of an agitated mind;
one should not scratch the ground with one's nails, nor with charcoal, nor with ashes.
One should not remain constantly prone to sleep, nor should one avoid physical exercise;
however, one must not sit upon husks, charcoal, ashes, bones, or potsherds.
She should avoid quarreling with people and likewise avoid contorting her limbs;
she should not remain with her hair disheveled, nor should she ever be impure.
She should never sleep with her head toward the north nor with her head downward;
she should not be without clothing, nor agitated, nor wearing wet garments.
She should not utter inauspicious speech, nor should she engage in laughter and the like;
instead, she should always be intent on auspiciousness and perform worship of her parents-in-law.
"She should remain with a serene countenance, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband.
Thus it is said; likewise, Kaśyapa spoke as stated in the Mātsya [Purāṇa]:
"A pregnant woman must especially avoid eating during the twilight hours."
One should never bathe, nor should one ever go to the roots of trees.
One should not remain constantly prone to sleep; one should avoid the shadow of a mango tree and perform a bath with all medicinal herbs or with lukewarm water.
Having performed the protection rite, being eloquent in speech, and intent on the worship of the sacred objects,
one who is generous and virtuous should observe the night vigil on the third lunar day dedicated to Pārvatī.
A woman should be devoted to her husband, especially when she is pregnant;
the son who is born to her shall live for a hundred years and be endowed with a means of livelihood.
Otherwise, she will undoubtedly suffer a miscarriage; of this there is no doubt. Thus it is said.

Suśruta also states: "From that time forward, she should avoid physical exertion, strenuous effort, over-satiation, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, grief, fear, riding in vehicles, suppressing natural urges, squatting (kukkuṭāsana), and bloodletting. "From that time forward" means from the moment of conception. That conception should be understood through signs such as fatigue and so forth. These too have been stated by him: "In one who has just conceived, there is fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, a sense of moisture in the thighs, and throbbing in the vagina upon the union of semen and blood. Whatever the pregnant woman desires should be given to her; otherwise, a fault is heard of [in the scriptures]. And thus says Yājñavalkya:

"By not granting her longings (*dohada*), the fetus may incur defects, such as deformity or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman. Thus says the *Śruti*: "They call a woman who has two hearts one who is experiencing *dohada*; one should grant her what she desires. She gives birth to a son who is vigorous and long-lived."
Thus end the duties regarding the pregnant woman.
Now follows the birth-rite (*jātakarma*);
concerning this, Viṣṇu says:

Then one should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) for the son born, as prescribed; the remainder [of the sentence] is "according to one's own *gṛhya* [tradition]. This means immediately after the bath. And so says Saṃvarta:
"When a son is born, a bath with one's clothes on is ordained for the father."
And that [bath] should be performed with cold water. Regarding this, Jābāli says:

"The occasional bath (naimittika) should be performed with cold water, as indeed should the optional (kāmya) one. And this must be performed even at night, because this rule is prescribed immediately after birth in the passage beginning, "When a son is born. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states:

"At the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, likewise at the transit of the sun, and during an eclipse of Rāhu, bathing is recommended; not otherwise at night. Here, "at a sacrifice" refers to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). The mention of "bathing" is intended to indicate "giving" as well. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:

"One should not perform a bath at night, nor especially a gift; however, one may perform occasional (naimittika) baths and gifts during the nights. Regarding that, he [the same author] states that even such a gift is an occasional one:

[49] Giving on occasions such as an eclipse, a wedding, the transit of the sun, a journey, illness, or childbirth is to be known as occasional (naimittika) giving; it does not incur fault even if performed at night.
"What is given on the birth of a son, on a journey, or during the night is inexhaustible.
Regarding the specific rule for bathing at night, Āśvalāyana says:
"Water that has been drawn during the day, having mixed it with gold..."
"But when the night-bath has arrived, one should bathe in the presence of fire.
Furthermore, the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) must be performed even before the cutting of the umbilical cord. As Manu says:
"The *jātakarman* for males is ordained to take place before the cutting of the umbilical cord."

There is no [impurity] until the umbilical cord is cut. Hārīta also stated that very same point with its underlying reason: "Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, they perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and acts for the sake of merit (*puṇya*); once it is cut, there is impurity (*āśauca*). The purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is the birth-rite (*jātakarma*). Acts for the sake of merit (*puṇyārtha*) are gifts (*dāna*). Jaimini also says:
"As long as the navel-string is not cut, one does not incur the state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
once the navel-string is cut, thereafter the birth-impurity is prescribed."
As for that which is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *śrāddha* on the birth of a son should indeed be performed while the umbilical cord is still uncut;
or else it should be performed by those of self-restraint once the period of impurity has ceased."
[50] Thus, this should be understood to apply in the absence of obstacles such as the loss of the substance [of the ritual]. For this very reason, Jābāli says:
"The birth-rite (jātakarma) must be performed according to the rules immediately after birth;
if, by chance, it has passed its time, it should be performed once the period of impurity (sūtaka) has elapsed."
This *śrāddha* should be performed with raw foodstuffs (*āmadravya*). As Pracetas says:
"A woman, a *śūdra*, and likewise a *svapaca*, even at a birth ceremony (*jātakarman*), should perform an *āmaśrāddha* according to the *pārvaṇa* rite."

"Svapakvaḥ" means one who cooks for himself. Satyavrata also states: "Upon the birth of a son, one who has performed the *jātakarma* before the cutting of the umbilical cord should perform the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, as stated by Vyāsa:
