"In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born [guests], during travel, upon the birth of a son, or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform a *hema-śrāddha* (gold *śrāddha*)."

This should be understood as applying when raw foodstuffs (*āmadravya*) are unavailable. Therefore, because of its inferiority, "foodstuff" (*dravya*) here is intended to mean that which is to be eaten; the "twice-born" (*dvija*) is the eater. However, in the *Ādipurāṇa*, a prohibition against cooked food (*pakvānna*) at a birth-śrāddha (*jātaśrāddha*) is shown:
"At a birth-śrāddha, one should not indeed give cooked food even to Brāhmaṇas, for their purification occurs through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and not otherwise."
Regarding the day of a son’s birth, Hārīta says by way of nature:
"When a son is born, that day is meritorious for the ancestors because of their joy (*āmoda*).
[51] Here, *āmoda* means delight. "Meritorious" (*puṇya*) means that it is praiseworthy for acts such as giving gifts and so forth. For this very reason, the Ādipurāṇa states:
When a son is born to the twice-born, both the gods and the ancestors come;
therefore, that day is meritorious and always worthy of honor.

"In that case, one should give gold, land, a cow, a horse, a chariot, an umbrella, a goat, a ram, a garland, a bed, a seat, and a house. Śaṅkha says that the acceptance [of gifts] occurs before the umbilical cord is cut; he states that what is done prior to that does not constitute a fault: "On the day of a son's birth, while the umbilical cord is still uncut, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, cows, or grain; some say this applies to one acting for the sake of a guru. Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"When a son is born, on that day one may freely accept gifts of gold, grain, cows, clothing, sesame seeds, food, molasses, and clarified butter. Thus says Vṛddhayājñavalkya.
"In that regard, one may accept all things except for cooked food;
if a twice-born man should eat it out of delusion, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

And this rule for accepting gifts applies only to those who are *sakulyas* (agnates). Thus says Śaṅkha: "One should give bipeds, quadrupeds, grain, gold, and so forth to all the *sakulyas*. And this should be done even during a period of impurity (*āśauca*). Thus says Prajāpati:

[52] "But when the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has arisen, there is immediate purification for the performer; he is purified by the preceding period of impurity. Thus ends the section on the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the naming ceremony, Yama says:
"One should have the naming performed for him on the tenth or the twelfth day."
"On an auspicious lunar mansion, on an auspicious day, or at a moment endowed with [favorable] qualities.
This means: under an auspicious lunar mansion, on an auspicious day, or at a praiseworthy moment. And so says Manu:
"One should cause the naming ceremony to be performed for him on the tenth or the twelfth day."
"On an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.

This means that on the tenth day from birth, the father should cause the naming to be performed; the word "should perform" (*kuryāt*) is used because he has the authority for the naming ceremony. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states: "The father, or another elder of the family, should establish a connection [for the name] with the family deity, the lunar mansion, and so forth. It should be understood that in the absence of the father, it is the family elder who acts. For this same reason, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: "Then, on the tenth day, the father himself should give the name."

And this is for the purpose of indicating the time mentioned in other treatises; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya says: "The naming ceremony on the eleventh day, and the first outing in the fourth month. In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa as well:
Some kings desire the naming ceremony on the tenth day;
others [desire it] on the tenth night, and still others when the month is complete.
"Likewise, other wise men say it should be on the eighteenth day," so it is said.

In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* it is also stated: "The naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) takes place on the tenth day, the hundredth day, or after a year from birth. Śaṅkha also mentions a specific rule: "Having raised [the child] on the tenth day, one should perform the *piṇḍavivardhana* [śrāddha] for the ancestors, because of the Vedic text stating that they are present there; having first offered an oblation to Brahmā and obtained the permission of the ancestors, one should perform the naming ceremony on that very day. The phrase "having raised" implies "from the previous bed. *Piṇḍavivardhana* refers to the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, Pāraskara says: "Having raised [the child] on the tenth day and fed the Brāhmaṇas, the father gives the name. Here too, the arrangement follows the respective *gṛhya* manuals. Manu describes its nature:
"A Brahmin’s [name] should be auspicious; a Kṣatriya’s should be endowed with power;

a Vaiśya’s should be connected with wealth; but a Śūdra’s should be contemptible. This means that their names, respectively, are those which signify auspiciousness, power, wealth, and reproach. Regarding the suffixes used here as well, he says the same:
"The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with *rakṣā* (protection);
that of a Vaiśya should be joined with *puṣṭi* (prosperity); and that of a Śūdra should be joined with *preṣya* (servitude).

This means that the words signifying *śarman*, *rakṣā*, *puṣṭi*, and *preṣya* are, respectively, the secondary suffixes (*upapada*) for these [classes]. And thus their names become: Bhadraśarman, Śaktipāla, Dhanapuṣṭa, and Hīnadāsa. Yama also mentions specific types of secondary suffixes.
"One should cause the names of a Brahmin to end in Śarman and Deva; those of a Kṣatriya in Varman and Trātṛ; those of a Vaiśya in Bhūti and Datta; and those of a Śūdra in Dāsa. Thus it is said.

In this regard as well, the names should be understood through the initial syllables mentioned by Manu: "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious. But Baijavāpa states the naming differently: "The father gives the name—one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, four syllables, or unlimited; beginning with a sonant (ghoṣavat), having a semi-vowel (antastha) in the middle, and ending with a long vowel or a visarga (abhiniṣṭhāna). This is the meaning: those syllables which are sonants—the third and fourth letters of each class—should be placed at the beginning. The semi-vowels (antasthā)—*y*, *r*, *l*, and *v*—should be placed in the middle. "Ending with a visarga" (abhiniṣṭhāna) means that the name should conclude with it. Alternatively, one may give a name connected with the grandfather or others, as Śaṅkha says: "The father, or another elder of the family, should give a name connected with the family deity or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Regarding women's names, however, Manu says:

"For women, this [name] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, charming, auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and containing a word of benediction. Thus it is said. "Easy to pronounce" means easy to utter. "Auspicious" means expressive of good fortune. "Ending in a long vowel" refers to the vowel *ā* or *ī*. For this very reason, Pāraskara states: "For a woman, a name derived from a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) should have an odd number of syllables and end in the vowel *ā*. Śaṅkha also says: "When a name for women thus ends in the vowel *ī*, that family becomes pure."
Thus ends the section on naming in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the rite of taking the child out of the house.
Regarding this, Manu says:

"In the fourth month, the child's departure from the house should be performed"—this is the rule; the word "in which" (yasmin) refers to the month of birth as understood from the context. Also in the Purāṇa:
"On the twelfth day, the child's departure from the house should be performed."
[56] "O Lord, it is the opinion of others that this should likewise be performed in the fourth month.
Then, as to what should be done after that, Śaṅkha says:
"The non-seeing of the child should be performed in the fourth month."
Yama also says: "Then, in the third month, the infant's sight of the sun should be performed;
in the fourth month, the infant's sight of the moon should be performed."

Logākṣi also states: "In the third month, the seeing of the sun. In this matter as well, the determination is according to one's own Gṛhyasūtra; however, for those followers of a Vedic branch (śākhin) for whom it is not prescribed, there is indeed an option. Thus ends the section on the first outing (niṣkramaṇa) in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the piercing of the ears (karṇavedha).
In that regard, the science of astrology states:
"The piercing of the ear is recommended in the months of Kārttika, Pauṣa, Caitra, or Phālguna, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day."
When the lunar mansion is auspicious, the moon is favorable, and the ascendant is a benefic head-ascendant,
and when it is free from the defects of the day, such as Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti.
A goldsmith should pierce the ears of an infant who has not yet grown teeth and is sitting on his mother’s lap,
using a needle with a double-threaded string.
The asterisms Hasta, Aśvinī, Svātī, Punarvasu, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Citrā, Hari (Śravaṇa), and Revatī;
when the Moon is favorable, on a Thursday or Friday, and in a Lagna presided over by Jupiter or Venus—the two ears [should be pierced].
"Bṛhaspati is the lord of immortality.
Thus ends the section on ear-piercing in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the ceremony of first feeding solid food (*annaprāśana*).
Regarding this, Manu says: "The first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) should take place in the sixth month, or at whatever auspicious time is desired in the family. Yama also says:

Then, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) should be performed according to the rules, either in the sixth month or in the eighth; or whatever auspicious rite is desired by the family should be done.

Logākṣi also says: "The first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place in the sixth month, or when the teeth have appeared. Śaṅkha also says: "The first feeding of solid food is in the [first] year, or in the half-year, according to some. In this matter, too, the arrangement follows one's own *Gṛhyasūtra*. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states a specific rule:
"In front of the deity, for the child who has been adorned and is seated on the lap of the nurse, food should be given in a golden vessel."
"One should have him eat that milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey, clarified butter, and gold;
then, once he has finished eating, the nurse should release the child from her lap. Thus it is said.
Immediately after the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), the same author describes the examination of the child's future livelihood:
Then, having arranged the crafts, all the vessels, as well as the weapons and the treatises before the gods, one should thereafter examine their characteristics.

"Whatever the child first touches, and likewise whatever vessel he touches himself, by that alone shall his livelihood be sustained. Thus ends the section on the *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*),
Manu says:
"The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes is indeed prescribed by dharma."
It should be performed in either the first or the third year, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Yama also says:
"Then, when a year has been completed, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) is prescribed;
it should be performed in the second or third year, according to the injunction of the Śruti."

Baijavāpa also says: "The *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) is performed in the third or the fifth year. Logākṣi also says: "When the greater part of the third year has passed, the *cūḍās* (tufts of hair) should be made. Here, *cūḍās* refers to the locks of hair. Śaunaka also says: "In the third year, the *caula*, or according to the family custom (*yathākuladharma*). [59] The meaning is that the *cūḍākarma* should be performed exactly as it is done in the family to which one belongs. In this matter, the arrangement is determined according to the respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Regarding the rules for the *cūḍā* and other rites based on the tradition of the sages (*ṛṣi-vyavasthā*), Logākṣi states: "The Vāsiṣṭhas have a lock on the right; the Atris and Kaśyapas have [locks] on both sides; the Bhṛgus are shaven; the Aṅgirases have five locks; some have a single braid (*vājī*); others have a lock for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala-arthāśikhin*); or they follow the family custom. This should be done on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight or on a festival day (*parvan*). *Kamuja* means a lock of hair. *Vājī* means a line of hair. Others, however, maintain a mere lock (*śikhā*) wherever it may be for the sake of auspiciousness. In this context, the number of years should be understood as starting from birth, because of the Smṛti of Āpastamba: "The *caula* takes place in the third year after birth, under the asterism of Punarvasu. The mention of Punarvasu is intended to indicate the prescribed lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For this very reason, Vyāsa says: [text follows].
One should have [the rite] performed under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, Citrā, Puṣya, Punarvasu, Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Hasta.
The word "shaving" (kṣaura) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Likewise, that same author states those [acts] which are prohibited:
"O Bhārata, one should not perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion in which a man was born; nor should it be done under the two Proṣṭhapadas, nor under Āgneya."

[60] One should avoid the first lunar day (pratipad), the empty days (riktā), the Viṣṭi yoga, as well as the days of Saturn, the Sun, and Mars, and indeed the night. Thus it is said; and also in the Jyotiḥśāstra:
The Sun should spend one month in the razor [period],
Saturn seven days, Mars likewise eight;
and the Preceptor (Jupiter), Venus, the Moon, and Mercury should grant [their respective periods] in sequence.
"Ten, eleven, seven, and five.
Likewise, in certain matters, an exception to the prohibition regarding a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is described in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*,
[to be applied] by the king's command or with the consent of the Brāhmaṇas.
"At the time of the release from bondage, at the initiations for sacrifices,
at the time of marriage, and during the birth or death impurities— for all these occasions, the performance of shaving (kṣurakarma) is recommended."
Thus ends the section on the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the sacraments for women;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
These rites for women are to be performed silently; however, their marriage is accompanied by mantras.

Those rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and ending with the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) should be performed for women without mantras. Prior to this, however, until the specific rule is stated, everything is indeed performed with mantras. Manu also says: "This entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without mantras."
"For the sake of the refinement of the body, at the proper time and in the proper order" (61).

*Āvṛt* refers to the rites such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*) and so forth. By this, he states that one must not allow the prescribed time for these rites to pass. For this very reason, Kātyāyana prescribes an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for such a lapse:
"In the case of a transposition of deities during the *homa* offerings, how should it be performed?"
Having performed the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta), one should again offer oblations in due order.
If, for some reason, the ritual preparations should be delayed beyond their proper time,
those rites which are to be performed prior to the initiation ceremony must still be carried out after having offered this very oblation.

The *sarvaprāyaścitta* (universal expiation) has also been stated by that same author: "And the *sarvaprāyaścitta* is performed with five [verses] verse by verse: 'tvaṃ no agne' (two verses), 'ayāś cāgne', 'ye te śatam', and 'ud uttamam'. In the case of the lapse of the time for initiation (*upanayana*), there is only the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice and so forth. Gobhila, however, states a specific rule: "These rites for women are performed silently; but the oblation (*homa*) is performed without mantras.
Manu, on the other hand, says that for women, marriage itself constitutes initiation (*upanayana*).
"The marriage rite for women is considered their initiation ceremony;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, household duties are their ritual fire-maintenance. [62] Thus it is said.

In this context, service to the husband means service to the teacher; the purpose of the household refers to domestic duties, and the performance of those consists of the tending of the sacred fire (*agniparicaryā*). Therefore, even here, prior to initiation (*upanayana*), the rules regarding eating whatever one finds, speaking whatever comes to mind, and consuming whatever is available, and so forth, are the same. As for what was stated by Hārīta: "Women are of two kinds: *brahmavādinīs* (female Vedic scholars) and newly-wed brides (*sadyovadhūs*). Among them, for the *brahmavādinīs*, there is initiation, the kindling of the sacred fires, the study of the Vedas, and the practice of begging for alms in their own homes. For newly-wed brides, once the marriage has arrived, the marriage ceremony should be performed after somehow performing the initiation and the [Vedic] mantras. This refers to the intention of another ritual manual (*kalpa*). And likewise, Yama says:
In former ages, however, the binding of the girdle of muñja grass for women was prescribed,
as well as the teaching of the Vedas and the recitation of the Sāvitrī.
Neither her father, nor her paternal uncle, nor her brother, nor anyone else should teach her;
for a maiden, the practice of begging alms in her own home is prescribed.

"One should avoid the deerskin, rags, and likewise the wearing of matted hair. Thus ends the section on the sacraments for women in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the duties of those who have not been initiated.

Regarding this, Gautama states: "Prior to initiation (*upanayana*), there is freedom of action, speech, and eating. Freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) means acting according to one's will; freedom of speech (*kāmavāda*) means speaking indecorous words and the like; freedom of eating (*kāmabhakṣa*) means consuming stale food and so forth. The intention is that there is no fault in these matters prior to initiation. Likewise, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* says: "In this period, there shall be no fault regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten, what may or may not be drunk, what should or should not be spoken, or even in falsehood—provided that he is not yet initiated."

One should not suspect that by the phrase "nor shall he drink," there is no fault in drinking liquor and the like; for, following the word "he should avoid," there is the traditional teaching of Gautama: "A Brāhmaṇa [should avoid] liquor always. The inclusion of the word "always" (nityam) is intended to establish the prohibition even for one who has not yet been initiated. Nor should it be suspected that before initiation there is no Brāhmaṇahood at all, for it is said:
"One should perform the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."

Since Manu has thus prescribed the rite of initiation (*upanayana*) for one who is a Brāhmaṇa, it should be understood that the statements of Gautama and others refer to cases other than those involving mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "There may be mention of eating according to one's desire, provided it excludes a great sin. Furthermore, regarding other matters, Gautama occasionally provides an exception concerning the eating of sacrificial remains (*huta*): "A student (*brahmacārī*) should not eat what is *huta*. *Huta* refers to what is offered in the fire and the remnants of such offerings, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*. One who eats these is *hutāt*; "not *hutāt*" is *ahutāt*. Thus he should be one who does not eat these. And so says Yama:

"The Vaiśvadeva cake and that which is offered into the midst of the fire—if a child should eat these, having been drawn away, he must be protected with great effort by his mother. [64] Thus it is said.

The *vaiśvadeva* is that which remains from the *vaiśvadeva* offering. Likewise, Gautama states an exception even to the rule of acting according to one's desire: "the religious student (*brahmacārī*). The meaning of this is that even when, for some reason, there is a delay in the initiation ceremony beyond the eighth year from conception, one must still remain a religious student. Nor should it be suspected that the term "religious student" here is intended to introduce the specific duties of a religious student; for Vasiṣṭha says: "Indeed, no ritual duty exists for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
he remains equal to a Śūdra in his mode of life until he is born through the Veda."

Gautama also states: "He is one whose urine and excrement are produced wherever he happens to be. This means that for him there are no such restrictive rules as facing north during the day or facing south at night, and so forth. When such universal non-restriction would otherwise apply, he himself says, for the sake of establishing a specific rule in certain cases: "No ritual procedure for sipping water (ācamana) exists for him. *Kalpa* here means "manner" or "method. By this, it is understood that while there is merely the act of sipping water on occasions requiring it, the full ritual procedure (*kalpa*) itself is prohibited. Therefore, by stating this, he implies that even upon touching someone who has not performed the sipping of water, there is no impurity for the father or others, saying: "There is no impurity from touching him" [65]. The intention is that he is already pure (*prayata*) by virtue of that very [act of sipping].
But if that were the case, then there would be no impurity even upon touching someone touched by a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, or the like.

Not so; for in the statement of Gautama, the *caṇḍāla* and others are not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛtatva*), and because no specific rule is mentioned in the passage: "Upon touching one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or a corpse, or one who has touched them, or one who has touched the latter, one becomes pure by touching water while wearing one's clothes. Therefore, the statements "there is no impurity (*āśauca*) from touching him" and "no rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) applies to him" must be understood as referring specifically to the *ācamana* that is the subject at hand. With this very intention, Āpastamba also says: "Until the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), embryos do not become impure (*aprayata*). Some say until one full year has passed; or until they cannot distinguish the directions; another view is until the initiation (*upanayana*). For it is here that eligibility (*adhikāra*) arises according to the scriptures. Regarding the phrase "for it is here that eligibility," the commentary on that text states that the three alternative views beginning with "some say" are presented as prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on the force of the reason. Likewise, Gautama mentions another form of purification: "Except for wiping (*apāmārjana*), washing (*pradhāvana*), and sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*). Wiping is the cleansing of the parts of the body defiled by food remnants with the hand using water. Washing is the rinsing of what is smeared with impure substances. Sprinkling is the pouring of water over what has been touched by something unclean. The meaning is that, other than these, sipping water is the cause of purification. Even if one has performed purification through such means as sipping water, one should not employ such a person in rites like the *agnihotra*. Thus says Gautama: "But one should certainly not employ him in the *agnihotra* or the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*). The intention is that he is devoid of the sacred formulas (*mantra*). Manu also says:

"Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor even one who is uninitiated (asaṃskṛta) shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*," so it is said. Furthermore, Gautama states that there is no application [of mantras] after they have been learned: "The *brahman* priest should not utter [Vedic texts], except when offering the *svadhā*. The offering of *svadhā* refers to funeral rites (*pretakarma*). The meaning is that in that context, the study of mantras by one who has not yet been initiated is not prohibited. The mention of the *brahman* priest is intended to include those things not forbidden by other Smṛtis, such as the auxiliary sciences (*smṛty-aṅga*). Manu also says:
"For no rite whatsoever is prescribed for him prior to the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
nor should he utter the Veda, except for the offering of the *svadhā*.
Thus ends the section on the duties of one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the commencement of learning,
Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"When the fifth year has arrived, while Janārdana is not yet asleep..."
One should likewise avoid the sixth, the first, and the eighth lunar days.
[67] On the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight when it is empty (the new moon), and likewise on a Tuesday;
having thus determined the auspicious time, one should perform the commencement of learning.
Having worshipped Hari, the goddess Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as the authors of the sūtras of one's own tradition and, in particular, one's own specific branch of knowledge.
One should offer clarified butter under the names of these very deities;
furthermore, the worship of the best of the twice-born should be performed here with sacrificial gifts.
The teacher, seated facing the east,
should first instruct the student— who is well-honored with the benedictions of the twice-born— while facing the west.
From that time forward, one should avoid those occasions on which study is forbidden:
both the eighth days of the lunar fortnight, as well as the two days at the end of each fortnight.
"In cases of impurity, during a festival of the senses, during an earthquake, at the sight of Rāhu,
during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise upon the fall of a meteor, [the study is suspended] for a day and a night.
Thus ends the section on the commencement of learning in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), Yājñavalkya states:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception."
"For kings in the eleventh year plus one, for Vaiśyas in the [eleventh] plus one, according to their respective families.

The term *upanāyanam* is simply *upanayanam*. That [initiation] for a Brāhmaṇa should be performed in the eighth year from conception or from birth. "Plus one" means that which exists together with one; thus, in that eleventh year, it refers to the twelfth. For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well, the calculation of years begins from conception:
"One should perform the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."
In the eleventh year from conception for a king, and in the twelfth year from conception for a Vaiśya.

Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*. On this point, Lōgākṣi says: "The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa is in the seventh year, of a Kṣatriya in the ninth, and of a Vaiśya in the eleventh. Or, one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the fifth year from conception, or in the eighth from conception; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh from conception; a Vaiśya in the twelfth from conception, or in the sixteenth from conception. Gautama, however, speaks of the optional initiation (*kāmyopanayana*): "The optional [initiation] is in the ninth or the fifth. Even there, the count of years begins from conception, because after describing both the obligatory and optional initiations, he himself stated: "The number of years is counted from conception. And this refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa class, as Aṅgiras has said.
"The binding of the girdle of muñja grass should be performed in the fifth year for a twice-born man desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), and in the ninth year for one desiring long life.
Thus says Manu as well.
"For a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), it should be performed in the fifth year.
Regarding Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, however, that which was spoken by Aṅgiras should be observed:
"Likewise, for a king, the ceremony for the increase of strength and longevity should take place in the sixth or the twelfth year."

"But for a Vaiśya, [the years] of exertion and life are the eighth and the fourteenth. Here, "exertion" (*īhā*) refers to activity concerning agriculture and so forth. In this context, it should be understood that strength is to be found in the sixth and eighth [years]. And so Manu says:
"For a king seeking power, in the sixth; for a Vaiśya seeking exertion, in the eighth."

In the same way, at other times as well, the rite should be performed with a view toward other specific results. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Now follow the optional rites (*kāmyāni*): in the seventh year, for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in the eighth, for one desiring long life; in the ninth, for one desiring splendor; in the tenth, for one desiring food; in the eleventh, for one desiring sensory power; in the twelfth, for one desiring cattle. And this applies equally to all three social classes (*varṇa*), because it is stated in the commentary on that [text] that these are prescribed immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*). Furthermore, in this case, there is a second birth for the Brāhmaṇas and the others. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"The first birth is from the mother; the second is the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
Regarding this, Manu states the reasoning:
"In that regard, his 'brahmin-birth' is marked by the tying of the muñja-girdle."
In this regard, Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, while the teacher is called his father.
"Because of the imparting of the Veda, they declare the teacher to be their father.

Āpastamba also says: "For he (the teacher) produces him through knowledge; that is the superior birth. Only the mother and father produce the physical body. Thus, the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) belongs only to the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and not to the Śūdra, because for the latter there is no second birth. And so Yājñavalkya states:
"They are born first from the mother, and the second time from the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass."
"Therefore, these—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—are remembered as the twice-born.

Regarding this regulation of the social orders (*varṇa*), Āpastamba states the rule for the seasons: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rajanya (Kṣatriya) in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. Alternatively, the five months beginning with Māgha may be accepted; for thus says the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"The initiation with the girdle of muñja grass is recommended during the five months beginning with Māgha."
And this is common to all three castes. As it has been stated in the very science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*):
"Spring is the season that bestows auspiciousness upon the first-born (Brāhmaṇas), summer for kings (Kṣatriyas), and autumn for Vaiśyas;
or rather, for the binding of the vow for all [castes], the five months beginning with Māgha are suitable."

Regarding the followers of the *Yajurveda*, however, it is stated in the *Dharmabhāṣya* (*Āpastamba Dharmasūtra* 1.19) that the mention of "spring" is for the purpose of restriction. Spring and the other seasons also occur through the Sun’s conjunction with two zodiac signs; this too has been stated in that very same work:
"Through the Sun’s conjunction with pairs of zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, there are six seasons:
Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, Varṣā, Śarat, and likewise the sixth, called Hemanta."

The deer is Capricorn (*makara*). By this, it is stated that Spring (*vasanta*) consists of Pisces (*mīna*) and Aries (*meṣa*). However, the *Śruti* says that Spring consists of Madhu and Mādhava alone: "Madhu and Mādhava are the two seasons of Spring. Madhu and Mādhava refer to Caitra and Vaiśākha. In this manner, the lunar days (*tithi*) and other factors are also to be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). [As it is said: "When the Moon has disappeared, when Venus is in its eighth house, when the Sun is without its digits (*niraṃśa*), and during the *anadhyāya* [periods] or the eclipse of water (the rainy season), the initiation (*upanayana*) must not be performed."

The Sun, being without degrees (niraṃśa), is situated in the first portion of the zodiac sign; the *galagraha* is also said to be in that very place. As it is said: "The fourteenth, the three beginning with the seventh, and likewise the solitary fourth—these eight are declared to be the *galagrahas*."
"The Guru [Jupiter], the son of Bhṛgu [Venus], the son of Dhātrī [Mars], and the son of Śaśadhara [the Moon]—these are, respectively, the presiding deities of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.

Thus: the son of Bhṛgu is Śukra (Venus); the son of Dhātrī is Aṅgāraka (Mars); the son of Śaśadhara is Budha (Mercury). These are the presiding deities of the Ṛgveda and the others in their respective order. The intention is that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) should be performed on the day (*vāra*) belonging to the specific Vedic school (*śākhā*) of the student.
[72] “In the three *hasta* nakṣatras, in Puṣya and Dhaniṣṭhā, and in the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Punarvasu, and Śravaṇa;
on an auspicious lunar day endowed with the strength of the moon—the binding and releasing of the vows for the twice-born should be performed.
Thus ends the section on the primary times for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the secondary periods of time,
Manu says:
"The Sāvitrī [initiation] does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until his sixteenth year."
"Up to the twenty-second year for a Kṣatriya, and up to the twenty-fourth year for a Vaiśya.
And this prefix *ā* is used in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), since Vyāsa says:
"The time for initiation (*upanayana*) extends up to the sixteenth year."
"The highest [period] for one is twenty-two [days], and the highest for another is twenty-four [days].

Here, "highest" means the last; the meaning is that beyond that, there is no longer even a secondary period. For this very reason, Yama states that there is a fall from caste (*pātitya*) upon its transgression: "And all those who have completely exceeded the prescribed time are indeed fallen."
Vyāsa also says:
"If this [prescribed] time has passed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī (vrātyas) and must be avoided with effort."

By saying they are "to be avoided," he states that these people are unworthy of social contact. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor engage in transactions with them. Manu also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa should never, even in times of distress, perform according to rule any ritual or matrimonial alliance with these impure persons."

"Brahmanical connection" refers to teaching and so forth. "By those who are unpurified" means by those who have not performed penance (*prāyaścitta*). For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states: "The initiation (*upanayana*) of a *vrātya* who has not performed penance must not be performed;
one should avoid teaching him, officiating at his sacrifices, and [arranging] his marriage and other such matters."
A penance has also been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Beyond this, these fall [from their caste], excluded from all religious duties;
they are *vrātyas* who have fallen away from the *sāvitrī*, except through the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice."

The *vrātyastoma* is a sacrifice intended for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) of those who have become *vrātyas*. The meaning is that having abandoned that [sacrifice], one has no eligibility for other rites. However, there is no contradiction in this regard, because there is a scriptural injunction granting eligibility even to one who is without a wife, has not studied the Veda, and has not performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). Vasiṣṭha, moreover, prescribes another form of expiation: "One whose *Sāvitrī* initiation has lapsed shall perform the *uddālakavrata*. For two months he should subsist on *yāvaka*; for one month on milk; for half a month on *āmikṣā*; for eight nights on clarified butter; for six nights on food obtained unasked; for three nights on water; and for one day and night he shall fast. Or he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *Aśvamedha*, or he may sacrifice with the *vrātyastoma*" [7.4]. The meaning of this is as follows: the *uddālakavrata* is so called because it was seen by Uddālaka. Regarding its nature, he states: "For two months on *yāvaka*, etc. *Yāvaka* is a gruel made from barley; he should subsist on that alone for two months. As for "unasked," he should eat sacrificially pure food (*haviṣya*) common to all vows, since no specific food is mentioned. And that [eating once a day] should be done only once [per day], because the nature of expiation is characterized by austerity. In the case of fasting, however, there is a cessation even of water, because the three-night period was previously prescribed specifically as subsisting on water.

Thus end the secondary times. Now, regarding skins, Gautama states: "The skins of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat. The *kṛṣṇa* is the black antelope; the *ruru* is the spotted deer; the *basta* is the goat. The skins of these belong respectively to the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. Bṛhaspati [says]:
"The black antelope skin for a Brāhmaṇa, the Ruru deer skin for a Kṣatriya, the goat skin for a Vaiśya, or for all [castes] the cowhide.
Thus [says the text]. Pāraskara, however, states: "Or for all, that of the cow. Yama also says:

"The black antelope skin for a Brāhmaṇa, the Ruru deer skin for a Kṣatriya, and the goat skin for a Vaiśya; however, the Ruru deer skin may be used by all. These are the upper garments, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "The skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are the upper garments. Pāraskara also states: "An upper garment of the skin of the Eṇa deer for a Brāhmaṇa, a Ruru deer skin for a Rājanya (Kṣatriya), and a goat or cow skin for a Vaiśya; or a cow skin for all. The *eṇa* is the black antelope.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [the section on] animal skins and then garments.

Regarding this, Gautama states: "Hemp, linen, bark-cloth, and *kutapa* wool are for all; or cotton that is unadulterated. Hemp (*śāṇa*) is a product of the hemp plant. Linen (*kṣauma*) is made from the fibers of the flax plant. Bark-cloth (*cīra*) is produced from *darbha* grass and similar materials. A *kutapa* is a blanket made from the wool of mountain goats. "Unadulterated" (*avikṛta*) means not dyed with colors. The meaning is that these are the garments for all [classes] without distinction. Vasiṣṭha also says: "Or for all, woven cloth that is undyed. Manu, however, prescribes the rules for clothing according to the specific caste system.
"They should wear, in due order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.

Vasiṣṭha also says: "The garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be white, unwashed, and made of cotton or dyed with madder; that of a Kṣatriya should be linen; and that of a Vaiśya should be yellow silk. Pracetās states the definition of "unwashed": "That which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and which has not been worn."
One should recognize that as unblemished, purifying in all ritual acts.

That which is dyed with madder (*mañjiṣṭhā*) is *māñjiṣṭha*. Some maintain that the garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be ochre (*kāṣāya*). Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Some prescribe an ochre garment; [an] *māñjiṣṭha* [garment] for a Kṣatriya, and a yellow (*hāridra*) one for a Vaiśya. That which is colored by an astringent decoction (*kaṣāya*) is *kāṣāya*; that which is prepared with turmeric is *hāridra*. However, Gautama states a specific rule regarding the ochre garment: "For a Brāhmaṇa, [the garment] is made from tree-bark; for the other two, they are *māñjiṣṭha* and *hāridra* respectively. That which is produced from the astringent decoction of trees is *vārkṣa*. Paiṭhīnasi, however, prescribes ochre for all: "The water-pot, the sacred thread, and the ochre garment—these are common [to all]. And this [ochre garment] is for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment.
One should not wear any white garment made of linen, cotton, kutapa wool, skin, bark, or woolen cloth as an undergarment.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, [the section on] garments; now, the staffs.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"According to the Dharma, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, [staffs] made of bilva and pālāśa wood; the third is likewise born of the plakṣa.
For a Kṣatriya, those of nyagrodha and khadira; and another, produced from the vetasa."

"For a Vaiśya, [staffs] made of *pīlu* or *udumbara* wood; likewise, the third is made of *aśvattha* wood. And this is not intended as a cumulative collection of staffs, but rather as an option (*vikalpa*). As Yama says: "For a Brāhmaṇa, a staff made of *pālāśa* or *bilva* wood is prescribed."
According to the law, the sacrificial post for a Kṣatriya should be made of Aśvattha wood or else of Khadira wood.

"Then for a Vaiśya, a staff of Udumbara wood or Plakṣa is prescribed. Pāraskara, however, states a specific rule: "The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is of Palāśa wood, that of a Rājanya is of Bilva wood, and that of a Vaiśya is of Udumbara wood; or all [types] may be used by all [classes]. Gautama also says: "Or [a staff] fit for sacrifice may be used by all. "Fit for sacrifice" means intended for sacrificial purposes. This refers to cases where the aforementioned types of staffs are unavailable. For this very reason, Yama says: "But if even these are not available, then for all [classes], any wood fit for sacrifice may be used."

With this very intention, Āpastamba says: "[78] 'The staff is made of wood,' so some teachers teach, provided it is not associated with a specific caste. Gautama also says: "Unwounded, curved like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and possessing bark. "Unwounded" means not damaged by being entwined with creepers and the like. "Curved like a sacrificial post" means having a tip bent downward like that of a *yūpa*. And thus Vyāsa says:
"Measured by the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose, they are bent like a sacrificial post. Manu also states the measurement of the staff:

"A staff for a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline (*keśāntika*); for a Kṣatriya it should reach the forehead (*lalāṭasammita*), and for a Vaiśya it should reach the nose. The term *keśāntika* means having the length of the head. For this very reason, Gautama says: "The measurements are [reaching] the crown of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose. Vasiṣṭha, however, states a distinction: "For a Brāhmaṇa it reaches the nose (*ghrāṇasammita*); for a Kṣatriya it reaches the forehead; for a Vaiśya it reaches the hairline. Śaṅkha also says: "They are declared to be, respectively, reaching the hairline, the forehead, and the shoulder."
Thus ends the section on punishments in the Smṛticandrikā [79].
Now, the girdles.

Regarding this, Gautama states: "The girdles (*mekhalā*) are made of *muñja* grass, bowstring, and *sautrī* [thread], respectively. A girdle made of *muñja* grass is the girdle of a Brāhmaṇa. A *maurvī*—made of *mūrvā* fiber—is the bowstring (*jyā*), the cord of a bow, for a Kṣatriya. One made of *śaṇa* thread is the *sautrī*; that is for a Vaiśya. And so Manu says:
"The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of *muñja* grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring (*maurvī jyā*); and that of a Vaiśya should be made of *śaṇa* fibers."

"Trivṛt" means threefold. Thus Preceṭas says: "The girdles are threefold and turned to the right. Vasiṣṭha, however, states a specific distinction regarding the girdle: "The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of muñja grass; that of a Kṣatriya is a bowstring; that of a Vaiśya is made of woven thread. Paiṭhīnasi also says: "The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of muñja grass or of *aśmāntaka* wood; that of a Rājanya (Kṣatriya) is made of *balvaja* grass or of bowstring; that of a Vaiśya is made of hemp (*kṣumā*) or of linen (*kṣauma*). *Kṣumā* is flax (*atasī*). This [rule] is to be understood as applying when muñja grass and the others are unavailable. For this very reason, Manu says:
[80] "In the absence of *muñja* grass, however, it should be made from *kuśa*, *aśmātaka*, or *balvaja* grass;
it should be triple-stranded with one, three, or five knots.
The term "triple-stranded" (*trivṛtā*) means having three strands. The mention of *muñja* is intended to include *mūrvā* and other such materials by implication. For this very reason, Yama says:
According to the Dharma, it is traditionally taught that the girdle of a Brahmin is made of muñja grass, that of a Kṣatriya is a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber,
and that of a Vaiśya is a cord of hemp.
"In the absence of even these, girdles should be made of kuśa grass, aśmātaka, or balvaja fibers, triple-stranded, with either one or three knots.
Thus ends the section on girdles in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
Manu says:
"The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward, and triple-stranded."

"Flaxen thread for a king, and woolen thread for a Vaiśya. And it is triple-stranded; it is "new thread," according to the Vedic revelation: "The *trivṛt* is indeed ninefold. Also, in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is the upper garment (*upavīta*), having an odd number of strands and being triple-stranded. "Having an odd number of strands" means having an odd number of threads—that is, three-fold. Furthermore, each individual strand consists of an uneven number of fibers; it must consist of exactly three fibers. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding its state of being ninefold. And Devala has said:
"One should make the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with a thread consisting of nine strands."

Thus, it is stated that the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) consists of nine threads and is triple-stranded. It should be wound upwards. Dattātreya says this: "It is triple-stranded by means of three threads wound downwards and again by three wound upwards.
Kātyāyana also [says the same].

"The triple-strand cord should be made with three threads wound upwards; [the other] with three threads wound downwards. Thus it is said. The author of the *Saṃgraha* states the definition of that which is wound upwards:
"It is tripled by the right hand moving upwards."

"The thread wound upon the person is remembered as *ūrdhvavṛta* in the scripture. This means that which is wound with the right hand raised upward and held aloft is called *ūrdhvavṛta*. And this is logical; otherwise, because going and winding would be simultaneous, the grammatical connection would have to be "wound by this [hand] while going. Regarding the application of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) here, Devala says:
"Having gone out from the village and having counted it upon ninety-six finger-breadths..."
Having washed the thread three times over with the three *ābliṅgika* mantras, [one should proceed] up to the point where it has been tripled.
In a temple of the gods, or in a cow-pen, or by a river, or elsewhere in a pure place, one should fashion a nine-stranded cord using the Sāvitrī mantra; it should be triple-stranded.
One should then bind a living branch from any one of the sacrificial trees, such as the *bilva* or *aśvattha*, while reciting "Salutation to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyo namaḥ*).
If one speaks [while eating], one should perform the *āveṣṭita* rite, for that causes distress to the ancestors;
one should strike the palm three times, as this grants satisfaction to the gods and others.
Having taken earth with his left hand, he should place it in this [vessel] while saying, "Bhūri";
likewise, he should cast a leaf, a flower, or even a fruit [into it] with the *vyāhṛtis*.
"Then, having consecrated it with the three verses beginning with *bhūr agniṃ ca*,
and having bowed to Hari, Brahmā, and Īśvara, he places it [there]. Now, the mantra for holding [the vessel] is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

"The sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is the supreme purifier, which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning. Put on this foremost, auspicious thread that bestows long life; may it be strength and splendor for you.

Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya*: "Thou art the sacrificial thread; I fasten thee upon for the sake of the sacrifice. Regarding this, Devala states the difference in deities for each individual strand:
The first thread is the syllable Oṃ; likewise, the second is Agni;
the third has the Nāgas as its deity, and the fourth has Soma as its deity.
The fifth has the ancestors as its deity, and the sixth is Prajāpati;
the seventh has Vāyu as its deity, and the eighth is Sūrya.
"The ninth is for all the deities; these are the nine threads.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the rule for the knot:
"The sacred thread (upavīta) should be threefold, and one knot is prescribed for it."
Regarding this, Devala says:
"The thread may have one knot, or it may be double or triple.
Pitāmaha states that for one who does not know this origin of the *upavīta*, all ritual actions become fruitless.
For one who does not understand this origin of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) as declared in the Vedas,
their bathing, giving of gifts, recitation of mantras, and other such acts are fruitless.
"The Brahmin who does not know the manner of wearing the sacred thread is a deluded soul; he bears the burden forever like a beast, such as a cow. Thus [it is said].
But Kātyāyana states another measurement.
"That which reaches the waist, being held at the spine and the navel, should be worn as the *upavīta*; it should be neither too long nor too short.

From this prohibition of being too long or too short, it is understood that if the [standard] measurement cannot be obtained for some reason, another measurement is not contradictory. For this very reason, Devala says:
"Nothing whatsoever should be done [with the sacred thread] above the breast or below the navel.
The phrase "below the navel" refers to [the thread] being too long. He (Yājñavalkya) says the same regarding the unavailability of the aforementioned [cotton] thread:
"[The thread] may be produced from cotton, flax, cow-hair, hemp, bark, or grass."
"The twice-born must always wear the sacred thread (upavīta) when performing their duties. Thus [it is said].

*Kṣumā* is flax (*atasī*). *Valka* is tree bark. *Tṛṇodbhava* is that which is produced from grass, made of *kuśa*. Thus Gobhila says: "One makes the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) from a cord, a cloth, or a rope of *kuśa*" [84]. Bodhāyana also says: "The sacrificial thread is a threefold cord made of *kuśa*. It should be understood that the cord is also used in the absence of a cloth, according to the traditional teaching of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: "Or one may use a cloth for the purpose of the sacrificial thread; in its absence, with a threefold cord. By this, it is stated that the sacrificial thread must be worn constantly. For this very reason, Bhṛgu says:
"One should always wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and always have the topknot tied.
Whatever one does without the topknot and without the sacred thread is as if it were not done.
Nor should it be suspected that, according to this [text], the state of wearing the sacred thread applies only at the time of performing ritual acts; for the same author says:
If a wise person desires their own welfare, they should not cross over a place where the sacred thread, purified by mantras, remains upon someone's body.
"A task that resides in the body must never be set aside;
by performing it even once, a twice-born man becomes purified.
Furthermore, this sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a student (*baṭu*) is indeed only one. Devala states this:
"For a religious student (brahmacārī), however, there is one [sacred thread], but from the time of his ritual bath onwards, there are two. Thus [it is said].
Bhṛgu also states: "One sacred thread is prescribed for a student; likewise, two are remembered for the other two [stages of life]."
"The scriptural conclusion is that for ascetics there should be only one [fire]" (85).
This means "for the other two," namely the householder and the forest-dweller. And this refers to the obligatory [fires], because many [fires] are heard of in the context of desire. Thus Devala says:
"Many [fires] are prescribed for one desiring long life," and so forth; this is called optional (*kāmya*).
Regarding the entanglement of hair, he says the same:
"If the thread should have hair upon it, then having removed that hair,
one should sprinkle it ten times with water consecrated by the Sāvitrī mantra."
"Or if it has been broken, fallen down, or used, one should discard what has been prepared.
Manu, however, states the rule for the disposal [of items] upon the loss of the girdle, the sacred thread, the staff, and so forth:
"The girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot..."
"Having cast those that have been spoiled into water, one should take up others accompanied by the sacred formulas.
Thus ends the section on the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
now follows the *agnikārya* (fire-ritual).
Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"And immediately after that, the wise man should perform the fire-rite.
This means immediately after the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsanā). And this should be performed at both times [of dawn and dusk]. To that effect, Yājñavalkya says:
"Then one should perform the fire-rite during both twilights. So says Sumantu as well:
"Then there is celibacy, the consumption of food, the twilight rites, and the fire-rite. [86]

Some desire that the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) be performed only in the evening. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Some maintain that the worship of the fire (*agnipūjā*) is only in the evening. The kindling of the fire is the worship of the fire. For this very reason, Lōgākṣi states: "Some say that one should kindle the fire only in the evening. And this [rite] consists precisely of the *homa* offering, not merely the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid*). For this same reason, Śaṅkha says:
"Having risen at the proper time, bathed, and offered oblations into the fire, one should, being pure and with devotion, perform the salutation (*abhivādana*) to one's gurus."
The intention is that because of the use of the word *huta*, this is indeed a *homa* (oblation). And the deity here is one indicated by the wording of the mantra. Manu also says:
"Having brought fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
evening and morning, he should offer oblations with them into the fire, unwearied."

"In the open air" means in a place such as a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), that is, from a distant location not belonging to anyone else. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "In whatever way one regards the property of another as one's own, he indeed becomes a thief. However, Baijavāpa prescribes a rule regarding the direction for fetching fuel-sticks (*samidh*): "Before sunset, having gone toward the north-eastern direction, one should fetch a fuel-stick from the forest without causing injury. A dry stick should be used by one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); a moist one by one desiring splendor (*tejas*); both types by one desiring both. By saying "before sunset," he indicates a prohibition once the sun has set. For this same reason, Āpastamba says: "[87] One should not go to fetch fuel-sticks after the sun has set" (ĀpDh 1.4.15). The specific rule regarding the fuel-sticks is also shown in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
"The fuel sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood; if those are unavailable, they should be of *khādira*;
in the absence of those, *śamī*, *rohitaka*, or *aśvattha*; and if even these are not available, *arka* or *vetasa*.
Kātyāyana, however, states the measurement for the fuel sticks used in the *sāvitra* rite.
The sacrificial fuel-stick should never be thicker than a thumb;
it must not be stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor split.
The sacrificial twig used by a wise person in fire-offerings should not be longer than a span nor shorter; it should not have side-shoots, nor should it be devoid of potency.

"Split, cracked, short, crooked, hollow, or thin; long, thick, or bitten by insects—such [fuel] destroys the success of one's ritual acts. Āpastamba also states a general rule: "One should not place un-consecrated fuel upon the fire. Hārīta also mentions the visible fault incurred by failing to perform the fire-rite.
In ancient times, Death indeed seized a religious student while he was practicing harm;
Agni liberated him from that [clutches], and therefore one should indeed attend upon him.
"But when the religious student (brahmacārī) does not place fuel-sticks into the fire,
then Death seizes him and places fuel-sticks [into his own fire] thereafter.
Thus ends the section on the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in the Smṛticandrikā.
[88] Now, the essential nature of the guru and others is being defined for the purpose of performing salutations and other such acts.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"He who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules,
and nourishes [the child] with food, that brahmin is called a guru."
*Niṣeka* refers to the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite). The mention of "providing food" is intended to illustrate the provision of the Veda as well. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"He is a *guru* who, having performed the [initiatory] rites, imparts the Veda to him."

The "rites" (*kriyāḥ*) are those beginning with *niṣeka* (conception) and so forth. Thus, it is meant that he who, having performed the rites from *niṣeka* up to the *upanayana* (initiation), and having imparted the Veda, sustains [the student] with food—he is called a *guru*. Furthermore, this status of being a *guru* belongs to the father alone and no one else, because he alone has the authority for the *niṣeka* and subsequent rites. Consequently, it is stated that the father alone has the authority regarding the *upanayana* and other such ceremonies. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "Having thus refined his son by means of the staff and other [initiatory rites], the father should diligently teach him the Veda as well as the scriptures of Manu and others."
And thus:
"He who, having initiated [the pupil], imparts the Veda is declared to be an *ācārya*.

This status of the *ācārya* as the performer of the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites is to be understood as applying when there is an absence of the father or a lack of fitness [in him]. For there is no reason to abandon a present and fit father; however, in the case of a lack of fitness, abandonment is indeed permissible. And so says Yama:
"He does not teach, nor does he study, and he persists in acts that cause a fall;
one who possesses these characteristics must be abandoned by the student observing his vows. Thus it is said.

In this context, the *guru* is the initiator (*upanetṛ*). For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "He who initiates one who is ignorant, and he who is himself ignorant, both enter from darkness into darkness; so says the Brāhmaṇa. One should seek such a preparer (*saṃskartṛ*) as is distinguished by noble birth and learning, and is composed. The meaning is that even he who initiates an ignorant person enters into darkness. This statement of the definition is intended to show that the status of being a *guru* for those other than a father is merely figurative. For this reason, Manu uses the word *guru* with the intention of denoting mere venerability toward those who have assisted him through Vedic study.
"Whether it be little or much, he who benefits another with sacred learning (śruta)—one should know that person here as a teacher (guru) by virtue of that benefit of learning.
This is the intended meaning because of the use of the word "api" (even/also). As for what was stated by Devala:
The preceptor, the father, the elder brother, and the sovereign;
the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, and the maternal and paternal grandfathers.
The eldest of one's caste, the paternal uncle—these are remembered as teachers among men;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the teacher’s wife, and the uterine sisters of both the father and the mother.
"The mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse are gurus among women.

Thus has this group of gurus been described, being twofold: on the mother's side and on the father's side. This, too, is intended to express their status as objects of veneration, just like the father and others. And so Vyāsa says:
The maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law, the teacher,
an elder brother, a Snātaka, and an officiating priest— these are always to be honored as gurus.

"A maternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a mother-in-law, a nurse, a paternal aunt, a grandmother, the wife of a paternal uncle, and the wife of a teacher—one should behave toward these as toward one's mother.
Thus [says Manu]; and Manu also [says]:

"One should maintain devotion toward one's father's sister, one's mother's [sister], and one's elder sister as toward a mother; however, the mother is more venerable than these. Yājñavalkya also states the definition of a teacher (ācārya):
"He who, having initiated [a student], imparts the Veda is called an *ācārya*.

The meaning is that he who, having performed merely the initiation (*upanayana*) for someone, bestows the Veda upon him, is his *ācārya*. The mention of the "Veda" is intended to include the *Kalpasūtras* and other such texts as well. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda..."
"They declare that teacher to be one who possesses the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*).

Here, "secret doctrine" (*rahasya*) refers to the *Upaniṣads*. Furthermore, this role of performing the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites should be understood as belonging to the eldest brother in the absence of a father; for it is said: "The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers just like a father."
And they should behave toward their eldest brother according to dharma, just as toward a father.

Thus, because Manu has extended the duties of father and son to these two [the preceptor and the teacher], he who teaches a portion of the Veda or the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) for the sake of livelihood is an *upādhyāya*. Regarding this, Manu says: "But he who, for the sake of livelihood, teaches a single portion of the Veda or the Vedāṅgas, is called an *upādhyāya*. (MDh 2.140)
Livelihood (*vṛtti*) means a means of subsistence. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:

"He who is a teacher for a fee is called an *upādhyāya*. Teaching for a fee is the act of teaching in exchange for payment. And thus Viṣṇu states: "But he who should teach this [Veda] for a price, him one calls an *upādhyāya*. The word "should know" (*vidyāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The definition of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) has also been stated by Manu himself.

"He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—he is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.

Furthermore, these aforementioned teachers (ācārya), sub-teachers (upādhyāya), and officiating priests (ṛtvij) are to be understood as worthy of honor in the order mentioned above. And so says Yājñavalkya:

These are to be honored as before, those for whom the mother is more venerable; "to be honored" means they are worthy of worship. "More venerable" means weightier, that is to say, most worthy of worship. Devala also says: "Of all gurus, five in particular are especially worthy of worship."
That which one cultivates, that which one gives birth to, and those by whom knowledge is taught.
"The eldest brother, and the husband—these five are remembered as gurus.
Among them, three are the most excellent; among those, the mother is to be highly honored.
(92) Regarding this, Vyāsa states the underlying reason:
Having carried [the fetus] within her womb for ten months,
she, overwhelmed by piercing pains and various agonizing sensations, gives birth while fainting from distress.

"A mother who is devoted to her children considers her sons dearer even than her own life; who is able to repay her for that, even in a hundred years? This is the intended meaning: she is most worthy of worship. "Repaying her" (*niṣkṛti*) means becoming free from debt to her. On this point, Śaṅkha says: "A son shall not be released from his debt to his father, nor from his debt to his mother while he is alive, except through the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Manu also states that the mother alone is the most venerable.

"An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya; a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya; but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in terms of reverence. This [statement] refers specifically to the biological mother who has not performed the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. Otherwise, however, the father alone is superior. Thus says the Purāṇa:
According to the Dharma, there are two gurus for a man in this world: his father and his mother.
Of these, the earth is more venerable, and the mother is even more venerable than that.

"Of those two as well, the father is superior because of the preeminence of the seed; in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother. Thus, the teacher is indeed more venerable even than the biological father alone. Regarding this, Manu says:
[93] Between the one who gives birth and the one who gives the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable.
It is the teacher (*ācārya*) who gives the Veda, and not the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*). For immediately thereafter it is said:
"For the twice-born man, the birth through the Veda is eternal both after death and in this world."

The meaning is that he performs that birth known as the initiation (*upanayana*) for the purpose of grasping the Veda (*brahman*). Viṣṇu states that even a child who teaches an elder is more venerable: "One should behave toward a teacher who is a child or of equal age as one would toward a guru. Regarding this, Manu relates an ancient account: "The infant Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his ancestors;
having encompassed them with his knowledge, he said to them, 'O little sons!'"
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant one is indeed a child, while the giver of the mantra is the father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child" and the giver of the mantra a "father."
The seers did not establish dharma by means of years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he who is learned in the Vedas is great among us.

They did not establish greatness based on age and so forth; rather, they held that he alone is great who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and a teacher (*pravaktṛ*). For this very reason, one should not bear malice toward him. As Manu says:
"He who fills both ears with the unerring Brahman is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear malice toward him."
[94] It covers and fills; the meaning is that it makes it unerring, free from discordant notes and the like. Vyāsa also said:

"Those who harbor malice toward their teacher, father, or mother, whether by thought or deed—their sin remains even after the slaughter of an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā). Therefore, there is no greater evildoer in this world than these."
Manu also says:
"The teacher, the father, the mother, and the elder brother must not be treated with contempt even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brāhmaṇa."
Devala says that he who always acts for the pleasure of his parents attains the full range of dharma:
"As long as both father and mother remain free from infirmity,
for that long the son should abandon everything else and be devoted solely to them."
If both mother and father should be well-pleased by the virtues of their son,
that son shall, through that very deed, attain the entirety of Dharma.
Transformation is death. Manu also says: "The suffering that parents endure during the birth of human beings cannot be repaid, even in a hundred years."
One should always speak kindly to those two and to the teacher at all times;
for when these three are satisfied, all austerity is fully accomplished.
[95] Service to these three is said to be the supreme austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For those three worlds are indeed these; those three stages of life are indeed these;
those three Vedas are indeed these; and those three sacred fires are said to be these.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇā fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire;
this triad of fires is most venerable.
By devotion to one's mother, one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one attains the world of Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all his ritual actions are fruitless.
As long as those three live, one should not serve another;
one should constantly perform service toward them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the next world, one should report that to them through thought, word, and deed without causing them any obstruction.
This is the supreme dharma directly; any other is called a secondary dharma.
"Pāratrya" means pertaining to the next world. Devala also says:
"There is no deity equal to a mother; there is no teacher equal to a father. Indeed, no recompense whatsoever exists for them."
Thus concludes the section on the definition of the Guru and others in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for salutation (*abhivādana*).
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
[96] Then the learned man should offer salutation, saying, "I am so-and-so.
The meaning is that this should be done immediately after the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). In place of the word "so-and-so" (*asau*), he should utter his own name. And thus says Manu:
"A Brahmin, when saluting an elder after the formal greeting..."
One should announce one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so by name."

Regarding the salutation, after the word "I salute" (*abhivādaye*), one should state one's own name, saying, "I am Devadatta by name. Furthermore, the word "O" (*bhoḥ*) should also be uttered following that. As he himself has said: "In a salutation, one should utter the word 'O' at the end of one's own name."

When this is the case, the formal practice is as follows: "I salute you, sir; I am Devadatta by name. Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "A Brāhmaṇa should salute, extending his right arm level with his ear; a Rājanya [Kṣatriya] level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist; and a Śūdra should remain low with his palms joined. And this must be performed with both hands, for otherwise a fault is heard of in the scriptures. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"Whatever dharma one may perform with the mind from birth onwards, all that becomes fruitless through saluting with only one hand."
This too concerns the learned; as he himself said:
"Then, one should bestow the blessing upon the disciples with hands in the shape of a lotus for the guru;
with the ear of a goat for the learned; and with a single hand for the ignorant."
The meaning is that the two hands are turned upside down like lotuses. Atri also says: "Having raised his right hand, one should salute a wall;
however, toward a *śrotriya*, one should perform the *añjali* gesture, and for a guru, one should grasp his feet."
Regarding the sequence of salutation in an assembly of Brahmins, Manu says:
"Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge— one should first salute him from whom one has acquired that knowledge."

And this must be done by rising up, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "In all cases, one should rise and offer a greeting. Manu also says: "For the vital breaths of a young man depart when an elder approaches;
he recovers them again by rising and offering a greeting."
He himself said that for one who possesses such moral discipline, even longevity and the other virtues increase:
"For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength. [98]
Manu himself has stated what should be said by one who returns a greeting:
"A Brahmin, when greeted, should be addressed as 'May you be long-lived' or 'May you be well-being';
and at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with the preceding syllable protracted."

The syllable *a* is intended as an indicator for the final vowel of the name, since there is no rule that a name must always end in the letter *a*. Therefore, whichever vowel beginning with *a* occurs at the end of the saluter’s name—that is, the vowel preceding the final consonant—it alone is to be protracted (*pluta*). A new letter *a* is not prescribed at the end of the name. The term "preceding the final syllable" (*pūrvākṣara*) means that which has a preceding syllable (*pūrvam akṣaram yasya*). Vasiṣṭha also states: "In an address, the final vowel of this [name] is protracted. This means that when an address is to be made, the vowel at the end of the saluter’s name becomes protracted; that is, it becomes three morae (*trimātra*). And thus the usage is: "May you be long-lived, gentle Devadatta! However, when addressing those who do not understand a return-greeting in connection with their name, one should say: "I, sir" (*ahaṃ bho*). This applies to all women as well. Thus says Manu: [Manu 2.126] "When greeting, one should say 'I, sir' (*ahaṃ bhoḥ*) to those who do not know one's name, and likewise to all women."
"Those who do not know how to respond to a salutation by name,
a wise man should address them as 'I am [so-and-so],' and the same applies to all women.
He further states that one who does not even know the nature of the response to a salutation is not to be saluted at all.
"A Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be greeted by a learned man; he is just like a Śūdra.
(99) Furthermore, the fault of one who, despite knowing the proper form, fails to perform the return greeting and so forth, is shown in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
But he who, when a salutation has been performed, does not return the salutation or does not offer a blessing,
certainly goes to hell.
"But he who, when a salutation has been performed [by another], does not return the salutation to that Brahmin,
is born as a tree in a cremation ground, frequented by vultures and crows. Thus says Yama as well.
But he who does not offer a blessing after being saluted first shall incur a share of whatever evil karma that person has committed.
"Therefore, one who knows the Dharma should be the first to speak even to a Caṇḍāla;
he should say, 'Drink liquor,' and in this way the Dharma is not lost. He stated this very same blessing as well:
A Brāhmaṇa should say "Svasti" (May it be well); a Kṣatriya, "Āyuṣmān" (May you be long-lived);
a Vaiśya, "Vardhatām" (May it increase); but a Śūdra should say "Svāgatam" (Welcome).

[100] And this applies in common to all castes (*varṇa*). Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*: "It is the established rule that a Brāhmaṇa should pronounce blessings (*svasti*) for all castes. Yama himself also explains the meaning of the word *svasti*:
That happiness which exists in the three worlds, free from disease and calamity,
and in which all desires are contained— that is designated as "well-being" (svasti).

And this salutation (*abhivādana*) is to be performed only toward those who are older in age, according to the traditional law of Manu: "One should salute one who is superior in age. For this very reason, Gautama states that although officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others are worthy of honor, they are not to be saluted by those who are younger: "In the case of officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger, one should rise to meet them, but they are not to be saluted. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"One should rise to meet and salute officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are of lower age"—that also intends merely verbal address, meaning "one should speak to them face-to-face. For this very reason, Baudhāyana says: "In the case of officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger, there is merely addressing them after rising. Even regarding such addressing, Manu states the rule: [text follows].

"One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*), a Kṣatriya about his health (*anāmaya*), a Vaiśya about his well-being (*kṣema*), and upon meeting a Śūdra, one should ask only about his freedom from disease (*ārogya*).

Āpastamba also says: "One should ask about the welfare of one who is younger or of equal age. A *vayasya* is one of the same age. This rule also applies specifically to a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), as he himself states: "One should not pass by a *śrotriya* without greeting him, nor should one pass by a woman in the forest. Manu also states a rule regarding conversation with women:
But toward a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth,
one should address her as "Madam," "O fortunate lady," or "Sister."

And thus, it should be understood that with one who is younger or of equal age, there is merely a formal address (*abhibhāṣaṇa*), whereas with one who is older, there is a salutation (*abhivādana*).
