When it is asked by how much time seniority (*jyāyastva*) is established in those cases, Manu says: "Friendship among fellow citizens is based on a ten-year difference; among artists, on a five-year difference; among Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), on a three-year difference; and among those of the same lineage, even by a very small amount."

Among those residing in the same town, one who is ten years older becomes a senior friend (*pūrva-sakha*); one older than that is a superior (*jyāyān*). Among those who possess arts—meaning those skilled in the sciences of song, dance, and so forth—one who is five years older is a senior friend. Among those devoted to sacred learning—meaning students of the Vedas—one who is three years older becomes a senior friend; one older than that is a superior. Among those of one's own kin, such as brothers and the like, even one who is slightly older in age is a senior friend; the meaning is that even one who is older must be saluted (*abhivādya*). And this refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas, as Manu says:
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a seventy-year-old king as father and son; yet, of these two, the Brahmin is the father.

Therefore, the intention is that only a Brāhmaṇa is to be saluted. For this very reason, Śātātapa says: "A Brāhmaṇa should always be saluted with reverence by those desiring prosperity—namely, by Kṣatriyas and others—and he should be honored with a bow of the head."
[102] "A Brahmin must never salute Kṣatriyas and others,
even if they are endowed with knowledge, ritual action, and virtues, and are highly learned.
For this very reason, that same author also states the penance for saluting a Kṣatriya or others:
Having saluted a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, what should be the expiation?
One becomes purified by saluting eighteen Brāhmaṇas.
Having saluted a Śūdra, a twice-born man should perform a bath with his clothes on;
by properly saluting one hundred Brāhmaṇas, he becomes completely purified.
One becomes purified by worshipping the lotus-eyed Lord or the three-eyed God,
or by saluting a highly fortunate Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu states that there are certain exceptions to the practice of salutation even among Brāhmaṇas:
"In all assemblies, at sacrifices, and in royal palaces,
one should perform a mere salutation (namaskāra) but should not offer a formal greeting (abhivādana)."

Regarding the specific procedure for salutation toward teachers and others, Gautama states: "The clasping of the feet of the teacher should be performed in the morning. Here, "teacher" (*guru*) refers to the *ācārya*, since he himself says: "Of one's mother, father, their wives, elder siblings, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those [latter]," and so forth. "Elder siblings" refers to older brothers; "teachers of knowledge" refers to *upādhyāyas*; and "their teachers" refers to the teachers of one's mother and others. The meaning is that the clasping of the feet must also be performed for these. "Clasping of the feet" (*pādopasaṃgrahaṇa*) means touching the feet. Manu describes the manner of doing so:
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with the right hand;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.

The meaning is that one should touch the left and right feet of the teacher with one's own left and right hands. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states a specific rule: "With palms turned upward, one should salute the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand. Bodhāyana also says: "Having touched the ears"—the word "salutation" (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. This [practice] must also be performed toward the wives of the teachers. As Manu says:
"The wives of teachers who belong to the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the teachers themselves;
however, those of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by verbal salutation."
In this same manner, the wives of one's brothers should also be saluted. Regarding this, that very [author] says:
"The wives of one's brothers, if they are of the same caste, should be saluted every single day;
however, the women who are relatives by marriage should be saluted only after returning from a journey."
When such a general rule of salutation has been established, the same author states an exception in a certain case:
[104] "But a young wife of one's guru should not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by one who is over twenty years of age and capable of discerning virtues and faults."
On this point, he himself states the reason:
"In this world, women are indeed capable of leading astray both the ignorant and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger."

The meaning is that women are capable—indeed, able—to lead even a learned man, or even one who is ignorant, onto a wrong path, as if under the sway of desire and other passions. Therefore: "But a young man should perform the formal salutation of the wives of his elders when they are young, saying, 'I am so-and-so.'"
A Brahmin, however, remembering the dharma of the virtuous, should perform the clasping of the feet and daily salutation toward the wives of his guru.

Regarding the procedure for salutation (*abhivādana*), Āpastamba says: "One should not salute while wearing shoes, with the head wrapped [in a turban], or with the hands tucked away. Here, "with the hands tucked away" means with the hands not extended. Pracetas also states: "One wearing shoes should avoid sipping water (*ācamana*), lying down, mounting a vehicle, saluting, prostrating, and so forth. Śaṅkha also says: "One should not salute with a water-pot in hand, nor while wandering for alms, nor with flowers, food, or in an impure state, nor while performing rites for the gods or ancestors, nor while lying down. Āpastamba further says: "[105] One should not be saluted by one who is unpurified; likewise, one should not salute one who is unpurified. And one who is unpurified should not return a greeting to those of equal or younger age, nor to women. Baudhāyana also says: "One carrying firewood, a water-pot, flowers, or food should not salute. This same rule should be understood to apply to the person being saluted as well. Thus says Āpastamba.

One should not pay homage to a twice-born man who is holding sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, clarified butter, water, clay, earth, or unbroken grains in his hands, nor while he is performing silent recitation (japa) or a fire sacrifice (homa).
Kātyāyana also says:
One should not salute one who holds a sacrificial ladle in his hand, one who is unknown, one who is incapable, an enemy, one who is ill, a yogin, one devoted to asceticism, or a younger person.
Śātātapa also says: "Having saluted a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a woman who has killed her husband, or a woman who has caused an abortion,
a twice-born man becomes pure after one day and night, even if he did so out of delusion."

One should never, under any circumstances, salute a heretic, an outcast, one who has neglected the initiatory rites, a man whose wife has committed a grave offense, a rogue, an atheist, or an ungrateful person.

An excellent twice-born man should not offer salutation to one who is running, to one who is intoxicated, to one intent on voiding urine, or to one who is eating or about to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should not offer salutations to one who is yawning, stretching, cleaning his teeth, having anointed his head, or about to bathe.
And likewise Jamadagni says:
"If one does not perform a salutation upon seeing an image of a deity, or seeing an ascetic carrying the triple staff (tridaṇḍin), one becomes pure after a day and a night."
Thus ends the section on salutation in the Smṛticandrikā; now follow the grounds for being honored, wherein Yājñavalkya says:

Those who possess learning, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth are to be honored in their respective order. "Learning" refers to the *śruti* and *smṛti*; "ritual action" refers to prescribed duties; "age" refers to being advanced beyond oneself; "kinship" refers to the excellence of one's own family; and "wealth" refers to property. Those endowed with these qualities are to be understood as worthy of honor according to this sequence; the meaning is that each preceding one is more venerable than the following. Thus says Manu: "Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning is the fifth."
These are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being more weighty than the preceding.

The meaning is that the grounds for respect (*mānyasthāna*) are the causes for being honored. Among these, learning (*śruta*) is weightier than wealth and the rest, because it is rooted in both the seen and the unseen. Thus said Gautama: "Learning, however, is weightier than all [others], because Dharma is rooted in it. Manu states that even one of low birth is to be respected like one of superior birth when endowed with these qualities, such as wealth and the rest: "Among the three [higher] castes, he in whom there are five [qualities], who are abundant and excellent, is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage."

The "tenth part" refers to the final portion of a hundred years; the meaning is that ninety years have passed. And this [designation of] old age is intended as an indication of the possession of wealth and so forth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even a Śūdra, when these [qualities] are abundant, deserves honor in his old age.
Manu, however, states that even for those who lack wealth and such, honor is due by virtue of giving way on the road.
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one in his tenth decade, to a sick person, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.

A *cakrī* is a cartwright; a *snātaka* is one who has performed the *samāvartana* ceremony; a *vara* is one intent on marriage. When these meet on the road, the way must be yielded to them; that is to say, one must move aside from the path. However, when they themselves meet on the road, among them the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored by the yielding of the way. Regarding this, the same author says: "But among those gathered together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored. And when those two meet, the *snātaka* alone is to be honored by the king. Thus he says.
Thus, between a king and a *snātaka*, the *snātaka* is entitled to the honor due to a monarch.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"For the elderly, the burden-carrier, the king, the *snātaka*, women, the sick, the eminent, and those carrying a wheel [or a load]..."
The path must be yielded to them by you, O King; however, one who has performed his ritual bath is to be honored even more than the monarch.

The mention of the "elderly" (*vṛddha*) is intended to include others such as children (*bāla*) as well. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states, following the rule that "the way must be yielded": "To children, the elderly, those afflicted by death, those whose bodies are burdened by loads, women, *snātakas*, and renunciants. Here, the "woman" (*strī*) should be understood as one who is pregnant. Thus says Baudhāyana:
"The way must be yielded to an elder, to one oppressed by a load, to a pregnant woman, and to the weak; likewise to a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, and a blind king."
Thus ends the section on the grounds for respect in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the wandering for alms;
regarding this, Manu says:
Having accepted his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.

The meaning is: "according to the śāstra. When the question arises as to how that is so, Gautama states: "The word *bhavat* should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end, according to the sequence of the castes (*varṇa*). This means that in the sentence requesting alms, the word *bhavat* must be used at the start, middle, and conclusion in accordance with the order of the castes. And so says Manu: "An initiated (*upanīta*) member of the highest caste (*dvijottama*) should go about begging for alms preceded by the word *bhavat*; a Kṣatriya (*rājanya*) should have the word *bhavat* in the middle; but a Vaiśya should have the word *bhavat* at the end."

In this regard, the formal application [of the rules] is as follows: a Brāhmaṇa says, "O lady, give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*); a Kṣatriya says, "O lady, give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*); a Vaiśya says, "Give alms, O lady" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*). On this point, Yājñavalkya states:
"One should go for alms among blameless Brāhmaṇas for the sake of one's own subsistence.
*Bhaikṣam* means a collection of alms (*bhikṣā*). The meaning is that one should practice [the act of] obtaining that. And this refers specifically to the case of Brāhmaṇas. Vyāsa says the same:
[109] Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas should go about begging for alms every day,
either only from the houses of their own caste or from houses belonging to all castes.

Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "A student, being self-restrained, should daily obtain alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, and who are praiseworthy in their own duties."
He (the same author) states an exception even regarding some of those [rules] mentioned:
"One should not beg from the family of the guru, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives.
"In the family of the guru" means in the house of the guru. Furthermore, as was stated by that very same author:
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever among these will not treat him with contempt.

Thus, that [injunction] refers to the subject of begging as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*upanayana*), and is not contradicted by the rule: "One should not beg in the family of the teacher. Gautama states that if begging elsewhere yields no result, wandering for alms in the teacher's family is not prohibited: "If there is no [alms] among the teacher’s relatives, the teacher himself, or one's own kin, then elsewhere. Here, "one's own" means among one's own kinsmen. In this case as well, one should abandon each preceding person if alms can be obtained at the houses of those following them. That too has been stated by him: "Among those, one should avoid each preceding one. Vyāsa, however, speaks of the practice of begging for alms among the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*).
[110] Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas should go about begging for alms every day,
either only in the houses of their own caste or among the houses of all castes.

The intention is that the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the three previously mentioned castes. This concerns the case where members of the aforementioned [castes] of the same class (*sajātīya*) are unavailable. Accordingly, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* states:
"Or, O mighty-armed one, he may wander through the village for alms among all [castes] except for the lowest, provided those previously mentioned are not available," so said the omnipresent Lord.

The last [category] is the Śūdra. As for that which was stated by Manu: "Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech with self-control, and avoiding those accused of crimes."

Thus, that [statement] also has the same meaning as the *Purāṇa*, and is not for the purpose of permitting [begging] even from a Śūdra, because it was stated by that very [text]: "for those who are not devoid of the Vedas and sacrifices. Furthermore, as for that which is in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:

"O descendant of Kuru, one should beg alms from the four castes; in case of failure to obtain [them], [one may seek elsewhere]," that too is to be understood as applying to times of distress (*āpad*) when each preceding [caste] is unavailable. For this very reason, Viṣṇu [states]:
"When a time of distress has arrived, one may practice the mendicancy of all four castes among virtuous Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas whose domestic rites are maintained.

This [practice] must be performed in the morning and evening, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "In the morning and evening, one should go on the begging round with a vessel (amatram). An *amatram* is a shallow bowl or similar utensil. For this very reason, Manu states the prohibition against eating food from a single person.
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person; this refers to times when one is not in distress. To this effect, Yājñavalkya says:
"Remaining in the stage of studentship, one should not eat the food of a single person except in times of distress."
Manu states the fruit of subsisting on alms:
"The livelihood of one observing a vow by means of alms is declared to be equal to fasting. Atri also says:
Those who subsist on vegetables, those who subsist on milk, and others who eat only barley—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of one who subsists on [the remains of] food.
One who drinks barley-gruel with cow's urine for twelve years, [the urine] having the color of molten gold— that would not be equal to alms-food.

*Yāvaka* is that which is made from barley; it is a barley gruel. Nor should it be said here that begging for alms is optional because no specific fruit is mentioned [for doing so], for Manu prescribes an expiation for its non-performance: "If one who is not ill fails to go begging for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin*."

Āpastamba, however, states that one should not refuse a student (*brahmacārin*) who is begging for alms: "When women refuse those who beg, they—though composed in mind—steal the merit of what is sacrificed, given, or offered, as well as offspring, cattle, Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and food. Therefore, one should indeed never refuse a group of students wandering for alms. This rule refers specifically to students engaged in vows, study, and other such practices; for this very reason, Manu says: "And one should give alms according to the rules to a student who is a mendicant."

By the phrase "according to rule," he states the prohibition for one who is devoid of that [rule]. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being without vows and not studying; for it provides sustenance for thieves. Thus [it is said].
Manu has stated regarding the giving of alms by its very nature:
"Alms, salt, and condiments which have been placed directly into the hand—
by eating these, one indeed becomes impure, and the giver does not go to heaven."
And this alms-food should be collected only as much as is required; otherwise, a fault is heard [to result]. Thus he himself says:
"One should never collect alms in excess of the mere amount of food;
one who collects more than that intentionally incurs the fault of theft."
He who, having collected [food] by the honey-gathering method (mādhūkarī), gives it to Brahmins, goes to a terrible hell; and the eater consumes his own sin.
Therefore, one should never offer alms that are in excess.

The *mādhūkarī* is alms-gathering from house to house. By specifying "intentionally," he implies that there is no fault in taking more than required when done unintentionally. For this very reason, Āpastamba prescribes the rule for the disposal of the surplus: "One should not leave a remnant; if unable to do so, one should bury it in the ground, or cast it into water, or present it to the teacher, or to an attendant, or to a Śūdra" (ĀpDhS 1.2.8.13). Here, "attendant" (*antardhin*) means the teacher’s servant. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the word "remnant" (*ucchiṣṭa*) here denotes an impure substance, because Manu prohibits giving such a thing away: "One should not give the remnant of one's meal to anyone. Having thus collected that alms-food and presented it to the teacher, one should eat it. And so says Manu: [1.107]
"Having collected that alms-food according to his needs without guile, and having offered it to his guru, he should eat while facing the east, pure and having sipped water. Thus [it is said].

But in the absence of the guru, one should announce it to his wife and others. Gautama states this: "In his absence, however, [one should offer it] to his wife, son, fellow-student (sabrahmacārin), or virtuous persons. A *sabrahmacārin* is a fellow student; "virtuous persons" refers to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). Likewise, Āpastamba says: "If the guru is away, [one offers it] to the teacher's wife; if they too are away, to other *śrotriyas*. Thereafter, one should eat with the permission of the guru and the others. And so Hārīta says: "Alms-food that has been sprinkled with water, circumambulated by fire, shown to the sun, and permitted—this they call 'equal to nectar' (*amṛtasammita*). Eating that, the religious student (*brahmacārin*) attains the perfection of Brahman (*brahmasiddhi*). Yājñavalkya also [says]:
Having performed his fire-ritual, he should eat with speech restrained, by the permission of his teacher,
preceded by the *āpośana* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.

The ritual of *āpośana* consists of reciting "Thou art the spreading of immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and so forth. Having performed that first, one should eat; the meaning is that one should do so with respect and honor. And thus says Manu:
"One should always honor food and eat it without disparaging it;
for food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor."

But food that is eaten without being honored destroys both [the eater and the giver]. "Kutsayan" means "without praising"; "anindayan" means "without censuring. Gautama also says: "One should eat in the evening and in the morning food that has been honored, without censuring it. By specifying "in the evening and in the morning," Manu implies a prohibition against eating in between: "For the twice-born, eating in the evening and in the morning is ordained by the Śruti."
One should not eat between [the prescribed meal times]; this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

By the phrase "equal to the *agnihotra*," he states that eating is obligatory during both time-periods. And so says the Śruti: "Therefore, one should indeed eat in the evening and in the morning. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Eight mouthfuls are to be eaten by a sage (*muni*), sixteen by a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), thirty-two by a householder (*gṛhastha*), and an unlimited amount by a student (*brahmacārin*)."
Āpastamba also says:
"The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three attain perfection only while eating; for them there is no perfection for those who do not eat. [115]

Nor should one suspect excessive eating by the phrase "not in measure" (*amitam*). Therefore, Paiṭhīnasi says: "At the proper time, one should eat food that is light, quickly digested, small in quantity, and rich in flavor. Manu also says:
"One should not eat excessively, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from a meal;
overeating is detrimental to health, longevity, and the attainment of heaven."
It is demeritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
Likewise, that same author states the rule regarding the direction for the eater:
"One who eats facing east gains long life; one facing south gains fame;
one facing west enjoys prosperity; and one facing north eats according to truth."

That which is beneficial for life is *āyuṣyam*. One should eat that facing east; the meaning is that one should consume it. Thus, it is stated that one who desires long life should eat facing east. Similarly, that which is beneficial for fame is *yaśasyam*; one should eat that facing south. Desiring prosperity (*śrī*), one should face west. *Ṛtam* means truth; desiring that, one should face north. Hārīta also says: "One desiring long life should eat facing east; one seeking fame, facing south; one desiring prosperity, facing west. As for that which was stated by Manu:
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed goes to the Rākṣasas.

Thus, this refers to the domain of the *śrāddha*, because it is recited in that context. Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for the vessel: "One should eat from a vessel made of iron or clay. And having eaten, one should wash it oneself. To this effect, Āpastamba says: "Having eaten, one should wash the vessel oneself. It has been stated: "One should always subsist on alms. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states an exception in certain cases: "A Brāhmaṇa may eat at a *śrāddha* as much as he desires, provided he does not violate his vow."

"Not causing pain" means avoiding honey, meat, and so forth, because these are prohibited for one who practices celibacy (*brahmacārī*). For this very reason, Manu says: "Honey, meat, and the like, which are forbidden, must never be consumed. Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha states that there is no fault at all in consuming honey if it has come to one unintentionally: "In the *Vājasaneyaka*, honey that is obtained unintentionally does not cause defilement. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu—"The performer of a *śrāddha* must avoid salt, fermented acids, and stale food"—that refers to cases where one has not been invited. For this same reason, Manu says: [as follows].
"If he should eat when invited at will, his vow is not violated.
Thus ends the section on "Wandering for Alms" in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the duties of one who has been initiated:
on this point, Saṃvarta says,
"One should perform the morning twilight devotion according to the rule, while the stars are still visible."
He performed the evening twilight ritual with the suns still present, when the sun was half-set.
Standing, the student, being composed, should perform the recitation for the morning twilight;
sitting, he should perform the recitation for the evening twilight without weariness.
Thereafter, the wise student should perform the fire-rite,
and then he should study the Veda while gazing at the face of his teacher.

A student of sacred knowledge, composed in mind, pure, and restrained in speech, should beg for alms in the evening and in the morning; having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing the east.
Manu also says:
"Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors;
one should also perform the worship of the deities and the twilight devotions."
On this point, Dakṣa says:
"Bathing in the morning and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders;
for the ascetic, it is declared to be three times a day; but for the student, it is once."

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "The immersion [in water] should be like a staff. By the phrase "like a staff," he indicates that one should not strive for the cleanliness of the limbs. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "One should not bathe in water while praising oneself. Regarding this, Manu states that those duties which are unique [to the student], such as kindling the fire and so forth, must be performed only until the completion of the *samāvartana* ceremony: "A twice-born man who has undergone the initiation (*upanayana*) should perform the kindling of the fire, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial for his teacher, until his *samāvartana*."
And this is intended as an illustration for others of a similar kind; therefore, it is said in the Purāṇa:
"A student (brahmacārī) should always wear a girdle, a deerskin, a staff, a sacred thread, a loincloth, and a waist-string."
Yama also says:
"Dwelling with his teacher, he should maintain celibacy, subsist on alms-food, and carry a staff, a water-pot, the Veda, and likewise a girdle made of muñja grass."
The "Veda" refers to the fistful of *dharma*; "in the house of the teacher" means in the teacher's residence. Vyāsa states the duties for one living there:
"In the teacher's house, he should sleep later and rise earlier;
furthermore, whatever task is to be performed by a disciple or even a servant [he must perform]."
Having performed all that as "done," he should stand at the side,
a servant skilled in all tasks and all duties.
One should not eat when another has not eaten, nor drink when another has not drunk; likewise, one should not sit while another stands, nor sleep while another is awake.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One should attend upon the teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study;
one should study when summoned and offer whatever has been obtained to him."

Hārīta also says: "Furthermore, he should follow [the teacher] with devotion as he goes, stands, lies down, or sits, by fetching the water-pot, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel, by sweeping and smearing [the ground], and by attending to his body; he should not desire [to use] his discarded garlands, bed, seat, shadow, or sandals. Āpastamba also says: "He should remain dependent on the teacher, except in cases that lead to loss of caste (*patanīya*). Bodhāyana also says: "In all matters, his word as a teacher is unimpeded, except in the case of a mortal sin (*pātaka*). Yama also says:
"Dependent on the teacher and lacking independence, he should rise before the teacher while in the teacher's house."
Always sleeping in the lowest position, he has conquered his genitals and conquered his belly.
One who has conquered sleep, conquered laziness, conquered anger, and mastered the self;
who is desirous of hearing [the teachings], free from egoistic speech, and devoted to the guru, the gods, and the forest.
Worshiping the guru means honoring the guru. Regarding its fruit, Śaṅkha says:
"Neither by bathing, nor by fire-offerings, nor by the service of the sacred fire does one go to heaven;
it is through the worship of the guru that the celibate student goes to heaven."
Manu also stated other rules:
[120] "In the presence of his guru, his bed and seat must always be low;
and within the range of the guru's vision, he should not sit as he pleases."
And this [prohibition] refers to objects other than cows and so forth, because sitting together is prescribed in those cases. Thus he himself said:
"One may sit together with one's teacher on a cow, a horse, a camel, a vehicle, a palace, a grass mat, mats, as well as on a stone, a wooden plank, or a boat."

Viṣṇu also states: "He should not sit on the same seat as [the teacher], except for stone slabs, wooden planks, or vehicles. Likewise, one must not listen to censure or the like directed at the guru. And so says Manu:
"Wherever censure or even reproach of the guru takes place, there one should cover one's ears or depart elsewhere from that spot."

Slander (*parīvāda*) is the proclamation of faults that do not exist; defamation (*nindā*) is the attribution of faults that are untrue. One should not engage in slander and the like even against oneself. As he [the author] himself said: "Through slander one becomes a donkey; indeed, through defamation one becomes a dog.
One who consumes another's property becomes a worm; one who is envious becomes an insect."
One who lives off the wealth of a teacher without permission is a consumer [of forbidden things]. Hārīta also says:
"He who disregards his teacher, the giver of the nectar of immortality—that Brahman burns him, and he is born in the womb of an animal."
Whether one receives a verse, or a quarter-verse, or a half-verse, or even a single syllable from someone, one must certainly show respect to that person.

[121] Likewise, even the names of one's teacher and others should not be uttered. And so says the Smṛti: "The teacher, his son, his wife, an initiated guru, as well as one's father, paternal uncles, mother, and maternal uncle."

"A wise man should not mention by name his father-in-law who seeks his welfare, nor a learned ascetic, nor likewise his mother's sister. However, where the mention of the name of a preceptor or similar person is necessary, he should refer to him by the title of *upādhyāya* (teacher) and so forth. Thus says Gautama: "One should indicate the name and lineage of a guru together with honor. "Together with honor" (*samānataḥ*) means along with respect. For this very reason, Manu states:
One should not utter his name alone even in his absence,
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Likewise, Viśvāmitra states that service must also be rendered to the wife of one’s guru and others:
"Service, prostration, and indeed devotion must be performed in every way toward his wife and daughters, as well as toward elders who are established in righteousness."

Nārada also says: "Until the completion of his studies, the disciple should be intent on serving the guru; he should follow that same conduct toward the guru’s wives and likewise toward the guru’s son."
Sumantu also stated the rules for the religious student (*brahmacārin*):
"Celibacy, austerity, begging for alms, performing fire-rites at the two twilights, Vedic study, and service to the teacher—this is the conduct of a religious student. [122]

By the word *tapas* here, the observances (*niyamas*) of the student (*brahmacārin*) are meant. Thus Āpastamba says: "The word *tapas* refers to the observances; if they are transgressed, knowledge and ritual action flow away. Therefore, the intention is that the performance of these observances is mandatory. For this very reason, Manu states: "While living with his teacher, the student, having fully restrained the collection of his senses, should observe these observances for the sake of increasing his own austerity (*tapas*)."
But if among all the senses even one sense leaks away,
through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.

And these were stated by Yājñavalkya: "One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, fermented acids, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth."

*Madhu* refers to honey; *māṃsa* (meat) refers even to that of goats and the like, which must also be avoided. This is to be understood as applying when one is free from disease; otherwise, however, one may consume honey, meat, and so forth, having made them the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) of the Guru, as prescribed by a physician. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "If he should become ill, he may at will consume everything as the leavings of his Guru for the sake of medical treatment. The phrase *vyādhīyīta* means "he experiences the state of being afflicted by disease. *Añjana* refers to the anointing of the limbs with oil and the like, and of the eyes with collyrium and the like. This too is permitted except in cases where there is a physician's instruction, because medicine does not destroy the vow. Thus says the Smṛti:
[123] These eight are non-destructive: water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial oblation, the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine. Thus it is said.

One should avoid the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) of anyone other than one's teacher. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "The leavings of one who is not a teacher are not to be eaten. By the phrase "not to be eaten by one who is not a teacher," he implies that the leavings of a teacher are indeed to be eaten. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "The leavings of one's father and of one's eldest brother may be eaten. Nor should it be suspected that because the mother is also heard to possess the status of a teacher—as in the statement, "The teacher is the best among teachers; some say the mother"—her leavings must also be eaten. This is because she lacks the specific characteristics of a teacher, which are defined as: "He is a teacher who, having performed the [initiatory] rites, imparts the Veda to him. Therefore, it should be understood that the word "teacher" is used for her only in a figurative sense. For this very reason, Manu [states]: * *guruvad vartitavyaṃ hi śiṣyeṇa sarvadā* || * *guruśuśrūṣayā vidyā sidhyaty āśu mahātmanaḥ* || * *na hi vidyā-samo bandhur na hi vidyā-samaṃ dhanam* || * *na hi vidyā-samo lābho na hi vidyā-samā gatiḥ* || For a disciple must always behave toward his teacher as toward a teacher; through service to the teacher, knowledge quickly reaches fulfillment for the high-minded man. There is no kinsman equal to knowledge, no wealth equal to knowledge, no gain equal to knowledge, and no goal equal to knowledge.
"The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste (savarṇā) should be honored just like the gurus themselves. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, Gautama also, having extended the rules for a teacher (*gurudharma*) by stating, "The same applies to his wife and sons," declares an exception regarding eating their leftovers: "There is no [obligation to perform] eating of leftovers, bathing, dressing, washing the feet, massaging, or clasping the feet" [GDh 2.32]. *Prasādhana* means adorning; *unmardana* means massaging the limbs. Thus, when the rule of eating the teacher's leftovers has been established as a general principle, Āpastamba states an exception in certain cases: "In the event of a lapse in dharma, it is not to be eaten. The meaning is that the leftovers of a father who is possessed of unrighteousness (*adharma*) are not to be eaten. *Śukta* refers to harsh speech; one should also avoid that. For this very reason, Gautama says under the recurring phrase "one should avoid": "Harsh words. Regarding looking at the light of the sun—that is, gazing at the sun—Manu states that even that should not be done.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising or setting,
nor when it has just emerged from the water, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.

*Upaspṛṣṭam* means eclipsed by Rāhu. *Aślīlam* is untruthful speech. *Parīvādaḥ* is the censuring of others. The inclusion of the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) is for the purpose of indicating other observances (*niyamas*) as well. For this very reason, Gautama says: “One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, idle chatter, bathing [for pleasure], brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, calumny, and fear. *Gandha* refers to sandalwood and the like; its prohibition applies to that used for personal enjoyment, not to that offered to the deities. Thus says the Smṛti: “The religious student (*brahmacārī*) should accept only what has been offered to the deities. The same should be understood regarding garlands. *Yāna* refers to palanquins and the like. *Vādaḥ* is excessive prattle. *Vādanam* is the beating of drums and similar instruments. *Snānam* is bathing for the sake of pleasure, since bathing as a daily duty (*nitya*) is already ordained. *Bhayam* is [the causing of] fear to another. Manu also says:
One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, carrying an umbrella,
as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
Gambling, gossip, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and the harming of others—thus [it is said].

The *rasas* are the juices of sugarcane and so forth. Although honey is also a *rasa*, its separate mention is for the purpose of indicating the gravity of the expiation required for consuming it. As for looking at or touching women, one should avoid these only where there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse; otherwise, they cannot be avoided. For this very reason, Gautama states, following the rule "one should avoid": "Looking at or touching women when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse. Likewise, he mentions other restrictive rules: "In the presence of a guru, one should avoid covering the neck, sitting with the knees bound together (*avasakthikā*), leaning against a support, stretching out the feet, spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. Here too, "one should avoid" is understood from the context. Covering the neck means wrapping the neck with a cloth or similar item. *Avasakthikā* is binding the area between the knees with a cloth or similar item. Leaning against a support means resting against a wall or similar object. Yawning is well known. Cracking the knuckles refers to slapping the arms and so forth. Laughing is also well known. If that [laughing] cannot be avoided, it should be done by covering the mouth. Thus says Āpastamba: "[126] 'If one should laugh, one should laugh while covering [the mouth],' so says the Brāhmaṇa. One should not kiss a woman with the mouth, nor desire her with the heart, nor touch her without cause. Again, Āpastamba says: "One should not speak of what has been given, nor recall what has been done; and one should avoid self-praise and disparagement of others. Hārīta also says: "One should avoid riding horses, elephants, or chariots, climbing trees or uneven ground, piling up [things], crossing great rivers or oceans, and acts of great rashness or what is forbidden. Āpastamba also says: "One should converse with women only as much as necessary; one should be gentle, peaceful, self-controlled, modest, and firm in resolve. Viṣṇu also says: "A student (*brahmacārī*) should avoid prepared salt. Prepared salt is salt from saline soil (*ūṣara*). Manu also says:
The sun should never set while he is in a village, nor should it ever rise while he is there;
for he who sleeps when the sun has already set, or when it has risen, is abandoned by the sun.
"One who does not perform penance shall be joined with great sin;

he may be shaven-headed, or wear matted hair, or else have only a single lock of matted hair on his crown. (127) Here, "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*) means devoid of even the top-knot (*śikhā*), according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "He may be shaven-headed or wear a top-knot. Kātyāyana also says:
"The student must have his hair shorn, including the top-knot, until the ritual bath;
however, he must maintain celibacy until the release from the body, provided that [celibacy] has not already been established.
This refers to the intention of the Chandogas. Thus, there is the statement of Bharata in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
With their tips recently severed by his teeth,
these blades of kuśa and kāśa grass shine like the reciters of the Sāmaveda at the foot of a banyan tree.
"One should sleep on the ground," so it was stated by Gautama. Regarding this, Yama states the specific rule:
"One should avoid beds, seats, and couches, as well as the cleaning of teeth. One should sleep alone upon *kuśa* grass and should never spill semen."
Manu also says:
"One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen;
for if one should spill semen out of desire, he destroys his own vow."

The *vrata* is celibacy (*brahmacarya*). He [the author] himself states that if one emits semen unintentionally, there is merely an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and no violation of the vow: "A twice-born student who has unintentionally emitted white semen in a dream, having bathed and worshipped the Sun, shall mutter the verse beginning with 'Again me' (*punar mām*). Thus it is said.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the duties of one who has been initiated [128]. Now follows the praise of the Veda.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—
all that has been, is, and will be— is established from the Veda."
Yājñavalkya also says: "For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for achieving the highest good, whether through sacrifices, austerities, or auspicious ritual acts."

Among the rituals such as sacrifices, the study of the Veda alone is the supreme, most excellent means for the twice-born to attain the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it is of the nature of austerity (*tapas*). Thus says Manu:
"The best of the twice-born, desiring to perform austerity, should always study the Veda;
even the study of the Veda is declared here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin."
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingernails,
who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.

The meaning is that he who studies his own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) daily according to his ability performs the highest, most excellent austerity even unto the tips of his fingernails. *Hey* is used here for emphasis. "Wearing a garland" means one adorned with garlands of ghee—that is, even if he is devoid of formal observances (*niyama*). Vyāsa also said: "Dharma is not known from any other source; it has shone forth from the Veda alone.
Therefore, one who seeks Dharma should study the Veda with every effort."
One who seeks the Dharma does so for the sake of knowing the Dharma. For this very reason, Manu says:
"The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
He also states the fruit for one who knows the Veda:
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Vedas burn away the defects of his own karma.
Likewise, that same [author] stated that all ritual actions of one devoid of the Vedas are fruitless:
"As a eunuch is fruitless with women, as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
and as a gift is fruitless for an ignorant person, so is a Brahmin who has not studied the Rigveda fruitless."
Vasiṣṭha also says: An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied— these three are mere bearers of names.

The meaning is that just as an elephant made of wood or similar materials is not fit for tasks such as battle, so too one who does not study is not fit for his own duties. For this very reason, he [the same author] says that such a person is not a Brāhmaṇa:
"One who has not studied the Ṛgveda is not a Brāhmaṇa; nor is he a merchant, nor a farmer;
nor is he one who serves Śūdras, nor a thief, nor a physician."
Manu also says:
"The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other matters,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his lineage."

Therefore, the meaning is that one must first engage in the study of the Veda. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states: "[130] 'One should not study another science without having studied the Veda, except for the Vedāṅgas and the Smṛtis. The intention is that even the Vedāṅgas and so forth are for the purpose of fully understanding the meaning of that [Veda]. Likewise, Hārīta says: "The Veda is indeed the knowledge of a Brāhmaṇa; the Vedāṅgas are for the purpose of its full comprehension. Thus ends the praise of the Veda in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follows the praise of what has been heard (the Veda).
Regarding this, Laghuvyāsa says:
"A wise man should not allow himself to be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Vedas;
for one who rests content with mere recitation sinks like a cow in the mud."
Also in the *Nirukta*: "This man is like a pillar, a mere bearer of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning. Laghuvyāsa also says:
"All study of the Vedas and all that of the Dharmaśāstra which is undertaken by one who does not know their meaning is like the threshing of chaff."
Just as a beast of burden does not partake in its fruit,
so a twice-born man who is ignorant of its meaning does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda.
The meaning is that he does not become a partaker of the fruits of Vedic rituals. For this very reason, that same [text] states his equality with a Śūdra:
"The Brahmin who, having studied according to rule, does not investigate the meaning of the Vedas, is equal to a Śūdra along with his lineage; he does not attain the status of a worthy recipient."
For this very reason, he [the same author] states that one should not perform even verbal worship toward these people:
"A wise man should not honor with even mere words those twice-born who are constantly intent on the mere recitation [of texts] but devoid of their meaning; he should treat them like beasts."

Therefore, the intention is that for one who has studied the Veda, an inquiry into its meaning is necessary. For this very reason, Dakṣa says: "First, the acquisition of the Veda; then, inquiry, practice, recitation, and the giving of it to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold."
"Reflection" (*vicāra*) refers to reflection upon the meaning of the Vedas. Laghuvyāsa also says:
"That which has been studied but is devoid of what has been heard (*śruta*) is of no use, just as [a son] is not [useful] who is not a true son;
however, even *śruta* alone is sufficient for one's ultimate liberation."

What, then, is the intention behind the term "combined"? He himself has said: "Just as knowledge and action joined together are declared to be for the sake of liberation, so too study joined with what has been heard is superior, and not alone."
"Even a small amount of learning that has been gathered and studied is superior to the mere recitation of the Vedas by one of the twice-born from among the four castes.
Thus Manu states the fruit for one who knows the meaning of the Vedas.
[132] One who knows the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras, in whatever stage of life he may dwell,
is fit for becoming one with Brahman even while remaining here in this world.
Hārīta also says:
A twice-born man who knows the meaning of the mantras, while muttering prayers, offering oblations, and likewise teaching, attains the heavenly world; but in the opposite case, he goes to hell.

In the *Nirukta* as well: "He who knows the meaning of all things attains prosperity; having shaken off his sins through knowledge, he goes to the heavenly realm (*nāka*). Manu, however, speaks of the scriptures that should be studied: "One should constantly examine those treatises which quickly increase the intellect, as well as grains that are beneficial, and likewise the Vedic *Nigamas*."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"The treatises on Dharma, as well as the treatises on grammar,
the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and whatever narratives there may be [should be studied]."
"And the conduct of the great-souled ones should always be heard.
Thus ends the praise of sacred learning in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the rule for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*).
Regarding this, Manu says: "The entire Veda, along with its secret portions (the Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule."

The secret is the *upaniṣad*. The meaning is that it is to be mastered and studied. And so says the Śruti: "[133] 'One's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied. This means that the branch [of the Veda] inherited through one's own family lineage is to be studied. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has come down through tradition, they should perform the ritual actions of that branch and likewise study that branch."

The intention is that by studying another Vedic branch (*śākhā*), one becomes a "branch-rebel" (*śākhāraṇḍa*). As he himself says: "He who, having completely abandoned his own branch, should resort to any one among the other branches even in part, is called a branch-rebel."
Regarding his fault, that very same [author] says: "He who,
having abandoned his own Vedic school, adopts that of another,
should be excluded from all ritual acts by virtuous men, just like a Śūdra."
He who abandons his own branch and dwells upon the branches of others is the destroyer of his lineage; he shall go to the Raurava hell.
"By him who has abandoned his own branch [of the Veda], Brahman itself is abandoned;
he should be known as a slayer of Brahman (brahmahā), perpetually censured by the virtuous. Thus says Lōkāksi as well.
He who abandons his own Vedic branch and adopts that of another should be excluded from offerings to the gods and ancestors by donors, just like a Śūdra.

[134] By this, he states that the study of another branch (śākhā) is not contradictory provided one does not abandon one's own branch. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having studied one's own branch, one may then study another branch.
Likewise, he also states another rule:
A Brāhmaṇa who has been consecrated by the sacraments belonging to a particular Vedic school should study that very school; by abandoning it, he becomes fallen.
Vasiṣṭha states that he who abandons the ritual acts prescribed in his own Vedic branch (*śākhā*) and performs those mentioned in another branch is also a "breaker of the branch" (*śākhāraṇḍa*):
"A wise man should never perform a ritual act prescribed in another branch;
one who performs what is prescribed in another branch is proclaimed a breaker of the branch."
The compiler, however, states the fault of this [position] as well:
"He who, having cast aside what is declared in his own branch of scripture, practices what is declared in another's branch,
makes the Sage non-authoritative and sinks into blinding darkness."
Kātyāyana also says:
"The fool who, abandoning what is based on his own Vedic school, desires to perform what is based on another's Vedic school, his exertion is in vain."

By this very fact—that one does not abandon the rites belonging to one's own branch—it is understood that resorting to another branch is not contradictory. That too has been stated by that same author:
"What is not prescribed in one's own branch, but is taught in another and is not contradictory, should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites. [135]
Now, with reference to the commencement of study, Manu says:
"The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable Oṃ,
and the Sāvitrī consisting of three feet, should be known as the mouth of Brahman."

*Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*—these are the three Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). *Tat savituḥ* is the Sāvitrī, which is the mouth of Brahman; that is to say, the beginning of the Veda. Gautama, however, states that five utterances should be employed: "The five utterances preceded by *Oṃ* and ending with *Satya*. This should be understood as to be performed daily. And so says Saṃvarta:
"One should first employ the Praṇava, immediately after that the Vyāhṛtis, then the recitation of the Sāvitrī, and thereafter one should begin the narrative."

The meaning is that this refers to the narrative currently under discussion. Furthermore, the utterance of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is to be understood as occurring after the three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). As Manu says:
"Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by purifiers [such as kuśa grass], and cleansed by three breath-restraints, one then becomes worthy of the syllable Om."

*Prākkūlān* means those whose tips point toward the east. *Pavitram* means purifying. Gautama stated: "The touching of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* grass. By "vital breaths," the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, are meant; the meaning is that one should touch them with *darbha* grass. The breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) were also mentioned by him: "Three breath-restraints consisting of fifteen *mātrās*" [136]. *Prāṇāyāma* is the restraint of the breath, which is to say, remaining without breathing. A *mātrā* is the duration of the pronunciation of a short syllable. By the phrase "consisting of fifteen *mātrās*," he indicates the exclusion of the rule "accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*. And this utterance of the *praṇava* must be performed even after having studied [the Veda]. Thus says Manu:
"One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*.
What is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away, and what is not followed by it falls apart.
He states another rule as well:
At the beginning and at the conclusion of Vedic recitation, one should always grasp the feet of the teacher.
Grasping the feet (*pādagrahaṇa*) means clasping them (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). As Aṅgiras says:
"When the daily recitation of the Vedas has commenced and when it has been concluded, [one should grasp the feet] of the teacher."
"And the formal greeting (upasaṃgrahaṇa) must be performed by one who has returned from traveling abroad.
Gautama, however, states a rule regarding the direction for the student: "The student [should sit] facing east or north, while [the teacher sits] to the south. Manu also says:
"One about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures, should face north."
With palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light-colored garments, and with senses subdued, he should be taught.

Because of the expression "when about to study," this sipping of water (ācamana) is an ancillary part of the act of study. He [the same author] also stated regarding the *brahmāñjali* (the student's gesture):
"Having joined the two hands together, one should study; for that is remembered as the *brahmāñjali*.
Regarding a specific detail here, Saṃvarta says:
[137] Then he should study the Veda while looking at the face of the teacher;
his hands should be joined together and placed above his knees.
By the phrase "gazing at the face of the guru," he states that the Veda must be studied from the mouth of the guru alone. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"That which is studied relying on a book, and not studied in the presence of a guru, does not shine in the midst of an assembly, like the offspring of an adulteress born to a woman."
Even in the presence of the guru, one should study only with his permission, for otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Laghuvyāsa:
"If a twice-born man takes up even a single ṛc, or a half-verse, or a quarter, or even a syllable, from another without permission, he incurs sin."
One who is guilty of stealing from a Brahmin falls into hell.
Likewise, one must not study even in the presence of a Śūdra. Regarding this, that same author says:
"That which is studied on forbidden days (anadhyāya) and that which is studied in the presence of a Śūdra..."
And that which is for the sake of receiving gifts is said to lead to hell.
Manu also says:
"One should not recite [the Veda] indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras;
nor, having finished his study of the Veda at the end of the night, should one go back to sleep while still exhausted."

"Indistinct" means lacking proper phonemes, accents, and so forth. "At the end of the night" means during the latter part of the night; the meaning is that even if one is exhausted from studying the Veda, one should not sleep again. Thus says Gautama: "Having studied during the latter part of the night, one should not go back to sleep" (GDh 1.59). Hārīta also says: "Having awakened during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, and having recited the *svādhyāya*, one should not go back to sleep. Nārada, however, speaks of the fault in studying without proper phonemes, accents, and so forth: "But he who studies what is deficient in hand-gestures (*hasta*), devoid of accents and phonemes..."
Consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, he enters a low womb.
But he who studies with haste, yet employing the correct accents and phonemes,
purified by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas, goes to the world of Brahmā.
And Laghuyāska says that this fruit of study and so forth belongs only to one who possesses the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *garbhādhāna*, and not to anyone else:
"The study of the Veda must be performed by twice-born men who possess the purificatory rites;
for a Śūdra, it may bear fruit [only through service], otherwise it is declared to be fruitless."
He has also stated other rules:
"The entire Veda must be mastered by celibate students who wear the girdle, the deerskin, and the staff, and who abide in the conduct of the true path."
Subsisting on alms and constantly devoted to the service of the guru,
the twice-born should perform the vow of Vedic study according to the prescribed rule until its completion.
*Śuśrūṣā* means service. Manu states its fruit:
[139] "Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water, even so does one who desires to serve obtain knowledge residing in the teacher."
Nārada stated the means for acquiring knowledge: "He who fears learning as one fears a debt, as one fears hell from over-satiety,
or as one fears ogresses from women— he acquires knowledge."
Just as a great anthill is built by insects with fine particles of dust, it is not there that strength or power is the cause; rather, diligent effort is the cause.
One should gradually acquire knowledge, gradually acquire wealth, and climb a mountain gradually.
*Tṛpti* means satiety. Furthermore, he [the author] stated those very causes for the removal of obstacles:
gambling, devotion to books, and attachment to drama.
Women, sloth, and sleep—these six are obstacles to learning.
*Śuśrūṣā* is the desire to hear; *tandrī* is laziness. Thus, Laghuvyāsa says that the absence of study is better than study devoid of the aforementioned rules:
"One who knows the Dharma should study even a single quarter-verse (*ṛkpāda*) according to the prescribed method, but never the four Vedas through an improper way."
Therefore, it is better for him to resort to silence than to the subversion of the Vedas;
for by subverting the Vedas, a Brahmin goes headfirst to hell.

Yama states the definition of one who violates the Vedas: "The wise call him a violator of the Vedas who, seeking wealth, gives [the Veda] to a twice-born man, or recites it according to improper rules, or to one who has not been initiated."

[140] On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "One who is grateful, free from malice, intelligent, pure, capable, and not envious— these, being virtuous, competent, trustworthy, and givers of their own wealth, are to be taught according to the Dharma."

One who is grateful is one who remembers a favor. One who is non-malicious is one who is free from offense. One who is intelligent is one possessed of retentive memory. One who is pure is one who is self-restrained. One who is healthy is one who is free from disease. One who is not envious is one whose nature is not to expose the faults of others. One who is virtuous is one who possesses good conduct. One who is capable is one who is able to perform service. One who is trustworthy is one who does not deceive. One who is "one's own" is a kinsman. One who provides wealth is one who gives for the sake of the teacher. These are to be taught according to dharma, that is, without exceeding the requirements of dharma. Now, it may be objected: "It is not fitting that one who provides wealth should be taught;
for [the scriptures state]: 'The taking of instruction from a hired person and the teaching of one who is hired—'"
This is because [teaching for wages] is listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

Do not say so; for it is only teaching preceded by the acceptance of a salary that is prohibited, as other forms of teaching do not conflict with it since they serve as a means of livelihood. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Where neither dharma nor wealth is found, nor even service of that kind..."
In that case, knowledge should not be spoken, just as a good seed [is not sown] in saline soil.
Yama also says:
Since there would be no acquisition of dharma, nor the attainment of learning or wealth, one should die with one's knowledge; one should not sow knowledge in barren soil.
But Manu says that even one who imparts knowledge may be taught:

"The son of a teacher, one who is eager to learn, one who imparts knowledge, one who is righteous, one who is pure, one who is trustworthy, one who is capable, one who provides wealth, one who is virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to dharma."
[141] Capable means competent to receive knowledge. A giver of knowledge is one who bestows learning. Nārada also said:
"Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, or by abundant wealth;
or else, knowledge is acquired through knowledge—a fourth means is not found."
By stating "these are to be taught," he implies that those who are envious and so forth are not to be taught. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Knowledge indeed approached the Brāhmaṇa, saying: 'Protect me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus may I be powerful.'"

"O Brahmin, teach me to that person whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy; to one who would not deceive you and who would not speak anything against you—to such a guardian of the treasure, O Brahmin, impart this. Here, *śevadhi* means a treasure or storehouse. Viṣṇu also says: "One should not cause one who has not been examined to sacrifice, nor to teach, nor to initiate. Yama states the specific rules regarding teaching:
Having risen constantly at dawn, and having first cleansed his teeth,
bathed, and offered oblations, a man should then engage in teaching his disciples.

Āpastamba also says: "[142] 'While lying down, one should avoid teaching, nor should one teach on that same bed upon which one lies down. Manu also says: "But when about to teach, the teacher, always alert, should say, 'Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, 'May there be a pause!'"

"One should take pleasure [in it]" means one should cause [the student] to desist from [negligence]. Furthermore, one who does not study with an undistracted mind should be disciplined through rebukes and other such means. To this effect, Gautama says: "Discipline of a pupil is by means of non-killing. "Discipline" (śiṣṭi) means instruction. "By means of non-killing" means without resorting to physical striking. The mention of the "pupil" is intended to include others as well, such as a wife or anyone else who is to be instructed. For this very reason, Manu states: "A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, they may be struck with a rope or a split bamboo cane."

And this [punishment] is to be understood as applicable when one is unable to discipline [the offender] through censure and other such means. For this very reason, Gautama states: "In case of inability, [one may use] thin cords made of rope or bamboo. The word "beating" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. Furthermore, that beating must not be administered on the head. Regarding this, Manu says:
"But it shall be on the back of the body, and never on the upper part;
for striking otherwise than this, one would incur the guilt of a thief."

Gautama states that one who strikes another with the hand or other means should be punished by the king: "[143] One who strikes with something other than a weapon should be punished by the king. Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha speaks of the fault of one who does not impart knowledge to a seeker: "For he who, having studied the science, does not bestow it upon a seeker, shall become unworthy of performing sacred rites. Yama also says: "If a teacher does not impart knowledge to a student who has resided with him for a year, the teacher takes upon himself the evil deeds of that student living with him."

And this [rule] refers to cases other than those involving a Śūdra disciple, because for him there is a prohibition against Vedic study. Thus Āpastamba says: "For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the formal initiation (upāyana), the study of the Veda, the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), and the fruit-bearing rituals. Furthermore, this study must be performed from a Brāhmaṇa alone, because only he has the authority to teach. Likewise Manu states: "The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; among them, the Brāhmaṇa shall be the teacher, and not the other two—this is the settled rule."
This refers to times when there is no distress. For in times of distress, even for Kṣatriyas and others, the rule for Vedic study is prescribed. Thus he [Manu] himself said:
"In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is ordained;
as well as following after him and serving the teacher for as long as the study lasts."

In this context, service consists merely in following [the teacher]. Its duration is intended to be exactly as long as the study lasts. Gautama also states: "In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa; [the duties are] following him and serving him; once the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes the guru. The mention of "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is intended to include other things such as jewels and so forth. For this very reason, Devala says:
"Jewels, water, women, knowledge, dharma, purity, well-spoken words, and various arts—these are to be accepted from anyone."
Manu also says:
"A person of faith should acquire pure knowledge even from a lowly person;
one should learn the highest dharma even from an outcaste, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family."
Nectar should be taken even from poison, a well-spoken word even from a child,
virtuous conduct even from an enemy, and gold even from filth.
Likewise, he himself has stated that the fruit of knowledge is also such:
"For a Brahmin, both austerity and knowledge bring about the supreme state of liberation;
through austerity one destroys impurity, and through knowledge one attains the immortal."
Devala also says:
"Knowledge, wealth, and austerity—these are the three splendors of embodied beings;
by means of these three, that which is beneficial both in this world and in the next is accomplished."
"Through knowledge, one attains stainless light; through the renunciation of wealth, the dawning of happiness;
and through austerity, pure prosperity—a human being may obtain these by means of the three.
Thus [it is said]. Yama states the fruit of the gift of knowledge:
[145] "A daughter and knowledge are equal to ten thousand well-trained draft-oxen yoked and employed for a worthy recipient.
Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
A cow is equal to a thousand [other gifts]; a bull is equal to ten cows;
a vehicle is equal to ten bulls; and a horse is equal to ten vehicles.
A maiden is equal to ten horses, and the gift of land is equal to that.
There is no gift superior to the gift of land; the gift of knowledge is even greater than that.
Manu also says: "Of all gifts whatsoever— water, food, cows, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter— the gift of the Veda is preeminent."
Saṃvarta also says:
"One who is well-disposed through the gift of knowledge is honored in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the section on the rules for study in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the Upākaraṇa ceremony;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"The commencement of the study of the chapters [of the Veda] takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa."
Or, in the absence of the medicinal herbs, [one should do so] on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

The term *adhyāyāḥ* refers to the Vedas, which are being studied. Regarding them, the ritual known as *upākarma* (the commencement of study) should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on the fifth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā or Hasta, provided that the herbs have appeared. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "Now follows the commencement of the courses of study (*adhyāya*), when the herbs have appeared—on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇā, or on the fifth [lunar day] under the asterism Hasta. However, when the herbs do not appear in the month of Śrāvaṇa, then it should be performed on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada. For this very reason, Śaunaka says: "That is called the *vārṣika* (the rainy-season rite). Vasiṣṭha also states: "Now follows the *upākarma* for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada. *Prauṣṭhapadī* is the full moon day of Bhādrapada. Regarding that, Vyāsa states a specific rule concerning the asterism Śravaṇā.
But by hearing [the Veda] under the asterism of Uttarāṣāḍhā,
the interruption of study committed during the year perishes at that very moment.
"One should perform that rite in conjunction with Dhaniṣṭhā during the month of Śrāvaṇa;

one should know that rite, known as the *upākaraṇa*, to be fruitful. However, Baudhāyana states that the *upākaraṇa* occurs specifically in Āṣāḍha: "Having performed the *upākaraṇa* on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or in Āṣāḍha, one should conclude [the term] on the full moon of Taiṣya or Māgha. *Taiṣī* refers to the full moon of the asterism Tiṣya. Having thus performed the *upākaraṇa* for the Vedas (*chandāṃsi*), one should study them for four and a half months during both fortnights. And so says Manu:
Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākarma*) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic hymns (*chandas*) for four and a half months.

Vasiṣṭha, being diligent and making an effort, states that one should study for five and a half months, saying: "For four and a half months, or five and a half months. This study is not contradictory even for a householder. For this very reason, Śaunaka, following the rule "one should study," says: "One who has returned home [from studentship] should follow the ritual of a student according to the rule; others, however, say that one may approach his wife. The term "others" refers to those who are still students.
Thus ends the section on the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and the conclusion (*utsarjana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"A twice-born man should perform the external dismissal (utsarjana) of the Vedas under the asterism Puṣya,
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon."

The phrase "on the first day of the bright fortnight in the forenoon" applies to both cases. Here, he who performs the *upākaraṇa* on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa should conclude his studies (*utsṛjet*) on the first day of the bright fortnight of the auspicious month (Śrāvaṇa) in the forenoon; the other, however, does so in Māgha. This is because that same author has stated: "One should study for four and a half months. Āpastamba, however, prescribes the conclusion (*utsarjana*) on the full moon of Taiṣa: "One should cease [studying] on the full moon of Taiṣa or under the asterism Rohiṇī. In this context, Rohiṇī must also be understood as belonging to the month of Taiṣa. Thus says Yājñavalkya:

[148] "On the Rohiṇī asterism in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the formal dismissal (utsarga) of the Vedic meters outside [the village] near water according to the rule. Regarding this, there is a Purāṇa:

"At the Upākarma and the Utsarga, having assembled at the proper time and fashioned the sages out of darbha grass, one should worship them and then offer libations. Having thus performed the Utsarga, one should thereafter study the Vedas during the bright fortnights (śuklapakṣa) and study the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights (kṛṣṇapakṣa). And so says Manu:
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should recite all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.

Vasiṣṭha also says: "From this point forward, one should study during the bright fortnights; however, one may at will study the Vedāṅgas. By using the word "at will," he indicates that the study of the auxiliary sciences (aṅga) is not prohibited even on days when study is otherwise forbidden. For this very reason, Manu states: "Regarding the accessories of the Veda and in the daily private recitation (svādhyāya), there is no restriction concerning days forbidden for study, nor indeed regarding the mantras for the fire-oblation (homa)."

The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are the instruments of the Veda. The daily private recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*) is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Kātyāyana states that these two acts are for the sake of preventing the exhaustion of the Vedic meters (*chandas*): "By that *upākarma* rite, performed annually according to rule along with the *utsarga* by the twice-born, there occurs a restoration of the Vedic meters."
[149] "Whatever rite is performed by the twice-born with Vedic meters that have not lost their potency,
even if they are engaged in play, that always becomes the cause of their success.
Thus ends the section on *utsarjana* (the ritual conclusion) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the days unfit for study,
Manu says:
"In the event of lightning, thunder, and rain, and when there is a falling of great meteors..."
Manu has declared that among these there is no interruption of study, even at the prescribed times.

*Stanitam* means the thundering of clouds. Regarding these phenomena beginning with lightning, the meaning is that for each one there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the same time on the following day, starting from the time the omen occurs. Furthermore, this triad beginning with lightning should be understood to apply at the time of twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*), except during the rainy season. As he himself says: "One should know that when these have appeared while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should know there is a suspension of study; and likewise when clouds are seen out of season."

*Prāduṣkaraṇa* means making manifest; by this term, the time of twilight (*saṃdhyakāla*) is indicated here. "Out of season" means other than during the rainy season. Now, following the rule that these occasions cause the suspension of Vedic study until the same time the next day (*ākālika*), Gautama states: "In the case of thunder, rain, and lightning, [the suspension lasts] when the sacred fires have been kindled. However, in the case of a meteor (*ulkā*), the suspension lasts for the entire day and night (*sarvadākālika*). Thus says Āpastamba: "In the case of a meteor and an earthquake (*agniyutpāta*), the suspension of all branches of knowledge lasts for the entire day and night. Regarding an earthquake, Manu also says: "When a village is plundered by thieves, or when there is a panic caused by fire..."
One should know that there is no time for study during all extraordinary portents.

Regarding the portents of rain, such as the falling of blood and so forth; for Vasiṣṭha likewise states: "In the case of rains of stones, blood, or dust, the suspension lasts until the same time the next day. However, when the triad of lightning and the others occurs simultaneously, there is no study for three days. For this very reason, Gautama says in his commentary on the rule for "three nights": "When there is a conjunction of rain, lightning, and thunder. This too should be understood to apply outside of the rainy season. As Āpastamba says: "Where lightning, thunder, and rain should coincide outside of the rainy season, there is no study for three days, or until the ground is dry, according to some; or, upon one or two of these occurring, the suspension lasts until the same time the next day. Bhāradvāja also says:
When there is a fire-omen, or when rain falls out of season, there shall be no study in the village;
