however, when there is lightning and thunder, the suspension lasts for three nights until the same time the next day.

But when there is lightning and thunder during the twilight in the rainy season itself, then there is a suspension of study as long as the light remains. And so says Manu: "When the fires have been kindled, however, at the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts; in other cases, it is as [regarding non-study] during the night as it is by day."

In the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*), when an omen or portent occurs, there is no study as long as the sun is visible; this means that during the day, study ceases until the sun sets. In the evening twilight (*aparasaṃdhyā*), however, it lasts as long as the stars are visible. During the remaining seasons, the meaning is that just as there is no study by day, so too there is none by night. Hārīta, however, states a specific rule regarding thunder: "If there is thunder at the evening twilight, they should not study during the night; but if there is thunder at the morning twilight, [the suspension lasts] for a full day and night. Āpastamba also says: "There is no study on a day accompanied by the evening twilight if there is thunder in the latter part of the night; according to some, [the suspension lasts] from the time of the thunder until midnight, and also when cattle are penned. The meaning is that if there is thunder—that is, the sound of rumbling—in the latter part of the night (*dahre*), which means in a small portion of the latter part of the night, there is no study for that day including the evening twilight. Manu, however, states that portents such as earthquakes (*nirghāta*) and the like cause a suspension of study lasting until the same time the next day (*ākālika*), even during the rainy season.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) lasting until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

*Nirghāta* is a specific kind of atmospheric sound. *Upasarjana* refers to the halo surrounding the luminaries, specifically the moon and the sun. Āpastamba, however, declares that there is a temporary suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) during halos and similar phenomena:
"In the event of twilight thunder, *nirghāta*, earthquakes, or the falling of meteors;
and after completing the Veda, or having studied the *Āraṇyaka* for a day and night."
"Day and night" means a full day and night (*ahorātra*). However, as it has been stated by Yama:
"Upon the falling of Indra’s banner, likewise upon the falling of a meteor, and similarly during an earthquake, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights."

Thus, this should be understood as referring to the occurrence of a meteor together with lightning. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "In the conjunction of a meteor and lightning, there is a three-night period [of impurity]. Regarding this, Manu states: "The new moon (amāvāsyā) destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) destroys the pupil;
the Aṣṭakā and the full moon (paurṇamāsī) destroy the Veda; therefore, one should avoid them."
And in this context, a period of non-study for a day and night is to be understood. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states in the continuation [of his text]:
"On the fifteenth and fourteenth [lunar days], on the eighth, during the birth of Rāhu, at the junctions of the seasons, after eating, and after accepting food offered at a Śrāddha."

"During Rāhu’s seizure," that is, during eclipses of the moon and sun; "during the junctions of the seasons," meaning at the transitions of spring and so forth, specifically on the first days (pratipad) of the lunar fortnights. Likewise, there is the statement of Hanumān in the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"By her very nature she is slender-limbed, and she has been emaciated by separation from you;
she has become as thin as the knowledge of one who practices recitation on the first day of the lunar fortnight."
Hārīta also says: "On the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnights, on the two festival days (parvan), on the day after a holiday,
on the day of the holiday itself, and during the night— one should never study."
Also in another Smṛti:
"One should not study during the evening of the thirteenth lunar day, nor on the first days [of the fortnights].

The term *śrāddhika* refers to that which is connected with a *śrāddha*. The meaning is that after eating such food or receiving it as a gift, there is a suspension of study for two nights. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
[153] Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, edible foods, or whatever else may be offered at a śrāddha,
Brahmins are traditionally enjoined to observe periods of non-study (anadhyāya).

And this [rule] refers to cases other than the *ekoddiṣṭa* (the offering for a single deceased person), because in that case a three-night period is prescribed. Thus says Manu: "Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa*, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the impurity caused by a king or by Rāhu (an eclipse)."

*Ketana* means an invitation. Regarding the sighting of Rāhu, Śaṅkha also states: "Upon the sighting of Rāhu, upon the falling of Indra’s banner, and when a teacher has died, there is a three-night [period of suspension]. Gautama, however, declares it to be until the same time the next day (*ākālika*): "The [periods of suspension] caused by a thunderclap, an earthquake, and the sighting of Rāhu last until the same time [the next day]. Thus, one should understand that regarding the sighting of Rāhu, there is an option between three nights and one day and night (*ahorātra*). Yājñavalkya also states a three-night period for the death of a teacher: "There is no study for three days in the case of deaths among pupils, officiating priests, teachers, and kinsmen."

In this context, the *guru* refers to the *ācārya*, not the biological father, because for the latter a ten-day period is prescribed. For this very reason, "relatives" (*bāndhava*) should also be understood as those who are not *sapiṇḍas*. Vasiṣṭha, however, prescribes a single day and night even for students, officiating priests, and others: "For the son of an *ācārya*, a student, and a wife, there is impurity for a day and night; likewise for officiating priests and blood relations (*yonisaṃbandha*). Blood relations refer to maternal uncles and the like. The same should be understood regarding a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*). Therefore, following the rule for a day and night, Gobhila states: "When a fellow student has died, and also when one's own king [has died]."

However, in the case of the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites, a three-night period should be understood [as the rule]. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states regarding the observance for three days:

"At the *upākarma* and the *utsarjana*, as well as when a *śrotriya* of one's own *śākhā* [is present]. Manu, however, states regarding the *utsarjana*, with options: a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night), one day, or three nights.
Having thus performed the *utsarjana* of the Vedic meters outside [the sacred fire] according to the scriptures,
one should cease [recitation] for a night with two days (a *pakṣiṇī*) or for a single day and night.

"At the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, a three-night suspension [of study] is prescribed. A night that has parts of two days on either side is called *pakṣiṇī*. The application of these terms, such as *pakṣiṇī* and so forth, is determined according to their respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Āpastamba, however, having begun with the *upākaraṇa*, states that there is no study during the evening (*pradoṣa*) for a month: "Having performed the *upākarma* on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the evening for a month. In that regard, one should not study from the thirteenth day onwards, even beyond the month. Thus says the Purāṇa:
One who desires intelligence should not remember nor recite [the name] on the thirteenth day, especially on the seventh, and on the fourth, during the evening twilights.
In this regard, Prajāpati says:

One should not study during the sixth and the twelfth lunar days, nor when it is less than half a nāḍikā before midnight; nor during the evening twilight, nor during the third lunar day for nine nāḍikās.

[155] “Less than half a *nāḍikā* at midnight” means diminished by one *ghaṭikā* from midnight. “Nine *nāḍikās* during the night” is the ellipsis to be supplied. “At *pradoṣa*” means during the first watch (*prahara*) of the night. As Uśanas says: “On the thirteenth day, one should not study during the first four *muhūrtas*. Dakṣa states that there is no study during the two middle watches of the night: “One should spend the first and last watches of the night in the practice of the Vedas; however, by sleeping during the two middle watches, one is fit for becoming Brahman.”
On this point, Śātātapa says:
"On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, during the Aṣṭakās, during a great festival,
at nightfall on the thirteenth, the eighth, and also on the first day."

During great festivals, such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the like, there are also the *aṣṭakā* rites mentioned by Paiṭhīnasi: "The three *aṣṭakās* occur in the dark fortnights beginning with Pauṣa; some say they begin with Mārgaśīrṣa. The full moon joined with the asterism Puṣya is *pauṣī*; the month in which that occurs is *pauṣa*. Śaunaka, however, states that the three *aṣṭakās* occur in the dark fortnights of both Hemanta and Śiśira: "The *aṣṭakās* are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of Hemanta and Śiśira. And in this regard, a cessation of Vedic study (*anadhyayana*) for a day and night should be understood to apply. Thus says Manu:
"On the *aṣṭakā* days, as well as on the nights at the ends of the seasons, there is [suspension of study] for a day and a night.

Gautama also says: "The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha; the three *aṣṭakās*; and for three nights. This means that starting from the aforementioned full moon days, there is a three-night suspension; likewise, for the three *aṣṭakās* beginning with the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*), there is also a three-night suspension of study. The same should be understood regarding the *mahānavamī* and other such occasions. And so says the Purāṇa:
"On the *mahānavamī*, on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), and on the *bharaṇī* constellation during a great lunar day..."
Likewise, on the third day of the lunar fortnight known as Akṣaya-tṛtīyā, a wise man should not teach his disciples.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, known as Rathasaptamī, one should avoid teaching;
likewise, one should avoid it at the time of anointing the body and bathing.
Upon seeing a corpse being carried along on the ground, O best of the twice-born,
or during unseasonable thunder and the like, or upon the impurity caused by another's death and so forth;
A wise man should observe a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during eclipses and similar occasions;

on the *Mahānavamī* (the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja); on the *Mahādvādaśī* (the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika); on the *Mahābharaṇī*, which is the day immediately following the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada; on the *Akṣayatṛtīyā* (the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha); and on the one called *Ratha*, the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha. It is also stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"During the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and on the days of Hari’s lying down (*śayana*) and awakening (*bodhana*)."
However, one must observe a suspension of study on the anniversaries of Manu and others, as well as on the beginnings of the Yugas.
Also in another Purāṇa: "On all the beginnings of the Yugas, as well as on the beginnings of the Manvantaras,
one should observe non-study (anadhyāya), as well as on any lunar day that has a prefix."
[157] The beginnings of the Manvantaras, however, are shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, likewise the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of the month of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada."
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh of Puṣya,
the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and likewise the seventh of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
and the fifteenth days of the bright fortnights of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha.
"And these, beginning with Manvantara and others, cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
Thus it is said. The beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*) should also be understood as they are described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, and that ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika..."
"On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the fifteenth day of Māgha. Thus [it is said].

Gautama, however, declares a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) upon the passing of a dog: "In the case of a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat, there shall be a three-day fast and a separation from one's residence. Here, "fasting" (*upavāsa*) refers to expiation (*prāyaścitta*), while "separation from residence" (*vipravāsa*) means the absence from one's dwelling. That [separation] lasts for exactly three nights, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Hārīta which follows the list of the dog, jackal, cat, snake, mongoose, and mouse: "If these very animals pass between those who are studying, there shall be a three-night fast and one should remain separated for three days. By this, it is effectively stated that there is a three-day suspension of study. Vasiṣṭha, however, prescribes a fast of one day and night: "But in the case of a dog, a cat, a mongoose, or a swift-moving animal, it is for a day and night. The word "non-eating" (*abhojana*) is to be supplied as the remainder, since that alone is the subject under discussion. And this should be understood to apply when one is unable to observe the three-night fast. Regarding the passage of a cat, Uśanas states a specific expiation: "If a cat passes between, however, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and fast for three days. Āpastamba, on the other hand, prescribes six months of non-study in the event of an encounter with a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapāka: "In the case of a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapāka, or a hare, [the suspension lasts] for six months. In the case of an elephant or a tiger, it should be understood that the period is one year. He himself says: "If it is an elephant, [the suspension lasts] for a year; likewise for a tiger. Manu, however, declares a suspension of study for a day and night upon the passage of domestic animals and the like.
If animals, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, mongooses,
or the like pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night.
Yājñavalkya also says: "When the interval is occupied by a dog, a frog, a mongoose, a snake, a cat, or a rat,
as well as during the fall or the rise of Indra, one must fast for a day and a night."

[159] The meaning is: "the time characterized by the rising of Indra. Regarding this, Garga states the time for the rising of Indra: "On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the king should raise up Indra under the asterisms of Viśva (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Śravaṇa, or Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā)."

By the word *viśva*, the lunar mansion *uttarāṣāḍhā*, which has the Viśvedevas as its deity, is denoted; by the word *vāsava*, the lunar mansion *dhaniṣṭhā*, which has the Vasus as its deity, is denoted. The fall of Śakra also occurs in that very month. Thus says the Purāṇa:
"O King, in the month of Bhādrapada, there is the falling of Indra’s staff.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
In the sound of a dog, a jackal, a donkey, an owl, a lute, or one who is distressed;

*kroṣṭṛ* means a jackal (*sṛgāla*); *ulūka* means an owl (*ghūka*); *vāṇa* means a lute (*vīṇā*), as seen in the *Mahāvrata* [section] where it says, "the *vāṇa* has a hundred strings"; *ārta* means one who is suffering. When the sound or cry of these is heard, one should not study for that duration, because it has been stated by that very same [author]: "They know these to be temporary [obstacles]. Manu also says: "In mist and in the sound of a lute, during both twilights..."

The same should be understood regarding the sound of kettledrums and other such instruments, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the sounds of dogs, kettledrums, clay drums, and carts... (*vānabherīmṛdaṅgagardārtaśabdeṣu*). Here, *garda* means a cart. However, in the case of the sound of the *Sāman*, there is no suspension of study for the *Ṛc* and *Yajus* alone, but not for anything else. As Manu says: "One should never recite the *Ṛc* and *Yajus* while the sound of the *Sāman* is heard. Yama also says:
"When the Sāman-chant is being sung, the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda are [heard], and when the wind blows excessively.
Regarding this, Manu states the reason:
"The Ṛgveda has the gods as its presiding deity; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans."
"The Sāman is remembered as belonging to the ancestors (pitrya); therefore, its sound is impure.

Thus, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) for the sound of the *mṛdaṅga* drum and similar instruments, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "And there is a suspension of the study of the Sāmans in another branch [of the Veda]. The same should be understood to apply when one is in the vicinity of impure things and so forth. And likewise Yājñavalkya says:
"In the vicinity of impure matter, a corpse, a Śūdra, an outcaste (*antya*), a cremation ground, or a fallen person..."

"In the vicinity" means nearby. Viṣṇu also states: "One should not study in the presence of a Śūdra or an outcaste, nor in a temple, a cremation ground, at a crossroads, or on a highway; nor near water, nor with one's feet placed upon a seat, nor when one has vomited, nor when one has purged, nor while suffering from indigestion. Manu also says: "[161] One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after putting on a garment worn during sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a śrāddha ceremony."
"Ante" means near. "Maithuna-vāsaḥ" means having put on that garment with which sexual intercourse was performed; this refers specifically to an unwashed garment. For this very reason, Yama says:
"For when sexual intercourse has been performed, [one must remain so] even while wearing an unwashed garment."

Vasiṣṭha also states: "On a bed free from sexual intercourse, with a garment free from sexual intercourse and unwashed, and when one has vomited within a village. Regarding vomiting, however, there is a cessation of study for a day and night, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the case of vomiting, at a Śrāddha, and upon eating at a sacrifice to humans (manuṣyayajña), there is a cessation for a day and night. Alternatively, one may recite after consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Āpastamba says: "Having vomited, [one should wait] until the end of sleep, or having consumed clarified butter. "Until the end of sleep" means until sunrise. Manu, however, says that one should not recite even in a village [if these conditions apply].
For those who desire perfection in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as wherever a foul odor is present.

Those who have mastered the Vedas desire proficiency in Dharma; others desire proficiency in secular knowledge (*vidyā*). By this, he states that for those desiring proficiency in secular knowledge, study in villages is not prohibited. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "In cities, at will, on ground sprinkled with cow-dung or swept clean. For this same reason, Manu also says:
"In a village where a corpse is present, in the vicinity of a *vṛṣala*, during weeping, and in a crowd of people, there is no study."

Vasiṣṭha also says: "During the twilights, [one should not study] in a place where a corpse is present or where a *divākīrtya* is present. A *divākīrtya* is a *caṇḍāla*. The meaning is that one should not study in a village where a *caṇḍāla* resides. This should also be understood to apply to crossroads and similar locations. Thus Pracetas states: "At crossroads, on highways, on carriage roads, in gardens, and near a deity"—the word "one should study" is to be supplied. Gautama also says: "In a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, on a highway, or during impurity. Regarding the cremation ground, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "In a cremation ground, there is no suspension of study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from all sides; nor is there a suspension when the village is settled by means of fields. A *śūdra* and an outcast (*patita*) are like a cremation ground. Some say this applies to a common house. However, in the case of a *śūdra*, there is suspension of study only while looking at her or being looked at by her. Likewise, one should not study while mounted on a horse. And so Manu says:

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor in a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor while sitting with the knees bound by a cloth; nor after eating meat, nor food provided during a period of birth-impurity.

[163] “Neither during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle; neither immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor during the period of birth-impurity. Thus it is said. *Iriṇa* means saline or barren soil. *Prauḍhapāda* refers to one whose feet are placed upon a seat or similar object. *Avasakthikā* is the binding of the knees and the middle of the thighs with cloth or other materials. “Immediately after eating” means as long as the hands are still wet. And so says Yājñavalkya:
In an impure place, or when one is personally impure; during a flash of lightning, a clap of thunder, or a downpour of rain;
after eating; with wet feet; while inside water; at midnight; or during an excessively violent wind.
"Repetition" (*saṃplava*) means arising again and again. Manu also says:
"In the midst of water, at midnight, upon voiding excrement or urine, and while eating the remains of a *śrāddha* meal—one should not even mentally contemplate [the Veda]."

Bodhāyana also states: "There is no study even when death or birth occurs [to oneself] in one's mind. Manu, however, says that one must not study even during dust-storms and the like: "During a dust-storm, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, and likewise when dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking, a twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] in a group."
The appearance of light everywhere is considered a "burning of the quarters" (digdāha). Yājñavalkya also states:

"During a rain of dust, a burning of the quarters, at the twilights, in mist, during times of fear, while running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at one's house [these are occasions for immediate purification]."

"Running" means going quickly. When a learned person (*śiṣṭa*) who possesses the aforementioned characteristics has arrived at one's house, the meaning is that there is a suspension of study until he grants permission. And so says Yama:
"Upon seeing a guest who has arrived, a wise man should certainly not study;
once he has given his permission, one may study according to the ancient tradition."
Manu also says:
"And having informed the guest, one may eat when the wind is blowing violently,
or when blood has flowed from the body due to a wound inflicted by a weapon."

Likewise, Gautama declares that there is no study even when clouds appear during the non-seasonal period: "And when clouds appear outside the rainy season. *Abhra* means a water-bearing cloud. In the same way, this should also be understood regarding the shade of specific trees. And so says Yama:
"One should never study in the shade of the *śleṣmātaka*, the *śālmali*, the *madhūka*, nor of the *kovidāra* and the *kapittha*."
Furthermore, as stated by Manu: "A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two things while reciting: an impure place for study and an impure self."

This refers to the study of the *brahmayajña*. Thus says the Śruti: "For this very sacrifice, there are two occasions when study is suspended: when one is impure from eating, and when the place is [impure]. For this very reason, Manu states:

"In the case of the Vedas' auxiliary sciences (*vedopakaraṇa*), in the daily private recitation (*svādhyāya*), and indeed in the daily oblations and mantras, there is no restriction regarding days when study is otherwise suspended. [165]

The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are the means for the Veda. Constant private recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*) is that which pertains to the *brahmayajña*. Śaunaka also says: "In the case of constant recitation, optional recitation, a sacrificial rite (*kratu*), or even a complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), there is no prohibition of study for the Vedas; it is traditionally taught that such a prohibition applies only to the initial acquisition [of the text]."
Having spoken thus, Likhita stated the fault of studying during improper times:
"Those periods declared as unfit for study are the vulnerabilities of Brahmins;
through these vulnerabilities, the sacred knowledge (brahman) that has been acquired by a Brahmin flows away."
At that time, the Rākṣasas take away his prosperity, sacred knowledge, fame, and strength—
taking all of these— and depart, leaving behind only the desired fruit.
Yama also says:
"I cut short the life, wisdom, cattle,
and intelligence of one who recites the Veda during improper times, as well as his merit."
Also in the dialogue between Indra and Nārada:
"O Śakra, did you not go to those who study during forbidden times—
those evil-minded Asuras, slayers of Brahmins, and defilers of the Veda?"
"For if Vedic study is performed during periods when study is forbidden, it is as if it were not studied at all;
they do not go to heaven after death—O Nārada, are they not destroyed?
Thus ends the section on "Prohibited Times for Study" (*anadhyāya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the limit of time for the period of studentship.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "[166] For one who has been initiated, there is residence as a *brahmacārin* in the teacher’s family for forty-eight years; or for three-quarters less, or for half, or for three [years]. Likewise, Devala says: "Beyond this, one should undertake the practice of Vedic vows for forty-eight years; if incapable, then for twenty-four years or twelve years. This too refers to each individual Veda. As Bodhāyana says: "The ancient Vedic *brahmacarya* lasts forty-eight years, or twenty-four, or twelve, for each Veda. Yama also [says the same].
He should dwell for twelve years, or indeed twenty-four, or thirty-six years; he should observe the vow for each Veda.
Manu, however, states that the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts until the Veda has been mastered:
"The vow for the three Vedas is to be observed under a teacher for thirty-six years,
or for half that time, or for a quarter, or indeed until [the Veda] has been grasped."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Traivedika" refers to that which pertains to the three Vedas, namely the collection known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. That [period of study] should be thirty-six years. Thus, it is stated that one should observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years for each Veda. According to the "half" (*ardhika*) view, it is six years for each Veda; according to the "quarter" (*pādika*) view, it is only three. Yājñavalkya also says: "Celibacy for each Veda is twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until [the Veda] is mastered, and the tonsure ceremony (*keśānta*) occurs at the sixteenth year."
[167] The *keśānta* is the ritual known as *godāna*. The meaning is that this should be performed in the sixteenth year. And this refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa; as Manu says:
"The *keśānta* is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year, for the Kṣatriya in the twenty-second, and for the Vaiśya two years after that."

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, [the section on] the limit of the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) and the twofold nature of the student (*brahmacārin*). There are two kinds of students: the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*). Among these, the duties of the temporary student have been stated. Now, the duties of the lifelong student are being declared. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
A lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), however, shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in the absence of the teacher, in the presence of the teacher's son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire.

A *naiṣṭhika* is one who, according to the rule prescribed for the *upakurvāṇa*, reaches the end—that is, the time of death—without returning home. He should dwell in the presence of his teacher and others; the meaning is that he does not undergo the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning). And here, the phrase "in the absence of that" applies everywhere. Thus, it is stated that in the absence of a wife, he should tend the sacred fire (*agni*). This refers to a situation where there is no *sapiṇḍa* relative. As Manu says:

"But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with virtues, or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a *sapiṇḍa*, as one would toward the teacher."
When these are not available, one who is capable of standing, sitting,
and moving about may perfect his own body by performing service to the sacred fire.

The meaning is that he possesses standing, sitting, and moving about, by resorting to specific times for rising, sitting, and walking. This also refers to the case of a learned (*anūcāna*) Brāhmaṇa teacher and the like, because otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus he himself says: "A disciple desiring the unsurpassed goal should not dwell permanently with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned."
Regarding the duties for one dwelling there, Bṛhaspati said:
"I have thus prescribed this vow for the *upakurvāṇaka* (the student who returns home);
now I shall explain briefly that of the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong student)."

"Performing the twilight rituals, the fire sacrifice, Vedic study, begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and practicing compassion—by doing these until death as a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), one shall attain the world of Brahmā. Thus it is said.

Vasiṣṭha also says: "Restraining his speech, eating only on the fourth, sixth, and eighth days, he should practice begging for alms. Dependent upon his guru, wearing matted hair—or matted locks with a single tuft—he should follow the guru when he walks, and stay behind him; if the guru is seated, he should remain standing, and if the guru is lying down, he should remain seated in attendance. He should study only when summoned, and having offered everything he has obtained, he should eat only with the guru’s permission. He should avoid beds, sleeping on them, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, anointing the body, shoes, and umbrellas. He should stand during the day and sit at night. Three times a day he should approach water. The meaning is that he should bathe three times a day, performing the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day (*triṣavaṇa*). Devala also says: "[169] Wearing the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), a rosary, a wooden staff, a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and a girdle of muñja grass; eating once a day; bathing repeatedly; performing the *agnihotra* and twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) twice daily; not letting the hair, beard, nails, skin, scent, garlands, oils, collyrium, ointments, dress, ornaments, umbrella, shoes, or vehicles become neglected; and avoiding jumping over, swimming across, running, medical treatment, astrology, palmistry, architecture, auspicious rites, nourishing rites, pacifying rites, music, joining assemblies, making pacts, binding, crafts, writing, artisan work, house-building, field-work, dealing with goods, wealth, grain, or household items, gambling, legal disputes, knowing the state of others' minds, play, laughter, affectionate dalliance, deception, causing wonder, mockery, quarreling, arrogance, lamentation, weeping, and rubbing the feet. Hārīta, however, states the rule for the service of the fire: "Having gathered sacrificial fuel, one should serve the fire through sweeping, smearing, kindling, arranging, adding fuel, circumambulating with fire, walking around, standing in attendance, offering oblations, chanting hymns, prostrating, and so forth. One should not step over the fire, nor drag it with one's feet, nor blow upon it with the mouth. One should not hold water and fire simultaneously. One who has not digested his food or who is seeking food should not give [fuel]; while giving fuel, one should not step over it, nor spit. Day after day, one should kindle the fire with various offerings of cooked rice and oblations related to Agni. Having addressed [the fire], one may go; having returned, one should report [what was done]. Manu describes the fruit for one who acts in this manner: [Manu 2.88–91] "One should always wear a lower garment and an upper garment, be clean, and have trimmed nails and hair. One should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot, and be devoted to the study of the Veda. One should not sleep on a bed, nor wash the feet, nor apply collyrium, nor use perfumes, garlands, or ointments. One should avoid dancing, singing, playing musical instruments, and other such amusements. One should not look at a naked woman, nor at an impure person, nor at a mixture of castes, nor at a dog, nor at a person of low birth. One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor over the shadow of a Brahmin, nor over urine, nor over excrement, nor over a fire, nor over a woman in her courses. One should not eat with one's wife, nor look at her while she is eating, nor at her while she is yawning, laughing, or weeping, nor at her while she is uncovered. One should not teach the Veda while lying down, nor while seated on a high seat, nor while wearing shoes, nor while holding an umbrella, nor while wearing a turban, nor while wearing a wreath, nor while anointed with oil, nor while engaged in business, nor while intoxicated, nor while distressed, nor while naked, nor while wearing wet clothes, nor while standing in water, nor while facing the south, nor while wearing a single garment, nor while the head is covered, nor while seated on a chair, nor while leaning against a pillar, nor while standing, nor while walking, nor while riding in a vehicle, nor while in a boat, nor while on a camel, nor while on a donkey, nor while on a tree, nor while on a mountain, nor while on a roof, nor while on a stone, nor while on a mat of grass, nor while on a wooden plank, nor while on a hide, nor while on a swing, nor while on a cot, nor while on a litter, nor while on a palanquin, nor while on a horse, nor while on an elephant, nor while on a chariot, nor while on a ship, nor while on a cloud, nor while on a snake, nor while on a crow, nor while on a dog, nor while on a jackal, nor while on a cat, nor while on a mouse, nor while on a rat, nor while on a lizard, nor while on a frog, nor while on a bird, nor while on a monkey, nor while on a goat, nor while on a sheep, nor while on a cow, nor while on a bull, nor while on a buffalo, nor while on a boar, nor while on a pig, nor while on a carnivorous animal, nor while on a beast of prey, nor while on a scavenger, nor while on a corpse, nor while on a funeral pyre, nor while on a cremation ground, nor while on a crossroads, nor while on a place where four paths meet, nor while on a place where three paths meet, nor while on a place where two paths meet, nor while on a place where many paths meet, nor while on a place where there is a ditch, nor while on a place where there is a well, nor while on a place where there is a pond, nor while on a place where there is a lake, nor while on a place where there is a river, nor while on a place where there is a sea, nor while on a place where there is a forest, nor while on a place where there is a mountain, nor while on a place where there is a cave, nor while on a place where there is a thicket, nor while on a place where there is a swamp, nor while on a place where there is a desert, nor while on a place where there is a snowfield, nor while on a place where there is a mist, nor while on a place where there is a whirlwind, nor while on a place where there is a thunderstorm, nor while on a place where there is lightning, nor while on a place where there is a rainbow, nor while on a place where there is a halo around the sun or moon, nor while on a place where there is a comet, nor while on a place where there is a meteor, nor while on a place where there is a falling star, nor while on a place where there is a portentous sound, nor while on a place where there is a portentous light, nor while on a place where there is a portentous smell, nor while on a place where there is a portentous taste, nor while on a place where there is a portentous touch, nor while on a place where there is a portentous dream, nor while on a place where there is a portentous thought, nor while on a place where there is a portentous action, nor while on a place where there is a portentous result. One should not speak ill of anyone, nor should one strike anyone, nor should one cause anyone to suffer. One should not be arrogant, nor should one be deceitful, nor should one be malicious, nor should one be envious, nor should one be greedy, nor should one be angry, nor should one be proud, nor should one be conceited, nor should one be boastful, nor should one be slanderous, nor should one be calumnious, nor should one be treacherous, nor should one be ungrateful, nor should one be faithless, nor should one be dishonest, nor should one be untruthful, nor should one be double-tongued, nor should one be crafty, nor should one be cunning, nor should one be hypocritical, nor should one be fickle, nor should one be unstable, nor should one be restless, nor should one be distracted, nor should one be negligent, nor should one be lazy, nor should one be indolent, nor should one be procrastinating, nor should one be forgetful, nor should one be confused, nor should one be deluded, nor should one be bewildered, nor should one be infatuated, nor should one be obsessed, nor should one be addicted, nor should one be enslaved by passion, nor should one be dominated by hatred, nor should one be overcome by greed, nor should one be possessed by pride, nor should one be gripped by envy, nor should one be seized by malice, nor should one be held captive by jealousy, nor should one be bound by attachment, nor should one be fettered by aversion, nor should one be shackled by fear, nor should one be
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes straightway to the eternal abode of Brahmā.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One who purifies the body according to this rule, having conquered the senses,
attains the world of Brahman and is not born again in this world."
Yama also says:
"Those who, until the fall of the body, live as perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas),
go to the abode of Brahman and are not born again on earth."
As for that which was stated by Hārīta:
"Those Brahmins who practice celibacy become immortal after death."

Thus, this refers to the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate student) who knows Brahman, according to the Śruti: "All these [others] attain worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality. All these four types of *āśramins*, while performing their duties, attain worlds of merit. However, he among them who is "established in Brahman"—that is, one who is fixed in Brahman—attains the fruit of immortality, characterized by non-return. And Viṣṇu states that this status of being a *naiṣṭhika* is permanent for those such as the hunchbacked and others:
"For the hunchbacked, the dwarf, the congenitally blind, the impotent, the lame, the distressed, and the diseased..."
[171] Their observance of vows shall continue for as long as they live, without any share of inheritance.
"Without a share" means due to the absence of a share. The author of the *Saṃgraha* also states:

"Because the lame and others have no share and lack capacity according to the scriptures, they must necessarily be perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika*), owing to their lack of entitlement to ritual acts."
[Objection: If that is so, then let the state of a perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhikatva) belong only to those such as the hunchbacked woman and others, and not to others. [Reply: Not so;
for if he should desire a lifelong residence in the family of the teacher, he should attend upon him diligently until the liberation of the body.

This is because it contradicts the *Anuvacana* which establishes that [the state of being a lifelong student] is optional (*pākṣikatva*). For there is no such thing as an optional lifelong studentship for those who are hunchbacked and so forth. [Objection: But if others also possess the status of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhikatva*), then the Vedic injunction prescribing the duties of a householder—"One should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives"—would be sublated. [Reply: Not so. Since the status of a lifelong student is optional, there remains another scope [for the injunction]. For this injunction regarding "as long as one lives" applies to those who, under the influence of passion for women, desire only the state of a householder; thus, there is no contradiction. And so says Jābāli: "A householder may enter the forest. If he should desire only the household life, then he should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as he lives. And this is logical; otherwise, passages such as "He may enter whichever [stage] he desires, or else he may renounce even from the state of a student" would be sublated. [Objection: Let the Smṛti-based status of a lifelong student simply be sublated by the Śruti-based *Agnihotra* and other rites. [Reply: Not so. For that too is based on the same Śruti passage: "The student who dwells in the teacher's family is the second [type]; he should spend his entire life in the teacher's family," and thus there is no difference. Therefore, it is impossible to deny the twofold nature of the student. And Hārīta has said: "The student is of two kinds: the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*). [Objection: If there are two types of students, then the statement of Āpastamba and others that "there are four stages of life" (*āśrama*) would be sublated. [Reply: Not so. Just as the obligatory and optional *Agnihotra* are not distinct despite a difference in intention (*saṃkalpa*), these two are established as non-different in this way. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:

"The second is the *naiṣṭhika*, who remains in that very same stage of life (*āśrama*). By stating "in that very same stage of life," he indicates the extension (*atideśa*) of its duties [to the *naiṣṭhika*]. For this very reason, Gautama says: "In that regard, what was stated for the *brahmacārin* [applies]. The meaning is that whatever was stated in the section concerning the *upakurvāṇa*—such as the kindling of the sacred fire, the practice of begging for alms, and so forth—that also pertains to the *naiṣṭhika*.
Thus ends the section on the *brahmacārin* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the combination and the alternative of the stages of life (*āśrama*), Manu speaks concerning their combination:
"The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and likewise the ascetic (*yati*)."
These four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.

The meaning is that they are dependent on the householder, being produced from him. By the word "gradually," he indicates that the reverse order of the stages of life (*āśrama*) is prohibited. For this very reason, Dakṣa says: "There may be the natural order (*ānulomya*) for the three [stages], but the reverse order (*prātilomya*) does not exist;
there is no greater evildoer than one who produces offspring through the reverse order."
For this very reason, the same author states that one whose wife has died, being unable to marry again, must not become a perpetual celibate (*brahmacārin*):
"He who, having entered the householder stage of life, should again become a celibate student— neither a forest-dweller nor an ascetic— he is excluded from all stages of life."

Āpastamba also states the very same combination: "There are four stages of life: that of the householder, the teacher’s household, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. By conducting oneself with undistracted focus in all of these according to the instructions, one attains security. It is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"O son, being vigilant, do not fall into a wrong path by means of [the duties of] the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant."

The *Jābāli-śruti*, however, speaks of the combination of four, three, or two stages: "Having completed the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from studentship, or from the household, or from the forest. Manu, on the other hand, sets forth a temporal arrangement for the complete combination of all stages: "Having lived the first quarter of his life with the teacher, the twice-born man, having taken a wife, should dwell in the home during the second quarter of his life."
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
The meaning is that one-fourth of the lifespan prescribed by the Vedic scripture, "Man has a life of a hundred years," is twenty-five years. Hārīta states the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
"He who indeed serves the stages of life according to this rule, having conquered all worlds, is fit for the world of Brahman."

As for that which was stated by Gautama: "The teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*), because the householder’s state (*gārhasthya*) is directly enjoined," that is intended to establish the preeminence of the householder’s state; for there is no distinction, as the others are also established by direct Vedic injunctions such as, "Having completed his studenthood (*brahmacarya*), he should become a householder; having been a householder, he should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, he should renounce (*pravrajet*)," and "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year," and so forth. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "Only the householder sacrifices; the householder performs austerities (*tapaḥ*)."
And among the four stages of life, the householder is distinguished as superior.
Manu also says:
"Of all these [orders], according to the injunctions of the Veda and the Smṛti,
the householder is said to be the best, for he supports these other three."
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder.

Vasiṣṭha, however, states an option regarding the four stages of life (*āśrama*): "There are four stages of life—the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he may enter whichever among them he desires. The phrase "one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas" is intended to indicate an increase in the abundance of results. The meaning is: having studied the Veda and having not violated his vow of celibacy, he may enter—that is, take refuge in—whichever among those stages of life he desires, and therein reach his final consummation. This is also stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
O protector of the earth, if one desires the householder’s life, he should take a wife;
or else, he should spend his time in celibacy according to a formal resolve.
Or he may become a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), or a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) according to his desire.
Gautama also says: "Some speak of an option regarding his stages of life (*āśrama*. Uśanas has also stated:
"Permitted by his teacher, [he may choose] one of the four stages of life."
"Until the liberation of the body, he should practice according to the rule.

Thus, it should be understood that this option applies to one who lacks the capacity to perform the combined practice (*samuccaya*). By the phrase "he should practice until liberation," it is stated that one must remain as a member of an order of life (*āśramin*). For this very reason, Dakṣa says:
"A twice-born man should not remain without belonging to an order of life for even a single day."
For he who remains without an āśrama must perform penance.
One who is always devoted to recitation, fire-sacrifice, charity, or self-study,
yet has fallen away from his stage of life (āśrama), does not obtain the fruit even while performing these acts.
Hārīta also says:
"The man who belongs to no stage of life, the one who has fallen away from his stage, the one who observes a stage in vain, and the one who practices a stage falsely— all such men indeed go to hell."

And this fourfold order of life (āśrama-catuṣṭaya) is to be understood as belonging to the classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, the author of the Kalpasūtras states: "The four orders of life pertain to the three classes. Thus, it should be understood that when Manu says, "This fourfold dharma has been declared for the Brāhmaṇa," the term is intended as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the twice-born (dvijāti).
Thus concludes the determination of the stages of life (*āśrama-nirṇaya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*).
In this regard, Dakṣa says:
"When he has mastered the Veda and observes the Vedic vows, he should remain a *brahmacārī*; thereafter, having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāta*), he shall become a householder."

The *vratas* refer to the student’s observances (*brahmacarya*). The mention of “mastering the Veda” is intended to indicate the investigation of the Vedic meaning as well; for this very reason, another *Smṛti* states: “Having studied the Veda and having understood the meanings pertaining to the meters, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). Laghu-Vyāsa also says:

“Having studied even a single quarter-verse of the *Ṛgveda*, and having understood its meaning according to the rules, and having properly observed the vows, one is entitled to the *samāvartana* (the return home).”

"According to the rule" means by the method prescribed for observing the teacher’s instructions and so forth. And this refers to a case where one is capable of accomplishing the entire collection [of vows]. Alternatively, the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) indeed takes place even upon the completion of the mere vow (*vrata*). To that effect, Yājñavalkya also says:
"But having given a gift to the teacher, or with his permission, one should bathe;
or having brought the Veda or the vows, or indeed both, to their conclusion."

The meaning is that, according to the logic previously stated, having brought both the Veda and the vows—or either one of them—to completion, and having given the desired gift (*vara*) to the teacher, one should perform the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home). By this, the threefold nature of the *snātaka* is established. As Hārīta says: "There are three kinds of *snātakas*: the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vrata-snātaka*, and the *vidyā-vrata-snātaka*" [178]. He who returns home after completing the Veda but not the vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*. He who returns home after completing the vows but not the Veda is a *vrata-snātaka*. Furthermore, he who bathes after completing both is a *vidyā-vrata-snātaka*. Thus, it should be understood that for a *vrata-snātaka*, the completion of study and the knowledge of its meaning occur after marriage. As for that which...
Having duly obtained knowledge through service to his teacher, the twice-born,
permitted by his teacher, should perform the ceremonial bath after giving him a cow as a sacrificial fee.
Thus the gift of a cow has been described by Vyāsa; that too is intended as an illustration for any substance that serves to produce satisfaction. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella and sandals at the very least, grain, garments, or even vegetables—one should bring these to the Guru to produce his satisfaction."
By this, it is stated that when possible, only the most excellent [gift] should be given. For this very reason, Laghuhārīta says:
"Even if a teacher should impart but a single syllable to a disciple, there is no object on earth by giving which one might become free from debt."
And this giving of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be understood to apply even upon entering another stage of life (āśrama). Thus says the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"Having given a sacrificial fee to the teacher, he may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires."

Furthermore, for one who lacks the capacity to give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there is bathing upon receiving permission from the teacher. Thus says Gautama: [179] "At the end of his studies, the teacher should be invited with a gift; or, having performed [the rites], there is bathing for one who has been permitted. The meaning is that at the end of his studies, the teacher should be invited—that is, questioned—with a gift as the motive: "What object should be given by me to you? Having given that object to the teacher, he should bathe. Or, if he is incapable, he may do so with the teacher's permission; this is the sense. By the statement "at the end of his studies he should give," he indicates a prior prohibition. For this very reason, Manu says:
One who knows the Dharma should not offer anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when he is about to perform the ceremonial bath and has been authorized by the teacher, he should provide for the teacher’s needs according to his ability.
This also intends the provision of wages, since there is no prohibition against the other [means]. For this very reason, Yama says:
"Since there would be no arrival of dharma, nor service, nor acquisition of wealth, one should die with one's learning; one should not sow learning in barren soil."

Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the return from the teacher’s house and marriage have been described; this concludes the section on the life of the *upakurvāṇa* (the student). Now, his marriage is discussed. Regarding this, Manu says:
Having been duly permitted by his teacher and having returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One who has not violated his vow of celibacy should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks.
"Violation" means a lapse. "Endowed with auspicious marks" means possessed of the [proper] characteristics. When it is asked what those characteristics are, he himself says:

[180] A woman who has not belonged to another before, who is beloved, who is not a sapinda relative, who is younger, who is free from disease, who has brothers, and who is not born of the same ṛṣi-lineage or gotra.

"One who has had no other [husband] before" means she who has not previously belonged to another person, whether by gift or by enjoyment. "Desirable" (*kāntā*) means lovely, in the sense that she brings joy to the mind of the husband. Āpastamba also says: "In her upon whom the binding of the mind and the eyes [is fixed], there is prosperity. "Sapiṇḍā" means one who possesses a common *piṇḍa* (funeral cake); "asapiṇḍā" means one who does not possess such a *piṇḍa*. And this state of being a *sapiṇḍa* arises from participating in a single *piṇḍa*-offering rite, either as the giver, as the deity, or as a partaker of the smeared remains (*lepa*). Thus says the Matsya Purāṇa:
The fourth and subsequent [ancestors] are partakers of the lepa (the smearings); the father and the others are partakers of the piṇḍa (the funeral cakes).
The giver of the piṇḍas is the seventh among them; thus, sāpiṇḍya extends through seven generations.

The four ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather—the father and those following him—are the three subsequent ones who are the recipients of the *lepa* (the scrapings of the rice); however, the three beginning with the father are the sharers of the *piṇḍas* (the ritual cakes), serving as the deities for the offering of the *piṇḍas*, while the seventh among them is the giver of the *piṇḍas*. Thus, these seven are the *sapiṇḍas*. The meaning is that they are *sapiṇḍas* because they participate in the single act of offering a *piṇḍa*. Now, one might object: if *sāpiṇḍya* arises from participation in the single act of offering a *piṇḍa*, then since brothers participate in different acts, there would be no mutual *sāpiṇḍya* between them due to the absence of such a single act. This is not so; for it is possible for them to be connected to a single act through the delimitation of a single intended recipient (*uddeśya*). For those ancestors, such as the father, who participate in an act to be accomplished by one son, participate likewise in the act produced by another son; thus, their connection to a single intended recipient is evident. It is for this very reason that the *sāpiṇḍya* of those born in the lineage of a grandfather and others is established with the grandson. This is because the grandfather and others, who are connected to the son’s act, are thereby connected to that [grandson’s] act. However, when even a single ancestor like the grandfather lacks a connection to that act—due to the difference in the act caused by the difference in location—then *sāpiṇḍya* ceases. As Manu says: [Manu 5.60] "Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the fifth or the seventh person. [Manu 5.61] "In the case of women, the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship extends to the third degree. Thus, the *sāpiṇḍya* of the paternal line is established through the commonality of the act performed for the same ancestors, while in the maternal line, it is established through the commonality of the act performed for the mother’s parents and so on. Therefore, the *sāpiṇḍya* of brothers is indeed established through their mutual connection to the single act of offering the *piṇḍa* to the same ancestors. Thus, the definition of *sapiṇḍa* is fully consistent.
"But sapinda-relationship ceases with the seventh person. Thus [it is said].

Gautama also states: "The cessation of *sāpiṇḍya* occurs in the seventh or the fifth generation. And because the wife is a co-performer [of the ancestral rites], her *sāpiṇḍya* is established. In this manner, the cessation and continuation of *sāpiṇḍya* are to be understood everywhere. [Objection: If that is so, then *sāpiṇḍya* would result between a son and a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*), since both participate in the same funeral rite (*ekapiṇḍakriyā*). [Reply: True; however, the intention is that where this daughter’s son shares the same lineage (*gotra*) as the son, the state of having a common lineage (*ekagotratva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*). For this very reason, we shall explain later that in cases such as adoption (*putrīkaraṇa*), the daughter’s son also possesses *sāpiṇḍya* with the [adoptive] son. Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. She must be younger [than the bridegroom] in terms of both birth and stature. She must be free from disease—that is, not afflicted by chronic illness—because other ailments can be remedied. She must have brothers, out of fear of being made an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). As Manu says: *(Manusmṛti 3.11)*: "One should marry a girl who is not a *sapinda*, who has brothers, and who is of a different lineage (*asagotra*)."*
A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother, or whose father is unknown, for fear of the practice of *putrikā-dharma*.

The meaning is that it should not be known whether he has the intention to treat her as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) or not. By this, it is understood that a girl becomes an appointed daughter through the father’s mere resolve, even without a son [already born]. For this very reason, Gautama states: “According to some, she is an appointed daughter by mere agreement. When it is asked how she becomes an appointed daughter, Manu says:

“A man without a son shall, according to this rule, make his daughter an appointed daughter, [stating]: ‘Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be for me the performer of the *svadhā* offering.’”
Vasiṣṭha also said:
"I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son."

Or, the act of making her a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) is expressed by the phrase "she is indeed my son," based on the Vedic revelation: "The Fire-god, instructing [her], went to the grandson of his daughter. This has been explained in the *Nirukta*: "The husband instructs the daughter for the sake of the work of progeny, [thereby establishing] her status as a son. Regarding the phrase "one not born of a family with the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra*": one whose *ṛṣi* (ancestral sage) or *pravara* (lineage) is the same is called *samānārṣa*. The meaning is that one should not marry a girl born of such a lineage (*samānarṣijātā*). For this very reason, Gautama states: "Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*. And this identity [of *pravara*] is to be understood from the name. As Bodhāyana says:
"As long as a single sage persists among the *pravaras*, so long does the state of having a common *gotra* exist, except in the case of the groups of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras.
Here, "having a common *gotra*" means "having a common *pravara*. When it is asked how this applies to the groups of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
[183] Because of the commonality among five [gotras] in three [groups], there is no marriage; among three [gotras] in two [groups], there is none;
and even within the *bhṛgu* and *aṅgiras* groups, one must exclude a single [gotra] from the remaining ones.

The meaning is that for those with five *ṛṣis*, there is no marriage among those who share three *ṛṣis* in common. Bodhāyana also states: "In the case of a meeting of two *ṛṣis*, there is no marriage; in the case of a meeting of three *ṛṣis* among those with three *ṛṣis*, there is no marriage; and [likewise] among those with five *ṛṣis*. Furthermore, a *gotra* is well-known through the lineage succession. Both *gotra* and *pravara* are individually the grounds for exclusion. In that regard, since marriage would otherwise be permitted between the Yāskas, Vādhūlas, Mānavas, and Maukās due to a difference in *gotra*, the mention of "not having the same *ṛṣis*" (*asamānārṣa*) is made so that this may not occur; for these [groups], the *pravara* is identical: Bhārgava-Vaitahavya-Sādevala. However, where there is an option regarding the *pravara*, even there, since marriage would be permitted due to a difference in *pravara*, the mention of "not having the same *gotra*" (*asamānagotra*) is for the purpose of prohibiting that. Thus, it is effectively stated that one should marry a woman born of a different *ṛṣi* and a different *gotra*. Nor should it be suspected that the mention of "same *ṛṣis*" (*samānārṣa*) is a qualification of the *gotra*.
Having married a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā) or likewise one with the same ancestral rite (samānapravarā),
the twice-born man should abandon her and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
This is because she is remembered as distinct [from the wife]. Furthermore, what is abandoned here is only her enjoyment, not she herself. As Śātātapa says:
"I shall declare the atonement for that fool who marries a maiden who has the same *pravara* or even the same *gotra*."
Having abandoned that wife in such a manner, he should protect her like a mother.
But regarding him who procreates offspring there, Āpastamba says that he is degraded from his own caste and so forth:
"Having married and approached a maiden of the same *gotra* and *pravara*,
and having procreated a Caṇḍāla upon her, he is indeed fallen from Brahminhood."

Now, one might ask: since the exclusion of a woman who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the bridegroom is already established by the rule "one not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*," why is it stated again that she must be "not a *sapiṇḍa*"? It is said in reply: True, this is so; nevertheless, it is stated in order to show that the mother’s own *asapiṇḍa*—that very person—is what is recommended for the rite of marriage. And thus says Manu: "She who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and not of the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of taking a wife for sexual union."

The meaning is that she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the bridegroom’s mother, nor of the same *gotra* as the bridegroom’s father, is recommended for the rite of marriage. Now, an objection is raised: at the very moment of her being given away, the mother abandons her *sapiṇḍa* relationship and her *gotra* with the father and instead acquires *sapiṇḍa* relationship and *gotra* with the husband. How then can it be said, “she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother”? To this it has been said: “She attains oneness with her husband regarding the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the *gotra*, and during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*).”

The intention is that the *sāpiṇḍya* of a wife is with the *sapindas* of her husband alone, and not with her own father and others. True; there is no *sāpiṇḍya* for a mother with her own father and others if her marriage were preceded by her renunciation (of her kin). For upon renunciation, just as property rights cease, so too do *sāpiṇḍya* and *sagotra* status cease. It is with this very intention that it has been said:
"She has attained oneness with her husband in the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), in the lineage (*gotra*), and in the period of impurity (*sūtaka*)."

For this very reason, the cessation of the father’s *gotra* and other attributes through the relinquishment of an adopted son (*dattaputra*) and the like is established. Otherwise, the mention of the "father" in the rule, "She who is of a different *gotra* from the father," would be purposeless. And the cessation of the *gotra* and so forth has been stated by Manu: "The son given away (*dattima*) does not take the *gotra* or the inheritance of the biological father; the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) follows the *gotra* and the inheritance, while the ancestral offering (*svadhā*) departs from him who gives [the son away]."

And thus, since the marriage of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is not preceded by the formal giving away (*pradāna*), there is no cessation of *sāpiṇḍya* or *sagotratva* in her case. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha also stated that for unmarried women, *sāpiṇḍya* extends through three generations: "For unmarried women, *sāpiṇḍya* extends through three generations. Nor should it be suspected that even in the marriage of an appointed daughter, there is a formal giving away (*pradāna*) of her; for if such a giving away were to occur, then just as the lineage (*gotra*) and other attributes would cease, so too would her status as an appointed daughter cease. And if that status were to cease, she would no longer perform the duties incumbent upon her. Yet, her performance of the duties of a son is indeed heard in scripture: "Like one without a brother, she goes toward the men" (RV 10.18.7). This has also been explained in the *Nirukta*: "Like one without a brother, she goes toward the fathers; facing them, she leads them to the act of procreation for the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). Therefore, due to the absence of a formal giving away, it is established that the appointed daughter maintains *sāpiṇḍya* and *sagotratva* with her own father. For this very reason, Loka-kṣi says:
A son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) should perform the offering of rice-balls and water for his mother according to the lineage of his maternal grandfather; thus said Prajāpati.

In this way, even in the case of marriages such as those with Asuras and others, the prohibition against marrying within the same *gotra* and so forth does not cease, because in those cases there is likewise an absence of the formal giving (*pradāna*). For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"In the Brāhma and other [approved] forms of marriage, whatever maiden has been wedded, the offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water must be performed for her by means of the husband's *gotra*."
In marriages such as the Āsura and others, according to the Dharma, [the girl's name] is given by means of her father’s lineage.

The meaning is: by the *gotra* of the mother’s father. And thus, in cases such as the appointment of a daughter (*putrikā*), since there exists *sāpiṇḍya* for the mother with her own father and others, it is rightly stated: “she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother. Now, an objection: since the son is also a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother, whatever is a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother is also a *sapiṇḍa* of the son; for what purpose, then, is the mention of the “mother”? It is said in reply: when, however, there is the abandonment of the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) by both his mother and maternal grandfather, then, because that *sāpiṇḍya* ceases, a marriage with one who is a *sapiṇḍa* of hers might otherwise occur; so that this may not happen, the mention of the “mother” is made. Similarly, in the case of an adopted son (*dattaputra*) and others, through that very abandonment, the father’s *gotra* ceases, and a marriage with one who belongs to that same *gotra* might otherwise occur; so that this may not take place, the mention of the “father” is made. Thus, everything is faultless. Some, however, do not accept even one who is of the same *gotra* as the mother. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
Some do not even permit marriage with a woman of the same lineage as one's mother.

This [prohibition] also applies to the case of appointing a daughter (*putrikā*), because for a mother there is no other lineage (*gotra*) than that of her husband. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition against one who shares the same lineage as the mother applies only by way of past status (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*); for when a present condition is possible, it is improper to resort to a past status. Thus, it is established that she who is not a *sapinda* of the bridegroom’s mother, and she who is not of the same lineage as the bridegroom’s father, is eligible for marriage. [Objection: If this is so, then in the case of a son born through *brāhma* or other forms of marriage—where the status of being a *sapinda* to the father has ceased—the daughter of his maternal uncle (*mātula-sutā*) would have to be married to him. [Reply: True. But by whom was it said that she is not to be married? [Objection: By Manu and others themselves. As Śātātapa says:
He who marries a girl of the same lineage, or the daughter of his maternal uncle,
or one equal to a seer (in status), must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Manu also says: "Having approached the daughter of his father's sister, the daughter of his own sister, or the daughter of his mother's sister,
as well as the daughter of his mother's brother, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

"A wise man should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of kinship, for by taking them he falls low. Here, "of one who is *āpta*" means "of a close *sapiṇḍa*. Vyāsa also says:
[188] Deluded by sin, Brahmins will marry a girl who is third in descent from the mother's side and likewise third in descent from the father's side for a bride-price.

The meaning is: on the mother’s side, a daughter of the third generation from the maternal uncle; on the father’s side, a daughter of the third generation from the paternal aunt. *Śulka* means the price. By this, it is implied that one should count starting from the progenitor (*kūṭastha*). Thus, there is the statement of Yayāti in the Purāṇa:
"O you who were born from my heart, since you do not give me [your daughter] in marriage, your offspring shall indeed be born of sinful unions with maternal uncles."

Sumantu also says: "All fathers' wives are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*); their daughters are sisters; and their offspring are sister's sons (*bhāgineya*); otherwise, they would cause a confusion of castes. It is replied: True, these [texts] are intended to prohibit marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle. Nevertheless, in the case of a son whose *sapiṇḍa*-status with his father and others has not ceased due to an *āsura* or other form of marriage, the daughter of his mother’s brother is a *sapiṇḍa* of the bridegroom’s mother, and thus she is indeed ineligible for marriage. Likewise, the daughter of a paternal aunt who is of the same *gotra* as the bridegroom is a *sapiṇḍa* of the bridegroom’s father and is also not to be married. However, in the case of a girl wedded through a *brāhma* or other [approved] form of marriage, since her *sapiṇḍa*-relationship with her own father and others has ceased, the marriage of her son with the daughter of his mother’s brother is not forbidden. The same should be understood regarding the daughter of a paternal aunt (*paitṛṣvaseyī*). This very point was stated by Manu: [Manu 3.5–6] "One should not marry a girl who is a *sapiṇḍa* of one’s mother, nor one who is a *sagotra* of one’s father. A *sapiṇḍa* is defined as one who shares particles of the body (*śarīra*) through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). [Manu 3.7] "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship ceases after the seventh person [in the line], and the *sagotra* relationship ceases after the fifth. [Manu 3.8] "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandfather, and it likewise extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandmother. [Manu 3.9] "A girl who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of one’s mother and not a *sagotra* of one’s father is recommended for marriage. [Manu 3.10] "In the absence of such a girl, however, one may marry a girl who is a *sapiṇḍa* of one’s mother, provided she is not a *sagotra* of one’s father. [Manu 3.11] "But a girl who is a *sagotra* of one’s father, even if she is not a *sapiṇḍa*, must never be taken as a wife. [Manu 3.12] "For those who marry girls who are *sagotra* or *sapiṇḍa*, there is a fall from caste, and the extinction of lineage, along with the destruction of sacrifices. [Manu 3.13] "Some say that the *sapiṇḍa* relationship ceases after the fifth person, while others say it ceases after the seventh. [Manu 3.14] "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship is declared to extend to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandfather, and it likewise extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandmother. [Manu 3.15] "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandfather, and it likewise extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandmother. [Manu 3.16] "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandfather, and it likewise extends to the third degree among the descendants of the great-grandmother. "She who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and not of the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage and sexual union.
The intention is that she who is a *sapiṇḍa* or of the same *gotra* on the mother's side or the father's side must be rejected, and no other. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"The twice-born must carefully avoid one who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother. For this very reason, Śātātapa also states a prohibition specifically regarding one who shares the mother's *gotra*:
"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, and likewise one who belongs to the mother's *gotra*..."
And a twice-born man who marries a woman of the same *pravara* lineage shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

Nor should it be asked: "Since the prohibition of the daughter of a maternal uncle who is a *sapiṇḍa* is already established by the phrase 'not [of] the mother's lineage' (*na mātṛgotrām*) alone, what is the purpose of mentioning 'the son of a maternal uncle' (*mātulasutā*)? For even if there were two alternative views, the objection would be identical. In that case as well, the prohibition of the daughter of a maternal uncle alone would be established simply by the prohibition of those belonging to the mother's lineage and so forth. If, however, both types of daughters of a maternal uncle are prohibited by the two alternative views, then the mention of "the son of a maternal uncle" alone would suffice; what is the point of mentioning "the mother's lineage"? Furthermore, Manu also states an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) only for the daughter of a paternal aunt who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the father.
Having approached a paternal aunt, a sister, a daughter of one's own sister,
a maternal aunt, or the daughter of a maternal uncle who is a close relative, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

"A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives. Nor should it be argued that the word *bhaginī* does not qualify the daughter of the father's sister; for [the text states]: "A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives."

"Whether she be the third or the fourth on either side..."
