[192] Thus, since the rule for marriage on the mother’s side is prescribed beyond the fifth degree, how can there be the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter? It is said in reply: By the rule, “One should marry a girl who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of one’s mother,” marriage with the mother’s relatives would generally be permitted; however, to prevent that contingency, the text specifies that one should marry beyond the fifth degree from the mother’s relatives on the mother’s side—thus there is no contradiction. This should be understood to apply to the father’s relatives as well. For this very reason, Gautama states: “Beyond the seventh degree from the father’s relatives and beyond the fifth degree from the progenitor’s mother’s relatives. The meaning is that one should marry beyond the seventh degree even from the progenitor—that is, the man who procreates through *niyoga*. Furthermore, the specific types of relatives are shown in another *smṛti*: [text follows].
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s mother’s sister are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu).
The sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava).

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"the fifth [generation] from the mother's kin and the seventh from the father's kin"—that is intended to mean "one may marry after passing beyond the fifth and the seventh," in order to achieve consistency with the text of Gautama; it does not, however, intend the fifth and seventh generations as the limit for marriage. As for that which was also stated by Nārada:
One should not marry a girl who is within five generations on the father’s side or seven generations on the mother’s side;
likewise, she must not be of the same *gotra* or the same *pravara*.
Thus it is said; and furthermore, by Viṣṇu:

"A twice-born man who marries a girl who is inferior [in status] by five or seven generations, as well as one who marries a girl of the same lineage (sagotrā), should be known as one who has violated the bed of his guru."
Thus, even in that case, the fifth and seventh [days] are not permitted, because a prohibition is heard regarding them. As Marīci says:
"Those whose marriage rite takes place on the fifth or the seventh day—even if they are devoted to sacred rites, they are outcasts who have fallen to the state of Śūdras."
By this, that which has been stated by some— namely,
"In the absence of [a wife] superior to the seventh, one should marry a seventh"—
is also refuted. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Paithīnasi:
Marriage is permitted after passing beyond three generations on the mother's side and five generations on the father's side.

Thus, that [text] also intends to prohibit [marriage] within the [specified degrees] below; it does not, however, intend the fourth and sixth degrees for marriage, because that would result in a contradiction with the statements of Viṣṇu and others. Now, one might argue: since it is stated by the rule "and she who is not a sapinda of the mother" that one should marry her who is not a sapinda of the mother, and since this would imply that marriage could occur without distinction even within one's own mother’s lineage, why should there not be a restrictive rule—namely, "one should marry beyond the fifth degree from the mother's side"—in order to prevent that? Consequently, how can the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter be justified? The same should be understood regarding the father’s side. And it has been stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A householder, O King, should marry a maiden from the fifth generation on his mother's side and the seventh generation on his father's side, according to the proper rite."

The meaning is "having passed beyond the fifth. Let it not be so, because Gautama and others have prescribed restrictive rules (*niyamavidhi*) specifically regarding kinsmen. Alternatively, even if there were no restrictive rule regarding kinsmen alone, there is nonetheless no contradiction, as this restriction is established in both cases by means of the exclusion of marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle or the daughter of a paternal aunt, which is permitted by Manu and others in the manner already stated. Or rather, it should be understood that the Yājñavalkya rule stating "from the fifth and the seventh" pertains to the case of appointing a daughter (*putrikā*) and similar circumstances; whatever is logical in this regard should be accepted. As for what was stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
The female lineage of women and that of men are both considered ineligible for marriage;
however, the offspring of a man and a woman may intermarry beyond the fifth and seventh degrees, respectively.

Thus, that [objection] also refers only to what has already been discussed, and is therefore without fault. Furthermore, Śruti also proclaims this very same point. Thus it is heard in the Vājasaneyaka: "Therefore, from the very same person, both the eater and the food are born. The meaning of this is as follows: from one and the same person (*puruṣa*), the eater (*attā*)—that is, the enjoyer—and that which is to be eaten—the object of enjoyment characterized as a wife—are born; that is to say, a husband and wife are born. Anticipating this, he says: "Then, in the third generation," and so forth. "Let us unite" means "let us marry. But is it not the case that this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intent on praising the act of weaving garlands and is not authoritative regarding its own literal meaning? It is said in reply: True, an *arthavāda* is not authoritative regarding its own literal meaning; however, where there is another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it functions as praise by relying on the fact established by that other means, as in the case of "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity. Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"That which has been performed by the gods, and that which has been performed by the sages—such should not be performed by men; one should perform the action as it has been prescribed."

In another Vedic text as well: "In our womb, the progenitor Savitṛ, the creator of the universe, made us a husband and wife, possessing all forms. The meaning is: "In our womb—that is, in our belly—the progenitor, the god who is the creator of the world, made us a *dampatī*, that is, a husband and wife (*jāyā-patī*). There is also a mantra: "Come, O Indra, by the paths praised by the gods; enjoy this sacrifice of ours, this portion allotted to you. May the offering be satisfying, like a maiden to her maternal uncle; the portion for you is like the omentum of a father's sister's daughter."

O Indra, come to this sacrifice of ours by the paths that are praised and lauded. Having arrived, enjoy this portion being offered by us. For this very reason, the sacrificers have offered—having relinquished—the *vapā* (omentum), prepared with clarified butter and other substances, intended for you. Here there is a comparison: just as the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātula-yoṣā*) is the share (*bhāga*) of her grandson (*dauhitra*), fit to be enjoyed and worthy of marriage; and just as the daughter of a paternal aunt (*paitṛṣvaseyī*) is so for her [grandson], even so is this portion called *uvāka* yours. By this, the marriage of the daughters of maternal uncles and others is established even by the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, we understand this from tradition (*ācāra*): for the learned elders of the South (*dākṣiṇātyas*), who are experts in the three Vedas and performers of Vedic rites, indeed practice the marriage of the daughters of maternal uncles and others. And the authority of such custom has been stated by Manu: [The verse regarding the authority of custom follows here. Thus, the marriage of the daughters of maternal uncles and others is established both by scripture and by tradition.
"The conduct of the learned, the Smṛti, and the Veda—these three are the characteristics of Dharma.
Here, "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) means "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa). Devala also says: "In whatever regions there are gods, and in whatever regions there are twice-born [brahmins]..."
In whatever regions there is water, and whatever soil exists in each respective place.
In whatever places there is a particular purity and whatever kind of religious practice exists, one should not despise those things; for such is the dharma in those very places.
"In whatever country, city, village, or even learned metropolis,
one should not subvert that dharma which has been ordained for that place."

[Objection: But has it not been stated by Vasiṣṭha that even local custom (*deśācāra*) possesses authority only when it does not conflict with other means of valid knowledge? He says: "Local customs and family laws (*kuladharma*) are authoritative provided they are not in contradiction with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*). [Response: True; the sacred tradition is the Veda, and thus authority belongs only to those things not in conflict with it. However, there is no conflict with the Veda here; on the contrary, it is favorable, as was stated below. [Objection: Even in the face of a conflict with Smṛti, custom is indeed weaker, because of the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha: "Dharma is that which is ordained by Śruti and Smṛti; in their absence, the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is the authority. And here there is a conflict with Smṛti such as: "Having married the daughter of one's maternal uncle," and so forth. Therefore, how can there be authority for custom in this case? [Response: Not so, because the conflict is resolved by the fact that those [Smṛti rules] concern the state of *sapiṇḍa-relationship* with the mother. Or rather, let it be that they do not have a specific scope; instead, they refer to those who practice marriages with the daughters of maternal uncles and others in the northern regions (*udīcyadeśa*), for it is precisely of them that the hearing of defects is recorded. Thus says Baudhāyana: "There is a fivefold disagreement in the South: eating together with one who is uninitiated, eating stale food, eating the leavings of another, and marrying the daughter of a paternal aunt or a maternal uncle. Likewise, there are five in the North: selling wool, drinking *śīdhu* liquor, transactions with double-edged coins, the profession of arms, and sea-voyaging. One incurs fault by performing in one region what is practiced in the other. One incurs fault by performing in one region what is practiced in the other. In each respective case, there is simply the authority of the region. The meaning is this: the "other"—the Southerner—incurs fault by performing practices such as marriage with a maternal uncle's daughter in the "other"—the Northern region—but not in his own region. Similarly, the "other"—the Northerner—incurs fault by performing practices such as drinking *śīdhu* in the "other"—the Southern region—but not in his own region. Why? Because of the authority of the region; the meaning is that the authority of custom is based upon the region. For this very reason, Devala says:
"In whatever region a particular custom is established as being seen to be consistent with justice, that very local custom must be observed; such is the tradition of Bṛhaspati.

Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, for northerners there is no contradiction in contracting marriages with maternal uncles' daughters, whether in their own country or abroad. For Āpastamba says:

Those for whom [customs] have been handed down through tradition and were practiced by their ancestors— only they, and not others, would be faultless regarding those practices, provided they have a leader.

Those who possess customs inherited through a lineage of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, and which were practiced by their ancestors who were experts in the three Vedas (*traividya*), would incur no fault by performing those very customs, but not others. For such customs do not exist among the northerners as they do among the southerners. Therefore, it is established that duties should be performed by those very people in their own region and not by others. The author of the *Vārttika* has stated that the authority [of these practices] is determined by regional restriction: "Thus, for all such [matters], there is a restriction according to each respective region."
"Āpastamba has established the state of being defiled or undefiled based on the [manner of] consecration."

As for what Bodhāyana stated after saying "the authority of the country": "Gautama says this is false; one should not respect either, because one observes contradictions with the tradition of the learned (śiṣṭa) and because one observes contradictions with the Smṛti of the learned"—that [objection] is not intended to refute what was previously stated, since Gautama is mentioned [specifically]. Rather, it is to show that, due to observing contradictions with the Smṛti of the learned, Gautama intended the non-marriage of a maternal sapiṇḍa. And thus it has been said by others: "This would indeed be so, if he had not immediately thereafter said 'this is false'"—that too is refuted. Therefore, the marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle and the daughter of a paternal aunt is established by Śruti, Smṛti, and custom; thus everything is faultless.
Thus ends the justification for the marriage with the daughter of one’s maternal uncle in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Regarding the characteristics of a maiden, some characteristics have already been stated in the passage beginning with "one who has not belonged to another, who is lovely," and so forth. Now, other characteristics are being stated. In this regard, Manu says:

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
Śātātapa also says:
A householder who marries a maiden with a voice like a swan, the complexion of a cloud, and eyes tawny as honey, prospers in happiness.

Āpastamba also says: "One should marry a woman who is endowed with [good] lineage, character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease. By the phrase "endowed with auspicious marks," he implies that one should not marry a woman who possesses the opposite characteristics. For this very reason, Manu states:
"One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown."
One who is talkative and speaks excessively; one who is tawny and has tawny eyes—Yama also says:
"Short, tall, thin, stout, tawny-eyed, or pale-white—such women are neither to be honored nor served; they bring about destruction and death."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"One who does not possess the characteristics of a beard, nor has the form of a man;
nor one with a hoarse voice, nor one who is emaciated, nor likewise one with a voice like a crow."
Likewise, a wise man should not marry one whose gaze is too fixed, nor one with round eyes; nor one whose shanks are hairy, nor one whose ankles are prominent.
One should not marry a woman who has pits on her cheeks even when she laughs,
nor one whose skin is excessively parched, whose palms and nails are pale, or whose eyes are reddish.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose hands and feet are swollen;
nor should he marry one who is a dwarf, nor one who is excessively tall, nor one whose eyebrows meet.
"Nor [should a man marry] one with excessively gapped teeth, nor one with a gaping mouth. Now, those to be avoided by name: as Manu says:
"One should not [marry] a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river, nor one named after a low-caste group or a mountain."
Nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant, nor one with a terrifying name.
*Ṛkṣa* is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). *Antya* refers to the Mlecchas. *Bhīṣaṇa* means terrifying. Āpastamba also says:
"One should avoid in marriage those named after lunar mansions, rivers, or trees, as well as all those whose names end in the letter *r*, the letter *l*, or a sibilant (*ūṣman*)."
Yama also says:
One should avoid for the sake of a wife a woman whose name is that of a deity, a river, a mountain, or a gandharva; nor one whose name is that of a bear, a tree, or a creeper.

Furthermore, a woman who has been previously married (*paunarbhavā*) is likewise unfit for marriage. As Kāśyapa said: "Seven types of women born of remarriage are to be avoided as the lowest of their families:
one given in word, one given in thought, and one for whom the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony has already been performed."
She who has been touched by water, she who has been taken by the hand,
she who has circumambulated the fire, and she who is born again from a remarriage.
Thus these [women] have been described by Kāśyapa as burning their family like fire;
yet even a tree burnt by fire may sprout again after a long time.
A family that has been consumed by rebirth never sprouts again anywhere.

"Punarbhavas" means those who have become [wives] again. And so says Bodhāyana: "One given in word, one given in thought, one who has circumambulated the fire, one led to the seventh step, one who has been enjoyed, one who has conceived, and one who has given birth—these are the seven kinds of *punarbhū*. Having taken such a woman, one shall find neither offspring nor merit. One who has been given in word becomes a *punarbhū* through the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that having taken her—that is, having married her—one shall not find, nor partake in, offspring or merit. For this very reason, Nārada says:
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has had her hand taken in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) in the rite of re-consecration.

[203] The phrase "defiled by the taking of the hand" (*pāṇigrahaṇadūṣitā*) is intended as an illustration for those who have been verbally betrothed (*vāgdattā*) and so forth. Yājñavalkya also states: "One who is both unblemished (*akṣatā*) and blemished (*kṣatā*), and one who has been remarried after being consecrated again (*punarbhūḥ*). Here, the "unblemished" refers to those who have been verbally betrothed and the like; the "blemished," however, refers to those who have already been enjoyed and so forth. Although the external signs mentioned here can perhaps be known in some way, nevertheless, because the internal signs are difficult to discern, their knowledge must be achieved through the method prescribed by Āśvalāyana. For this very reason, Āśvalāyana also says that these signs are difficult to discern.

Having made eight lumps [of earth], he should consecrate the lumps with the mantra: "In the beginning, *ṛta* (Cosmic Order) was born first; upon *ṛta*, *satya* (Truth) is established. What this maiden has been born toward—that let her attain here. Let that which is true be seen. Having thus addressed the lumps, he should say to the maiden: "Take one of these. If she should take from a field that yields crops on both sides, he should know: "Her offspring will be rich in food. From a cow-pen: "She will be rich in cattle. From the soil of a Veda-altar: "She will be devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*). From an inexhaustible spring: "She will be endowed with everything. From a gambling ground: "She will be a gambler. If from a crossroads: "She will be a wanderer. From barren soil: "She will be barren. From a cemetery: "She will be a killer of her husband. Thus it is said.

"Vipravrājinī" means one who wanders about in various ways; that is to say, a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*). Since marriage would thus apply without distinction to a woman possessing the aforementioned characteristics, Yama states an exception regarding lineage in certain cases: "One should specify these fourteen families as ineligible for marriage.
Among Brāhmaṇas, one should avoid those who lack a *ṛṣi* lineage and those who lack officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)."
One should avoid those who are excessively tall or excessively short, those of extreme complexion,
those with deficient limbs, those with redundant limbs, and families afflicted by disease.
One should avoid those families that suffer from leucoderma, leprosy, and the like;
one must always avoid the family of Kāma and those families that are excessively hairy.

"And whatever family may be epileptic, and whatever family may be afflicted with jaundice. Thus [it is said]. A family that lacks a lineage of ṛṣis (anārṣeya) is one whose ancestral lineages (pravara) are unknown. A family in which there are those who are excessively tall or excessively long is an "excessively tall" family. One in which there are those who are excessively short or excessively hunchbacked is an "excessively short" family. One in which there is an excessive degree of skin coloration is an "excessive color" family. And this exclusion of families with diseases is for fear of the transmission of hereditary defects. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says: "Even from a prosperous family, one should not take [a bride] if it is possessed of the defect of contagious diseases."
"From a prosperous [family]" means from one that is flourishing. "Defects" refers to moral degradation. Manu also says:
"Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten families in forming alliances with women."

"One who is devoid of religious rites, one who lacks male progeny, one who is devoid of the Vedas, one who is excessively hairy, one afflicted with hemorrhoids, and families that suffer from bedsores, epilepsy, leucoderma, and leprosy. "Devoid of religious rites" means lacking the performance of sacrifices and other such duties. "Lacking male progeny" means being destitute of sons. "Devoid of the Vedas" means lacking the study of the Vedas. "Excessively hairy" means having an overabundance of body hair. "Afflicted with hemorrhoids" means suffering from a specific disease. The others should be understood in the same manner. This avoidance of those devoid of rites and so forth is for the purpose of preventing the birth of such offspring. Indeed, the birth of such offspring is recorded in the Purāṇas.
A son takes after his maternal uncles, and a daughter takes after her paternal ancestors.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Just as the mother is of such character, so shall the daughter be of that same character."

For this very reason, Manu said that one should cultivate relationships only with the virtuous: "One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form connections with the most eminent; he should abandon those who are inferior."
Yājñavalkya also says:

"From a great family renowned for ten generations among Vedic scholars (śrotriya)... The meaning is that one should marry a girl from such a great family—one in which five generations on both the mother's and father's sides are renowned—and which is prosperous with sons, cattle, and so forth. Furthermore, she must be of the same caste (savarṇā). As Vyāsa says:

"Having bathed, one should marry a girl of the same caste who is endowed with auspicious marks. This refers specifically to the first marriage. For this very reason, Manu says: "For the twice-born, a woman of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage at the outset."
By this [verse], he states that marrying a woman of a different caste after having previously married a woman of the same caste is not prohibited. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Three, two, and likewise one, in order of their castes, are the wives of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya respectively; for one born a Śūdra, she is his own [caste]."

According to the sequence of castes (*varṇa*), a Brāhmaṇa has three wives: a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra; a Kṣatriya has two: a Vaiśya and a Śūdra; and a Vaiśya has one: a Śūdra. Furthermore, for all, a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) remains the primary one. Nor should one suspect that the explanation—that a Brāhmaṇa has three wives, namely a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, and a Vaiśyā—is intended here; for if that were the case, the statement "those of his own [caste] for one born as a Śūdra" would have its meaning rendered redundant, since there would be no distinction as this would apply equally to a Vaiśya as well. Therefore, the previously mentioned interpretation alone is superior. For this very reason, Manu says:

"A Śūdra woman alone is the wife of a Śūdra; she and one of his own [caste] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and one of his own [caste] may belong to a Kṣatriya; and those three and one of his own [caste] belong to the first-born (Brāhmaṇa). This, however, refers to the case of one who acts out of desire. As he himself says:
"But for those who proceed out of desire, these [wives] would be inferior in successive order.

Here, "inferior" means "lowest. By this, it is stated that for the sake of dharma, one should marry a woman of the same caste. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "A Śūdra woman can never be the wife of a twice-born man for the sake of dharma."
"She is proclaimed for the sake of pleasure alone for him who is blinded by passion.
This means that she would not exist for the sake of dharma, nor would she enter into religious duties. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But he whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are centered primarily upon her..."
The ancestors and the gods do not eat his offerings, nor does he go to heaven.

The meaning is that those [other castes] are dominated by it and dependent upon it. As for what was stated by that same author: "Even in times of distress, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who remains [in his own station], a Śūdra wife is not prescribed in any traditional account whatsoever."

[207] Thus, this refers specifically to the subject of marrying a Śūdra woman immediately after [the others], because that same author [Yājñavalkya] prescribes the sequence with the words, "These [wives] should be in order, each lower than the last. And Yājñavalkya has stated: "Three [wives] according to the order of the castes. The phrase "even when staying in distress" means even for those who do not obtain a wife of their own caste (*savarṇā*). This is for the purpose of an absolute prohibition against these two [cases], and not for the purpose of permitting a Vaiśya [to marry a Śūdra]. For he himself says:
"Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry a woman of a lower caste, quickly lead their families, along with their descendants, to the state of Śūdras."

Paiṭhīnasi, however, states that in the absence of a bride of equal caste, one may marry a Kṣatriya woman or others: "In the absence of a [suitable] maiden, one should observe the vows of a Snātaka; or else, he may procreate sons with a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman—so say others. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"That which is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born—that is not my opinion, because in her the self (ātman) is born of its own accord."

Thus, that too has the same meaning as the text of Manu. Nor can it be argued that, this being the case, the statement "there the self is born of itself" is consistent as a logical reason (*hetu*); for by that [text] as well, the marriage of a Śūdra woman is mentioned in the phrase "three [wives] in the order of the castes. Furthermore, if the marriage of a Śūdra woman were never accepted on the grounds of such a reason, then the marriage of Kṣatriya women and others would also not occur, since in those cases too, the self itself is produced. Therefore, this is not a logical reason, but should be understood as a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). As for what was stated by Yama:
A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman remains impure for three days;
if he then conceives a child by her, he is indeed deprived of his Brāhmaṇahood.
Thus, as for that which was stated by Manu: "By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
having procreated a son upon her, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood itself."

Thus, by that [statement] as well, marriage performed in the reverse order (*vyutkrama*) and approaching her for intercourse are prohibited, and not merely the procreation of a son in her. For if it were otherwise, the statement regarding the division of inheritance—“The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their caste, are entitled to four, three, two, and one shares”—would not be possible. For this very reason, Manu also declares the fault [of such a union] solely on account of having a child by a Śūdra woman.
By means of crafts, trade, and the exclusive occupations of Śūdras—
namely, cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
"Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, as well as through atheism regarding the efficacy of ritual acts.
This means [perishing] by selling cows, horses, and so forth. Furthermore, he (the same author) states other opinions as well:
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.

The meaning of this is as follows: "A Brahmin who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste]. In this regard, the opinion of Atri and Gautama—the son of Utathya—is stated; therefore, according to their view, there is no marriage with a Śūdra woman. For Śaunaka, however, degradation does not result from the mere act of marriage, but rather from the procreation of offspring. Thus, in his view, one should not approach a Śūdra woman during her fertile season (*ṛtu*). But for Bhṛgu, there is no degradation even through the procreation of offspring therein; rather, it is by virtue of having such offspring—that is, he whose offspring are those very ones born of a Śūdra woman, the state of being such is "tadapatyatā"—by that state. Therefore, in his view, one should not approach a Śūdra woman during her fertile season while a Brāhmaṇa wife has not yet borne children. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also states a prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman: "Some [allow] even a Śūdra woman, excluding the sacred mantras (*mantra-varjam*). One should not do so, for [in that case] there is certainly a degradation of the lineage through sins, and moreover, it is not conducive to heaven."

Thus concludes the section on the characteristics of the bride in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the characteristics of the groom. Regarding this, Gautama states: "One should give [the daughter] to one who is endowed with learning, conduct, kinship, and character. Here, "learning" (*vidyā*) refers to the Veda and sacred tradition (*śruta*). "Conduct" (*cāritra*) refers to ritual performance. "Kinship" (*bandhu*) refers to a praiseworthy lineage. "Character" (*śīla*) refers to moral behavior. The meaning is that one should give the daughter to one who is endowed with these qualities. Āpastamba also says: "The excellence of a groom consists in being endowed with kinship, auspicious marks, and character, as well as being learned and free from disease. Yama also says:
[210] "The wise should bestow a daughter after examining these seven qualities: family, character, physical form, age, learning, wealth, and a protector; everything else is not to be considered.
As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu:

"The family of a Brāhmaṇa is to be accepted, not his Vedas nor his recitation of the *padapāṭha* and *kramapāṭha*; likewise, in the giving of a daughter in marriage and at a *śrāddha*, learning is not the determining factor"—this statement is intended to establish the primacy of family, but it is not for the purpose of rejecting learning altogether. For this very reason, Āśvalāyana says: "One should first examine the family. Likewise, Yājñavalkya states that his virility must also be examined.
One who has been carefully tested for virility, who is young, wise, and beloved by the people—Kātyāyana also says:
"Women were created for the sake of offspring; women are the field, and men are the seed-bearers."
"A field should be given to one who possesses seed; one without seed does not deserve a field.
This is the sense: therefore, that [seed] must be examined. Nārada, however, states the means for examining it:
"The seed of which floats in water, and whose urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy..."
"A man shall be recognized by these characteristics; one who is the opposite is a eunuch.
Here, "seed" means virility. It is "gladdening," meaning it possesses sound. Yājñavalkya also says:
"One whose urine is gladdening and frothy, whose semen is heavy and white, and whose voice is like that of a bull..."
Otherwise, he would be a eunuch; a mouth-vagina is difficult to cure.
The term *mukhebhaga* refers to a specific type of eunuch. Śātātapa also states the characteristics of a bridegroom (*vara*):
"A bridegroom is one who is sought after, who possesses wealth, and is endowed with noble lineage and good character; he should be handsome, learned, wise, young, and free from defects."
"He should be chosen" refers to the father of the girl; this is the ellipsis. The defects [of a groom] have also been stated by Kātyāyana:

"One who is insane, one who is fallen (patita), one afflicted with leprosy, likewise one who is impotent, one born of the same lineage (sagotra), one deprived of sight or hearing, and likewise one corrupted by epilepsy."
These are indeed remembered as the defects of a groom, and they are proclaimed as the defects of a bride;
[these apply] to those who are far away, to the ignorant, and to those following the path to liberation.
"A daughter should not be given by the wise to those who are brave or to those who are destitute.
Thus ends the section on the characteristics of a bridegroom in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the times for the giving away of the daughter (*kanyādāna*).
Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"In the eighth year she becomes Gaurī; in the ninth, she becomes Nagnikā;
in the tenth, she is called Kanyakā; and in the twelfth, she is known as Vṛṣalī."
A *vṛṣalī* is a woman in her courses;
a barren woman is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*, as is one whose children have died.
Furthermore, another is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*: a maiden who has reached puberty.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Devala: "And this refers to the general case; it does not mean that she becomes *rajasvalā* (menstruating) at exactly twelve years, for in some cases the appearance of menses may occur even before that. For this very reason, Yama says:
"An eight-year-old girl is a *Gaurī*, a nine-year-old is a *Rohiṇī*, a ten-year-old is a *Kanyā*; beyond this age, she is *rajasvalā*."
Furthermore, it has been stated by Āpastamba: "A girl of eight years is a Gaurī, while one of ten years is a Kanyā;
when the twelfth year arrives, the menses begin for women."
Thus, as for that which was stated by Yama: "When the twelfth year has arrived, the menses appear in women";
and also that which was stated by Yama:
If a man does not give his daughter in marriage when she has reached her twelfth year,
his father drinks her menstrual blood month after month.

This [statement] also refers to the general case, since for some women even at that age the appearance of menses is impossible. For this very reason, Manu says: "A thirty-year-old man should marry a pleasing twelve-year-old girl, or a twenty-four-year-old man an eight-year-old girl, if he is one who acts with haste lest his dharma suffer."

"Satvara" means one who is young in age. Thus, it is stated that as long as the appearance of menses (*rajo-darśana*) has not occurred, the marriage of a girl is not prohibited. For this very reason, Yama says:

"One should marry off a girl before she becomes menstruating. Gautama also says: "[213] 'The giver is at fault for not giving her away before puberty; some say he is at fault even before she has put on the [marriage] garment. Saṃvarta also says:
When the time of puberty has arrived, Soma enjoys the maiden;
at the time of menstruation, Gandharva; and when the breasts appear, Agni.
Therefore, one should marry off a maiden before she reaches puberty;
thus says Vasiṣṭha as well:
"A father, giving away his daughter while she is still a *nagnikā* (pre-pubescent), does so out of fear of her reaching the time of menstruation."
"For while she remains in her menses, the fault falls upon the father. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *nagnikā* (the girl who is "naked") is described in the *Purāṇa*:
"As long as a maiden, in the presence of a man, does not [conceal] her limbs out of shame..."
"As long as she hides herself behind firewood and the like, she remains naked"— so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"As long as she does not take up a garment, as long as she plays with dust."
As long as she does not perceive a fault, so long does she remain naked.

Amarasimha, however, states that a girl is *nagnikā* until the appearance of her menses, saying: "A *nagnikā* is one who has not yet reached puberty. Likewise, Manu also specifies the time for the bridegroom's marriage:
"A thirty-year-old man should marry a pleasing twelve-year-old girl, or an eighteen-year-old an eight-year-old; he should act with haste if his duty is failing."
Bṛhaspati also says:
A man thirty years of age should marry a girl ten years old who has not yet reached puberty;
or a man twenty-one years of age may take a seven-year-old bride.
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"A man who possesses three times [the wealth] should marry a wife who possesses one time [the wealth].
Thus ends the section on the timing for the giving away of a maiden in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage: Manu states the fruit for one who bestows a daughter according to the aforementioned procedure:
"That [fruit] of a Brahmin would not be so inexhaustible as that which comes from the Agnihotra and other such rites."
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving a maiden in marriage according to the prescribed rule, [he obtains that same fruit by giving land].
Marīci also said:

"One who maintains the sacred fire does not go to hell, nor does the giver of a daughter, nor her son. The sacrifice equal to the Viśvajit is the gift of a daughter; the giving of a daughter yields great fruit."
Saṃvarta also says:
"By giving away a maiden consecrated with *homamantra* mantras, one obtains the merit of a hundred times a hundred *jyotiṣṭoma-ati-rātra* sacrifices."
Bṛhaspati also says:
A cow is equal to a thousand [other gifts], a bull is equal to ten cows;
a vehicle is equal to ten bulls, and a horse is equal to ten vehicles.
A maiden is equal to ten horses, and the gift of land is equal to that; gold, a horse, sesame seeds, an elephant, a female slave, a chariot, land, a house,
a Kapila cow, and a maiden— these are indeed the ten great gifts (mahādānas).
Yama also said:
"A daughter and knowledge are equal to ten thousand sacrifices that draw the chariot-pole, when they are bestowed upon a worthy recipient."
"By giving away a fair-complexioned girl (gaurī), one attains the summit of heaven; by giving Rohiṇī, Vaikuṇṭha;

by giving a maiden, the world of Brahmā; but by giving a menstruating woman (rajasvalā), one goes to Raurava. Thus, he [the author] states that the same fault applies to the one who marries a menstruating woman as well.
The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three go to hell upon seeing a daughter who has reached her menses.
That Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by intoxication, would deflower such a maiden is indeed unfit for conversation and excluded from the row of diners; he is a Brāhmaṇa who has become the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
"For that Brahmin who, deluded by intoxication, consorts with a *vṛṣalī*,
there is constant birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) day after day.
Furthermore, he states the same fault for one who consumes her [liquor]:
A twice-born man who commits sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī* for even a single night removes that sin by subsisting on alms and reciting [sacred texts] constantly for three years.
Furthermore, by engaging in sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī* continuously for one month,
one attains the status of a *śūdra* in this very life, and after death, one is born as a dog.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Vṛṣalī, who has been defiled by her breath,
and who has begotten offspring upon her, no atonement whatsoever exists.

[216] But when a maiden becomes menstruating while still a virgin, Bṛhaspati declares that her father incurs the sin of foeticide: "If a maiden sees her menses at her father's house while remaining uninitiated, her father incurs the sin of foeticide; that maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*."
"Bhrūṇahatyā" is the killing of a fetus; and that is to be understood as occurring at every menstrual period. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"By not giving [the wife] away, he incurs the guilt of bhrūṇahatyā at every ṛtu.
Nārada also says:
As many seasons as pass for her without a husband,
so many sins of foeticide shall belong to him who does not give her away.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
"A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house at will until death;
but he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities."

Thus, this statement is intended to mean that one should give [the bride] to a man endowed with qualities, and not to one devoid of qualities; it is not, however, for the purpose of an absolute prohibition against giving her to one lacking qualities. Therefore, Bodhāyana says:
"One should give a maiden who is still naked (*nagnikā*) to a virtuous man who is a celibate student (*brahmacārin*);
or else, even to one devoid of qualities, but she must not be detained once she has reached puberty."
Yama also says: "One should give a maiden who is still naked (i.e., very young) to a man of merit according to one's ability;
but one should never give her to one devoid of merit, nor should one allow her to remain beyond the time when she reaches puberty."

But when he does not give her away even then, she, as a maiden, should choose for herself a husband suitable to her; thus says Yama: "If a maiden remains in her father's house without being given away at the age of twelve, her father incurs the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā); that maiden shall choose a husband for herself."
And this period of waiting is to be understood as being from the onset of her menses until three years have passed.
Thus says Bodhāyana:
"A woman who has reached puberty should wait for the command of her father for three years."
Then, in the fourth year, she shall find a suitable husband.
If a suitable [bridegroom] is not available, she may resort even to one who lacks good qualities;
for a suitable [match] possesses good qualities. Manu also says: "A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years."
But after this time has passed, she may find a husband of equal status.
If she should find a husband on her own when she is not being given away,
she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she marries.

The meaning is that even the husband whom she approaches does not incur any fault. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu—"A maiden, having waited until three menstrual periods have passed, may choose her own husband"—that is intended as a prohibition against choosing a husband before those three periods have elapsed. On this point, Manu says:
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any jewelry belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brother; if she should take it, she would be a thief.

Yājñavalkya states that he who, having verbally given away a maiden, subsequently takes her back, shall be punished by the king: "A maiden is given only once; he who takes her back incurs the punishment of a thief. Manu also says:
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once.

The meaning is that the portion falls [to the heirs] only once; that is, one receives the share from the father and others only once. And this refers to the case of a bridegroom who is not defective. As Nārada says:
"If a man has given a maiden to a bridegroom according to the law and does not give her to him, and the bridegroom is not defective, he shall be punished by the king there like a thief."

By this observation of the fault, it is implied that one should not give [the girl] back to the previous suitor even if she has been verbally betrothed. For this very reason, Gautama states: "Even after having promised her, one should not give her to one who is joined with unrighteousness. With this same intention, Yājñavalkya also says:
"One may take back even a betrothed maiden if a more excellent groom should come forward.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
But this is what neither others nor other virtuous men have done:
that having first granted permission to one person, it is then given to another.
Thus, even that [view] intends an unobjectionable bridegroom. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"In the case of a man and a woman, the formal choosing (*varaṇa*) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), for the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is indeed distinct."
"Of those two, the betrothal is said to be non-binding because of the possibility of perceiving defects.

[219] Between those two—the betrothal and the taking of the hand—it is the betrothal alone that is non-binding due to the possibility of perceiving defects, not the taking of the hand. The sense is that the status of being a husband does not arise for either of them by mere verbal agreement (*vāgdāna*). Therefore, Yama says: "A girl's husband is not declared [to exist] by water [libations] nor by word."
Husbandhood arises at the seventh step from the sacrament of taking the hand.

By this, it is stated that even if the groom dies before the seventh step [of the marriage rite], the bride does not become a widow. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "If the groom should die first after she has been given by water and word, but she has not yet been led away by the sacred mantras, the maiden belongs to her father alone."

The meaning is that [the bride-price belongs] to the father alone, not to the receiver [of the girl]. Kātyāyana also says: "But when a man, having chosen [a bride], should perish, after three menstrual periods have passed, the maiden may choose another groom."
The arrival of blood refers to the appearance of menses. This should be understood to apply even when [the groom] has gone to another country. As Nārada says:
"But if a groom, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country, after three menstrual periods have passed, the maiden may choose another groom."
Manu, however, states a specific rule regarding the payment of a bride-price:
"If the giver of the bride-price dies after the price has been paid for the girl, she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided that the girl consents. [2.20]

Thus, it is stated that from the giving of the word (*vāgdāna*) until the seventh step (*saptapada*), if a defect is perceived or in the event of death and so forth, one may give the maiden to another; but not after that point. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "When she has been betrothed to many, but remains unmarried, if suitors arrive from all of them, the first suitor shall receive her."
Now, if [other suitors] should arrive after she has been wedded, the first suitor shall not take her back;
the meaning is that the first suitor shall take only the bride-price (*śulka*) he himself gave, but not the girl. Manu also says:
"A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again."
He who, having given, gives again, incurs the sin of human falsehood.
That too was stated by him:
"One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men."
The meaning is "five relatives," because they alone are the subject under discussion. Vasiṣṭha, however, states that even after the taking of the hand (marriage), she may be given to another:
"Once the taking of the hand has been performed, a maiden is consecrated solely by the mantras;
if her womb remains unviolated, she deserves the performance of the sacramental rite again."
Nārada also says:
"Even a maiden who has been married, if she has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, deserves to undergo the marriage rite again; she is just like a maiden."

This too should be understood as a view of the faults [of marriage]. For this very reason, Yama says: "If a suitor is in no way endowed with noble birth and good character, neither the sacred formula (*mantra*) is the cause in that case, nor would there be falsehood regarding the maiden."
"Having forcibly abducted that maiden while her virginity remains intact, one may give her again to a virtuous man; so said Śātātapa."
Kātyāyana also says:
"But if he belongs to another caste, is an outcast, or is a eunuch; or if he follows forbidden occupations, or is a sapinda, or a slave, or even one afflicted by a chronic disease."
Even if she has been married, she may be given to another, along with her veil and ornaments. Manu also says:
"When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste..."
In five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.

Thus, those [texts] which, after the period of the *saṃskāras*, prescribe remarriage for women whose wombs have not been violated, should be understood as having in view other ages (*yuga*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*: "In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a woman already wedded, the taking of the eldest son’s share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother’s wife, and [carrying] a water-pot."

Also in another Smṛti: "But Devarāta says that one should avoid five things in the Kali age: the procreation of sons, the Gomedha sacrifice, the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), unhusked grain, and the Pauruṣamedha."
Manu, however, states that upon discovering a defect, even a maiden may be abandoned:
"Even after accepting a maiden according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon her if she is blameworthy,
diseased, corrupted, or was obtained through deception."
[222] "Exceedingly corrupted" means corrupted in various ways. Nārada also says:
"One should not defile an uncorrupted maiden, nor should one defile an uncorrupted groom.
If a fault exists, there shall be no blame for the two who mutually abandon each other."
This too should be understood as occurring before the seventh step, since it is precisely there that the status of wife is established. For this very reason, Manu says:
"The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion should be recognized by the learned at the seventh step."
Nārada states that he who gives away a maiden without disclosing her defects shall be punished by the king:
"But for him who gives away a defective maiden without having declared her such,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence."

Two hundred and seventy *paṇas* constitute the first *sāhasa*. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya—"If one gives [a girl] away without declaring her defects, the punishment is the highest *sāhasa*"—that refers to cases where the defects are numerous. Eighty-one thousand *paṇas* constitute the highest *sāhasa*. Furthermore, Nārada states that he who abandons even a faultless girl is likewise subject to punishment.
But a man who, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her, must be punished;
even against his will, he shall marry that very same girl again.
"One who is to be disciplined" (*vineya*) means one who is subject to punishment. He himself has also stated what that punishment is:
"Having accepted a girl who is faultless, if he then abandons her, he shall pay the highest fine" (YDh 1.66).
The faults of a maiden have also been described by him alone:
Afflicted by long-standing or loathsome diseases, deformed, having engaged in sexual intercourse, impudent, and one whose heart has gone to another— these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden.
Thus concludes the section on the fruits of giving a maiden in marriage in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of who is the giver of the maiden;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

The father, the grandfather, a brother, a paternal kinsman, and likewise the mother— each subsequent person among these, provided they are of sound mind, becomes the giver of the daughter in the absence of the preceding one.

One who is "in his natural state" (*prakṛtistha*) is free from defects such as insanity. However, when one is not in his natural state, even an act performed by a father or others is as if it were not done at all. As Nārada says:
"Even if he is independent, whatever act a person performs while having fallen into an unnatural state shall be as if undone, because of the absence of independence."
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
"To whomsoever her father may give her, or her brother with the father's consent,
she should serve him while he lives and must not disregard him when he has passed away."
This is for the purpose of establishing the preeminence of those two, and not for the sake of excluding others; for this very reason, Nārada says:
"The father himself should give the daughter, or the brother with the father’s consent, as well as the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a kinsman of the same lineage, or a relative."
"But if the mother exists and remains in her natural state, she shall give [the girl in marriage];
if she does not remain in her natural state, those of her own caste shall give the girl.
When there is, however, the absence of all [these], then the king shall give [her]. Regarding this, that same author says:

But when there is no one at all [suitable], the maiden should approach the king; and when even he, due to being preoccupied with the protection of the realm and other duties, does not grant her permission, then the maiden herself, with his authorization, should choose a husband suitable for herself. That too has been stated by that very same author:
"With his authorization, having gained his consent, she should choose a husband for herself."
Yājñavalkya also states:

"In the absence of givers, however, a maiden may choose her own husband from among eligible suitors. The word *gamya* means "one who is fit for approaching" (i.e., a suitable suitor). Accordingly, Nārada says, following the phrase "she may choose": [he should choose].
"One should practice the dharma together with a wife who is of the same caste and similar in lineage, character, and extensive learning; and from her, one should procreate sons.
Thus ends the determination regarding the giver of the bride in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the appointment of a widow, Manu says:
"By a brother-in-law or by a sapinda relative, a woman who has been properly appointed..."
The desired goal is to be attained upon the complete exhaustion of the continuum.

The meaning is that a woman, having been authorized by her father-in-law or others, should produce with her husband’s brother—whether the elder or the younger—or in his absence, with a *sapiṇḍa*, the desired offspring characterized by masculinity. Yājñavalkya also says:

"Authorized by her elders, and desiring a son, the husband’s brother (*devara*), or a *sapiṇḍa* or one of the same lineage (*sagotra*), shall approach her during her fertile period after being anointed with clarified butter."
The phrase "by her desire for a son" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]; otherwise, because of the prohibition against *niyoga* (the practice of levirate). And so says Yama:
"A woman who does not desire [a son] should not be appointed; one who desires a son should be appointed.
Nor should it be suspected that a woman must have the desire for a son simply because a childless woman lacks heaven and other such rewards.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Only one son should be begotten, not a second. To that effect, Manu says:
"One appointed to a widow, anointed with clarified butter, restrained in speech, and acting at night, shall procreate only one son, never a second."

Some, considering that even a man with an only son is as good as sonless, believe that the purpose of the *niyoga* is not fulfilled and thus desire the procreation of another son. This too has been stated by that same [author]: "Those who know the law, seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* for those two remains unfulfilled, consider a second procreation on their wives to be lawful."
Regarding this, Yama states the procedure for approaching her:
"When she has bathed during her fertile period, he, remaining silent at night after sunset,
should approach her without touching his nails or body hair, and without making known the scent or touch."
Alone, his limbs smeared with ghee, foul-smelling, sorrowful, and dejected,
he avoided face-to-face contact and did not let his limbs touch one another.
One who has restrained his self may take a wife; but once a wife has been taken, he should renounce [worldly life].
"Renounce" means that he should not return again. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"He may go [to her] until conception occurs; otherwise, he would become fallen."
A son born according to this procedure shall be his *kṣetraja* (field-born) son.
The meaning is: "of this former husband. As for that which was stated by Manu: "A widow must not be appointed to another [husband] by the twice-born;
those who appoint her to another destroy the eternal dharma."
Thus, regarding that [point], another Smṛti states:

"A second husband is nowhere prescribed for virtuous women. This [contradiction] is resolved by understanding that [the latter statement] refers to a prohibition specifically for the Kali age. For this very reason, Kratu says:
In the Kali age, there shall be no procreation through the husband's brother, a daughter given in marriage shall not be given again,
no sacrifice involving the slaughter of a cow shall be performed, and the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) shall not be used.
Bodhāyana also says:
"A rule that was not previously established but is now being performed here at present is a 'purākalpa' (ancient practice), just like the marriage of a widow."
Thus ends the section on the appointment of widows in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the different types of marriage.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Understand these eight forms of marriage for women in brief:
the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and likewise the Āsura."
"The Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"The Brāhma marriage consists of giving away the bride, adorned according to one's ability, after having invited her [and the groom]."

The meaning is that when a bridegroom possessing the aforementioned characteristics is brought to one's own home and an adorned maiden is given to him according to one's capacity, that is the *brāhma* marriage. Manu also says: "Having invited a man of learning and good conduct and having honored him with gifts and clothing, the giving away of a daughter by oneself is proclaimed as the *brāhma* dharma."

"Having honored" means having worshipped with ornaments and so forth. One born of such a woman liberates ten ancestors beginning with the father, ten descendants beginning with the son, and himself from sin. And thus says Gautama: "The son of a Brāhmaṇī purifies ten preceding and ten succeeding generations, as well as himself," provided that he is of good conduct—this is the understood implication. Likewise, Manu says: "The son of a Brāhmaṇī who performs meritorious deeds liberates twenty-one groups—the ten preceding, the ten succeeding, and himself—the fathers from their sins."
Gautama also says: "Virtuous sons purify. Yājñavalkya states the definitions for the *daiva* and *ārṣa* forms as well:
"The *daiva* is when [the bride] is given to the officiating priest at a sacrifice; the *ārṣa* is after taking two cows.
When a sacrifice has commenced, the giving of a daughter to the officiating priest after she has been adorned is the *daiva* marriage. And so Manu says:
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) rite.

Furthermore, that marriage in which a maiden is given after taking two cows is the Ārṣa marriage. The mention of "two cows" is for the sake of illustration; therefore, Manu says: "Having taken from the groom one pair of cattle, or two [pairs], according to the law, the giving of the maiden in accordance with the rule—that is called the Ārṣa dharma."
The pair consists of the bull and the cow. Yājñavalkya states their fruit:
"The first-born purifies fourteen, and the later-born six.

The first-born is one produced through the *daiva* rite; he purifies seven ancestors and seven descendants. The later-born is one produced through the *ārṣa* rite; he, moreover, purifies three on each side. And so Manu says:
A son born of a Daiva marriage purifies seven generations before and seven after;
a son born of an Ārṣa marriage purifies three before and three after; and a son born of a Kāya marriage purifies six before and six after.
The *prājāpatya* form belongs to Prajāpati. He himself has described its essential nature as well:
"Having addressed the couple with the words, 'May you both perform dharma together,' and having honored them, the bestowal of the daughter is recorded as the *prājāpatya* rite" (229).
Likewise, Yājñavalkya describes the four beginning with the Āsura:
"The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva from mutual consent;
the Rākṣasa from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca from the deception of the maiden."

The Āsura marriage consists of taking wealth from the groom and then giving away the daughter by her father and others, without a formal gift (*dāna*). Thus says Manu: "When a man gives wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to his ability, and gives away the daughter of his own free will, that is called the Āsura dharma."

"Non-giving" (*āpradāna*) means taking [the girl] by force; "by one's own will" (*svācchandyāt*) means by one's own desire. The *gāndharva* [form], however, is the mutual union of the maiden and the groom through their own desire. And so Manu says:
"The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through their own desire—this should be known as the *gāndharva* [form], which arises from passion and involves sexual intercourse."

"Suitable for sexual union" means beneficial for sexual intercourse. As for the *rākṣasa* [form], it is the abduction of a maiden by means of combat. And so says Manu: "Having slain, having cut, and having pierced [the guardians], while she is crying out and weeping, the forcible abduction of a maiden is called the *rākṣasa* rite."

"By force" means by compulsion. The *paiśāca* form, on the other hand, occurs through deception (*chala*) regarding a maiden. Deception is *chala*; the meaning is that the abduction of a maiden while she is in a state such as sleep under a pretext is the *paiśāca* form. And so Śaunaka says: "The *paiśāca* occurs in the abduction of those who are asleep or intoxicated. Regarding these [marriages], beginning with the *āsura*, Manu states the defects of their progeny:
"In the four marriages, beginning with the *brāhma*, in their proper order, sons endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasvin*) and esteemed by the learned are born."
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and qualities, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining improper marriages, cruel and untruthful sons are born who hate the Veda and the dharma of Brahman.

A *nṛśaṃsa* is a cruel person; *brahmadviṣaḥ* are those who hate the Veda. Nor should it be suspected that in the case of *āsura* and other such marriages, the status of husband and wife cannot arise because the ritual of "stepping the seven steps" (*saptapadī*) and so forth is absent; for even in those cases, the performance of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is prescribed immediately after the formal acceptance [of the bride]. Thus says Devala:
"In the Gāndharva and other types of marriages, the marriage rite must again be performed by the three castes according to the rule, with fire as witness."
Also in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"The Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa forms of marriage—
among these, the enclosure [of the fire-altar] is prescribed first, and the oblation afterwards."
*Parigraha* means acceptance. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha also states that wifehood does not arise merely through forcible abduction:
"If a maiden has been taken by force but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she is to be given to another according to the prescribed rule; such is her status, just like [any other] maiden."
In this regard, Manu states the rule for marriage according to the system of castes:
"One should know that for a Brāhmaṇa, six [wives] in the direct order [of castes] are lawful; for a Kṣatriya, the four following [him];
and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, those same [wives], excluding the Rākṣasa form."

One should know that for a Brāhmaṇa, those beginning with the *brāhma* and ending with the *gāndharva* are lawful (*dharmya*), meaning they do not deviate from dharma. For a Kṣatriya, there are the others beginning with the *āsura* and ending with the *paiśāca*. For the Vaiśya and Śūdra as well, these same [latter four] apply, excluding the *rākṣasa*. Regarding these, he himself states which are recommended:
"The wise know the first four to be recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the *rākṣasa* alone for a Kṣatriya; and the *āsura* for the Vaiśya and Śūdra."
In another Smṛti as well:
"Four types of marriage are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa: the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa;
likewise for a Kṣatriya, the Āsura; for a Vaiśya, [the same]; but for a Śūdra, the last one is censured."
The meaning is that it is censured by no one and is not praised. For this very reason, Yama says: "The eighth among marriages, the Paiśāca, is declared to be the most base.
Therefore, Vyāsa prescribes the Paiśāca rite only when other forms of marriage are unavailable.
"A maiden who cannot be won by any other means should be married by a man through a clandestine marriage, even by way of theft, while she remains in seclusion.
Some do not even accept the Ārṣa form as commendable, because in that case too there is the taking of a bride-price; and so Manu says:
"Some say that in the *ārṣa* marriage a pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*), but that is indeed false;
for whether it be small or great, it remains nothing other than a sale.

(232) "False" means untrue. This is not in accordance with Dharma, because even by that much alone, this [act] constitutes a sale—this is the meaning. Devala, however, states that a pair of cattle is not the bride-price.

"Thus, these four forms of marriage are righteous and bestow prosperity; they are free from a bride-price and are worthy of the Brāhmaṇa and the others. From them, [the offspring] lead both families [to excellence]. And thus, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Āsura and Gāndharva forms should be understood as permissible when the recommended forms of marriage are unavailable. The same should be observed for the Kṣatriya and the others. As for that which was stated by Kāśyapa:
A woman who has been purchased with wealth is not called a wife;
she is neither for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors—Kaśyapa declared her to be a slave.
Thus, that [statement] refers to the possibility of a praiseworthy marriage. Furthermore, regarding this, Manu has stated with reference to praiseworthy marriages:

"Through ill-contracted marriages, through the omission of sacred rites, through the neglect of Vedic study, and through the transgression against Brahmanical status, noble families fall into the state of being base."
Thus, that also refers to the same subject matter as previously stated. Likewise, regarding the taking of a bride-price (*śulka*), he declares the very same fault:
"A wise father of a maiden should not accept even the slightest bride-price;
for a man who accepts a bride-price out of greed becomes a seller of his offspring."
Indeed, we have never heard of such a thing even in previous births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
Yama also says:
"That man who desires wealth through the sale of another human being shall subsist upon that person's urine and excrement in the next world."
"Fools who sell their daughters, being evildoers in this world, fall into a terrible hell and burn their lineage down to the seventh generation.
This should be understood to apply to the taking of wealth for one's own sake; however, Manu states that there is no fault when [wealth] is for the sake of the daughter.
"That for which the kinsmen receive a bride-price is not a sale;
that is merely an honoring of the maidens and an act of compassion.

The meaning is that the bride-price received for the sake of the girl is solely an honoring—that is, a form of worship—of the maidens. "Compassion" (ānṛśaṃsya) means freedom from cruelty. On this point, Yajñapārśva says:
When the ritual procedure for a marriage has been set in motion and the time for the fire-oblation has arrived,
if the girl reaches her menses, how do the officiating priests act?

"Having bathed that maiden and worshipped her according to the rule, the practitioner, having offered the oblation while in a state of meditative union, should then set the ritual procedure (tantra) in motion.
Thus [ends the work] by the son of the venerable Keśavāditya Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge...
The section on sacraments (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*) is completed in the *Smṛticandrikā* composed by Yājñika Vedana Bhaṭṭopādhyāya; herein ends the chapter on marriage (*vivāhaprakaraṇa*).
